Five big names to look out for at Glasgow 2026

BBC News Wed, 22 Jul 2026 07:46:47 GMT

Scotland's Josh Kerr, England's Kadeena Cox and South Africa's Chad le Clos are among the biggest names competing in Glasgow

With 215 golds up for grabs at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, highlighting just five medal hopefuls is no easy feat.

Scotland's largest city is set to welcome more than 3,000 athletes from 10 sports, all of whom have the ambition of leaving with a slab of metal resting on their chest.

For some, a podium-finish is paramount. The bare minimum. For others, competing at the Games is a win in itself.

Much has been made of the reduced programme, the city's readiness and the 'what next?' once Glasgow has passed on the hosting baton again, but for now, the attention - finally - is fully on the athletes.

Here, BBC Scotland highlights some of the biggest names set to compete in the upcoming Commonwealth Games.

Is Glasgow ready for the Commonwealth Games - and does the city care?

Can Wales find new Commonwealth legends in Glasgow?

Keep up to date with the Commonwealth Games here

We couldn't start with anyone else, could we?

Even before he walked the walk after talking the talk, new mile world-record holder Josh Kerr was the poster boy for his home Games.

The brazen - arguably gallus - boy from Edinburgh has won the hearts of many Scots, and athletics fans generally, in recent years for his no-nonsense, bullish approach on and off the track.

He set out his stall months ago, targeting the men's mile world record - which had stood for 27 years - at London's Diamond League on Saturday.

Kerr didn't just break it, he smashed it by nearly half a second, running a simply sublime three minutes 42.66 seconds.

The Scot now heads to his homeland for his second Games appearance, competing in the Commonwealth Mile in search of his first medal for Team Scotland.

The 28-year-old told BBC Scotland earlier this year that "gold in Scotland is what I grew up thinking about" and you'd be a brave soul to wager against him when he's in this mood.

Men's one mile final: Scotstoun Stadium on Saturday, 1 August.

This video can not be played

'Oh my word!' - Scotland's Kerr breaks mile world record

It's hard to believe Kadeena Cox has not yet competed at a Commonwealth Games.

The para-cyclist, who won gold in athletics and cycling at the 2016 Paralympics in Rio, has missed the last two Commonwealth Games because of injury.

But the 35-year-old, who was a contestant on I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here in 2021 after winning Celebrity Masterchef earlier that year, will be hopeful of cooking up a storm at the ever-rowdy Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome for Team England.

In an expanded para-track cycling programme, Cox will compete in the C4-5 event with her sights set on another podium finish.

Cox made the watching world sit up and take notice 10 years ago in Brazil. Sure to be well-backed in Glasgow, it would be right on brand for the vivacious Cox to star in the Glasgow velodrome.

Women's C4-5 4000m individual pursuit final: Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on Thursday, 30 July.

Kadeena Cox won gold in the women's C4-5 500m time trial at the Rio Paralympics 10 years ago

When it comes to the Commonwealth Games, names don't get much bigger than Chad le Clos.

The South African swimmer is one medal away from becoming the most decorated male athlete in the Games' history. His current haul of 18 - seven gold, four silver and a further seven bronze - is deeply impressive.

A good number of them were collected in Glasgow 12 years ago when he equalled the legendary Ian Thorpe's record of seven medals in one Games.

At 34, Le Clos won't compete in as many races this time but is set to be on the blocks for the men's 50m and 100m butterfly events.

He won gold in the 100m butterfly here back in 2014 and also pocketed a bronze in the 50m - but he claimed a gold in that distance on the Gold Coast in 2018.

Any medal will secure the record for the man from Durban and Glasgow, where he produced such a remarkable show in 2014, is the perfect stage to make history.

Men's 50m butterfly final: Tollcross Swimming Centre on Wednesday, 29 July.

Men's 100m butterfly final: Tollcross Swimming Centre on Sunday, 26 July.

Chad le Clos won seven medals at the last Commonwealth Games held in Glasgow

This rising superstar is more a 'if you don't know, get to know' athlete.

Remember the name: Seine Stowers.

A junior Commonwealth Games champion, Stowers marked her 18th birthday earlier this year with four gold medals - breaking 12 records along the way - at the Universal Weightlifting Championship in her homeland of Samoa.

Competing in the women's 77kg - as she will in Glasgow - she lifted 142kg in the clean and jerk category as she established herself as one of Samoa's most exciting medal prospects for years.

Weightlifting runs in the family, too, with her sister, Feagaiga, a gold medal winner on the Gold Coast and a silver medallist in Birmingham four years ago.

Already, though, Seine appears to be taking centre stage.

American Olivia Reeves holds the world record at 77kg in both snatch (123kg) and clean and jerk (155kg), but with Stowers on the scene, who knows for how much longer?

Women's weightlifting (77kg) final: SEC Armadillo on Wednesday, 29 July.

Rhys McClenaghan made history for Team Ireland at the Olympics two years ago

Rhys McClenaghan has done it all.

A European, World, Commonwealth and Olympic champion on the pommel horse, he is undeniably one of the sport's greats, but we've been warned to expect 'Rhys 2.0' in Glasgow.

Northern Ireland's gymnastics golden boy - who secured Ireland's first Olympic gymnastics medal with his gold in Paris two years ago - was forced into a spell on the sidelines last year with a shoulder injury, but he is ready to bring a new routine over to Glasgow.

"The Commonwealth Games is a good chance to show your work in progress. At the Olympic Games, you want to see your finished product," he said.

"It's going to be a work in progress, but hopefully one that is the best in the world too.

"Part of me is striving be like a younger Rhys, but the reality is I'm doing a completely new routine and the rule changes have pushed me into that direction - that's the Rhys 2.0 there."

McClenaghan won gold eight years ago, pipping England's Max Whitlock - who has had to withdraw from these Games with injury - before collecting silver in Birmingham four years ago.

He was the first gymnast to complete the Grand Slam and so arrives at these Games as one of Team NI's wise heads - despite only being 26 years old.

It's a frightening prospect for the rest of the field. Even more frightening is the fact he's rebooting for version 2.0.

Men's pommel horse final: The Arena on Monday, 27 July.

Will your job be replaced by AI? Here are the roles most affected

BBC News Wed, 22 Jul 2026 07:40:33 GMT

Artificial Intelligence (AI) companies are making vast claims about the ability of their tools to replace human labour.

Some jobs will be automated, others will be "augmented". The bosses of the world's biggest companies are diverting vast sums into these tools, partly with the knowledge that they could save money on headcount.

"Flat is the new up", we are told, in terms of the size of a company's workforce as investors ask whether jobs should be done by new recruits - or, instead, armies of "AI Agents", virtual workers tasked with doing specific roles, some of them relatively skilled.

If even half true there will be an impact on us all, across sectors and individual careers, and perhaps it will happen sooner than we think.

Nobel prize-winning economists recently warned the world “must act now” to ensure that AI leads to rising living standards and not large-scale job displacement, and last month London businesses warned they were struggling to find the skills they need as AI disrupts the jobs market.

It is early days yet, but there are already some notable patterns in the data.

This chart is the industry benchmark for how various models can perform the tasks previously done by humans, in this case using and developing computer software.

This measure showed that three years ago, large language models (LLMs) were only able to reliably complete tasks humans took seconds or minutes to do. Now they are increasingly able to complete fairly complex tasks taking an hour or so.

Now, some of the LLMs can find problems in a cryptocurrency contract and even develop and streamline the model itself, which would take a human several hours.

The latest generation of models could start to entirely develop themselves in the next year or so. This is just software coding, but the same type of pattern is being seen, at an earlier stage, with financial analysis, early stage legal work, even some entry level creative industry jobs.

What does that mean for jobs? The most thorough analyses out there come from the United States, using four years of data on employment outcomes by age among a range of occupations most exposed to AI (including software developers and customer contact reps) - and least exposed to AI (health workers, childcare workers, hairdressers).

Stanford University's analysis of wage and jobs data finds a hit to employment for 22 to 25-year-olds of 2.7% since ChatGPT became widespread, rising to 12.8% in the most AI-exposed sectors such as finance, software and creative industries.

Not all economists agree, arguing that other factors such as interest rate rises can explain this.

Online jobs postings have also been affected since the launch of ChatGPT and other LLMs.

There are many other factors here, from interest rates to taxes, however there is something of note in the OECD's recent analysis of the difference in jobs posting between its slightly different measure of highly exposed sectors (eg telemarketing and legal services) and less exposed sectors (construction, cleaning and food prep).

The UK was hit quite notably on this measure at a time when rates were stable or being cut. It also predates last year's National Insurance rise. On most international measures, the UK's service sector concentration leaves it exposed to potential AI jobs losses.

AI usage is measured in "tokens", which are small chunks of text that AI systems use to understand, analyse and generate language. On average, one token is roughly equivalent to three-quarters of an English word.

There have been astonishing increases in AI use in 2026, and the increase in token use has vastly outweighed the declining “per token cost”.

The world's top companies that are using AI had deployed "token leaderboards" to try to get their employees to create as much gain in productivity as possible from the most advanced models.

Trillions, and sometimes thousands of trillions of tokens (quadrillions) have been used over the past few months primarily for “agentic use”, which is for agents that can perform tasks automatically. The problem here is that incredible bills were racked up, so much so that many of those companies have now begun to ration the use of these models.

This is important. It might show that there are limits to how much work could be automated. The virtual workers might be more expensive than the human ones. It depends on the task.

One factor to watch out for however, is that many companies, including Western ones, are diverting to much cheaper forms of AI, derived from Chinese models that are provided freely on to the market.

So there is much uncertainty here, but some clear trends emerging.

The borough where families are slowly disappearing

BBC News Wed, 22 Jul 2026 05:15:39 GMT

Islington seems, on the surface, a family-friendly area. Parents push buggies through quiet leafy side streets of this popular neighbourhood that is also within easy reach of central London.

But this north London borough has one of the lowest fertility rates in the country and mothers are older on average here than in most other parts of the capital.

Islington is a snapshot of a trend also playing out not only in inner London but also other parts of the world.

The situation has been described by the London Assembly as an "existential challenge" for the city as a whole, so what are the reasons behind this and what can be done about it?

Keen to find out more about family life in Islington, I joined a Zip-Zap baby music class to speak to parents.

Tiphanie Frutuoso and her husband had their first baby this year.

"My husband and I have a one-bedroom flat – a two-bedroom is super expensive.

"Childcare is £2,000-£3,000 a month."

They are moving back to Luxembourg, partly because childcare is free.

"It's really sad because we love London. We have better job opportunities here," Frutuoso added.

Tina Meschino had her first child at 41.

"I've always been career-driven. I moved to London from Australia for career opportunities.

"It's taken a while to get to where I want to be – an executive position – which felt like the right time to start a family."

But she added that it was very difficult to find a suitable home with enough space, within budget.

Samantha Nagaratnam had her daughter at 35.

"I was moving forward in my career and was really, really focused on that. But nobody tells you how hard it is [to fall pregnant]. It took about three years when we started trying."

Originally from Toronto, she said it was much harder to find a family home in Islington with enough space.

Zip-Zap co-founder Laura Edwards says families are moving out of Islington to other boroughs for better schools, more affordable homes and more space.

"It's going to have huge implications in 40-50 years when there's nobody to do the jobs and support the economy."

Some families have told me they have decided to stay in the borough but it is proving to be really difficult.

Father-of-two Patrick Penny-Annang has lived in Islington all his life and now shares a one-bedroom flat with his family.

"Our living room becomes our bedroom... our one bed becomes the kids' room," he said.

"Islington is a lovely area to live in but because of that it's really expensive.

"Schools have been closing, schools that I used to go to."

Between 2013 and 2023, London's population of 0–9-year-olds fell by 99,100, despite the capital's overall population growing by 506,000. The decline has been steeper in inner than outer London.

"It's an existential challenge for London," says Bassam Mahfouz, chairman of the London Assembly's Economy, Culture and Skills Committee.

His committee's recent report recommends pursuing UNICEF Child Friendly City status, introducing child-friendly housing standards, and mapping play and recreation spaces across boroughs.

"We need to tackle this as an absolute emergency.

"What's happening in Islington is happening right across London," he said, warning the trend threatens the city's workforce.

He is urging the government and the mayor to "redouble their efforts" to ensure "children are growing up in every postcode".

The fertility rate measures the number of children born per woman of childbearing age.

At 0.99, Islington has the second-lowest total fertility rate in the capital after the City of London, and one of the lowest in England.

To put it in perspective, the estimated number of children born per woman fell to just under 1.4 for England and Wales in 2025, down from 1.9 in 2010.

BBC England's data unit analysed some of the factors that may be contributing to Islington's low rate:

Francesca Baker-Brooker, 39, who works in PR, and her husband Andy, 41, an accountant, have decided not to have children.

The couple live in a two-bedroom flat in Islington. They both say they shared a "gut instinct" early in their relationship that parenthood was not for them.

"We like our lifestyle - we like running, going to festivals and gigs," Francesca said.

Soon after that conversation, they moved from a three-bedroom house in Kent to a two-bedroom flat in Islington and Andy had a vasectomy.

"I don't know how feasible it would have been to move to London if we'd wanted to start a family," Andy said.

When people ask if he has a family, Andy says his answer is: "I have a family – my wife."

They say about half of their friends in London do not have children, although they believe that is far less common outside the capital.

"I think it definitely is easier to be child-free in London," he added.

Katie Beck, a policy fellow at the London School of Economics' LSE Cities, said: "People want to have children in London, but there are barriers – namely the cost of living and childcare.

"People are not able to stay in London to have children, or once they do they're moving to outer boroughs or leaving London altogether."

Beck says London's falling rates of children reflects a wider global trend, driven by housing and childcare costs, more women entering higher education and the workforce, changing parenting expectations, fewer teenage pregnancies, and growing concerns about the future.

She points to boroughs such as Islington, where high poverty, limited green space, expensive housing and dense populations contribute to particularly low child populations.

I was keen to find out what the younger generation think, so spoke to a group of students.

Jess Rolf, 23, says having children was "never something she worried about", and trying to build a settled life was "very stressful with the cost of living and the job market".

"I'm from Lincolnshire and people my age back home are buying houses with their partners and talking about starting families.

"I don't think that's on the cards for me."

Charlotte Ward, 26, has said planning ahead is difficult.

"A lot of people our age are quite disenfranchised.

"You put all your energy into school, university and work, then wonder, 'do I want to bring somebody else into that if I can't even support myself right now?'

"When parents or grandparents ask 'what happens when you have children?', I can say, 'I might not'.

"There's a small element of emancipation from the expectation that you definitely will have children but if I'm progressing in my career and my male counterparts don't have to take time out to have a child, that could put me at a disadvantage."

Millicent Angel, 24, says it is hard to envisage a future when the world feels "so unstable" but she still definitely wants children.

She adds there's "a million and one things" she would like to do first, including developing her career.

Beck argues that "children are an indicator species".

"They are a sign of a healthy city. If you see a dearth of children, that rings alarm bells that a city is not functioning as it should," she added.

She describes a child-friendly city as one that is accessible, with active transport and safe affordable housing.

As the independent think tank Centre for London points out: "London is not becoming a city without families with children, but it is becoming a place where the realities that families with children face are increasingly unequal."

A spokesperson for the Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan said: "The mayor wants London to remain a city for everyone – where people can afford to put down roots, raise a family and build a future.

"That is why tackling London's housing crisis and increasing the supply of genuinely affordable homes is one of his top priorities, alongside measures to support families with the cost of living, including funding free school meals for every child in a state primary school."

They added that he would "continue working with the government to build more affordable homes, support public services and ensure London remains a great place for families and children".

A government spokesperson said: "We've made paternity and unpaid parental leave day one rights through our Employment Rights Act, and have rolled out 30 hours of funded childcare a week to working families."

The government added that it was also building more council homes to back "families at every stage".

I've got a motorway in my garden - it's my shelter in hot weather

BBC News Wed, 22 Jul 2026 05:13:07 GMT

Narelle Cowan and Aimee Lipley's gardens have a few things in common.

Both have pretty plants, chairs for al fresco dining - and one of the UK's busiest motorways.

About 75,000 vehicles travel over the elevated concrete monolith hanging about 45ft (14m) above their plot every day on the main route between London and south Wales.

"I call it my free gazebo," said Aimee. "I love it under here, when it's raining you can walk to the shops without getting your hair wet."

The two-lane carriageway in the sky was one of the first sections of the M4 and a relic of the 1960s freeway building boom after the explosion in post-war car ownership.

There are many examples of motorways built close to people's homes in the UK's biggest cities such as London, Birmingham and Glasgow but few are more stark than in Port Talbot where the M4 - which opened on 22 July 1966 - cuts the Welsh industrial town in half.

"I've got three pillars of the M4 in my back garden, I use one to help hang my washing line up," said Narelle.

"It's convenient because the motorway covers the back half of the garden so I've a dry area and it acts as my sunshade, which has been handy in recent weeks."

The 34-year-old mum-of-one told the BBC she "doesn't really notice vehicle noise especially when you've got the music on and enjoying yourself".

"The M4 is like a background murmur, you get used to it," added the property developer.

"I call it ambience. I know some wouldn't want a motorway in your garden but it doesn't bother me or my neighbours, we've got a lovely community and many have been around here for years and years. We love it."

This Port Talbot stretch of the M4 is a congestion hotspot which can frustrate drivers - but many passing over the 4.25 mile (6.8km) long section between Cardiff and Swansea may not think of the people living almost underneath them.

"We do get a lot of rubbish in our garden from people throwing things out of the vehicles on the overpass above," added 39-year-old Aimee, who has lived in the shadow of the M4 for eight years.

"We get to see what people are eating, sometimes you get cigarette ends and it's interesting to see what crisps people are eating."

Under the section initially built as the Port Talbot bypass - before the M4 was bolted on at either end - the main noise is the rushing of the nearby River Afan.

"Yeah we hear the river and the road directly outside our house more than we've ever heard the motorway," said Aimee.

"It's almost like the noise of the motorway is kept up there above us."

There's an area about 80ft (24m) wide running through the town that provides a man-made concrete canopy and a unique shelter from the elements.

"Kids can play underneath the M4 even when it's raining because they're protected," said Aimee.

"I had a childhood playing underneath the motorway. It's somewhere safe for the community."

Homes were demolished, chapels flattened and communities displaced in Port Talbot when Wales' first stretch of motorway was built at a cost of more than £5m.

Despite imposing itself over the whole of Port Talbot with no compensation for affected locals, the motorway was widely welcomed because the old A48 main road through the town couldn't cope.

"Port Talbot was a congestion blackspot and a logical choice for Wales' first motorway," said history professor Martin Johnes.

"The A48 snaked through the town on a route that dated back to the days of horse and carts and had to cross a railway which meant it was shut for three hours a day causing tailbacks of several miles.

"The result was that for a five-and-a-half mile stretch on the A48 the average car speed was 18mph."

It took 13 years from the Port Talbot bypass being commissioned in 1953 to opening in 1966 when it cut journey times between Bridgend and Swansea by about 20 minutes.

Swansea University professor Johnes wrote that Wales' national newspaper, the Western Mail, produced a six-page supplement to mark the Port Talbot bypass' opening and called it a £5m miracle that would end the stop-go misery.

Historians recall the scheme - known locally as the road on top of a town - was seen as a symbol of progress by many although some suffered.

One side of the terraced row of houses on Llewellyn Street was demolished and replaced by the motorway, leaving the remaining side staring at either a huge concrete embankment or pillars propping up the M4.

Some felt the M4 had ripped the heart out of the town and a community had been broken, contributing to a feeling that disaffected locals should be compensated - and seven years later the 1973 Land Compensation Act became law.

That meant governments had to compensate people if public works like roads and aerodromes affected the value of property.

It therefore made it expensive to build so close to houses so contractors have to find cheaper routes away from urban areas.

While it may be scant consolation for those in communities around old urban motorways, bypasses like the one at Port Talbot are less likely to be built now.

Many authorities have enforced a 50mph speed limit - another thing that irritates motorists.

Both Aimee and former lorry driver Narelle feel the 50mph limit on the M4 above their back gardens has reduced vehicle noise while official data shows pollution has dropped to below the legal limit.

Cutting speed on the M4 was imposed after the UK and Welsh governments were taken to court as Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) levels exceeded legal limits around several stretches of road - including at Port Talbot.

Breathing air with high levels of NO2 can irritate airways, cause coughing, wheezing or make it difficult to breathe and worsen diseases like asthma.

But since the speed limit, levels of NO2 have dropped below the legal threshold. Other factors such as vehicle efficiency and more people working from home has helped but analysis shows the limits had the biggest immediate change.

"Occasionally we could smell stuff in the air but I think that was from steelworks, not from the M4," added Narelle.

"We don't smell it any more, I guess that's because the blast furnaces have gone."

"Where we are has allowed us to get on the property ladder as the house with a driveway and garage is more affordable here than in another part of town," added Aimee.

Are flies following a strategy when they keep hitting a window? Part 2

New Scientist July 22, 2026

When wasps, bees and flies continually clatter against the glass of my conservatory attempting a means of escape, are they following a strategy? (continued)

Alan HardingLondon, UK

I think the previous answer to this question misses an important difference between flies, wasps and bees (4 July).

Advertisement

Moving towards light has served flies well, but when confronted by glass – a relatively recent innovation – it can be fatally futile

In my experience, wasps and bees continually buzz around in more or less the same part of a window and are very easy to catch – for example by trapping them under an upturned glass, covering it with a piece of paper and releasing them through an open window.

With flies, on the other hand, this is almost impossible, as they tend to buzz around randomly. I don’t think this is a strategy for escaping (as was previously said, they have no concept of glass), but rather a strategy for not being eaten.

Bees and wasps have stings and stripy bodies to warn predators ‘”eat me at your peril”. I think flies’ random flight paths have evolved to make it much harder for predators to catch and eat them.

Jonathan WallaceNewcastle-upon-Tyne, UK

It was suggested by your previous correspondent that flies and bees banging against the window to escape from a room aren’t following any specific strategy. This is probably incorrect.

If you observe a fly as it moves around a room, you won’t see it repeatedly flying against the wall in the way that it does against the glass of a window. This suggests that the fly (or bee) clearly “sees” the window as the way out.

Flying insects don’t reason their way out of the room in the way that we would, but are likely to have evolved a strategy of instinctively flying towards the light when inside a dark space.

In most circumstances, this simple strategy works well for them, but when confronted by glass – a very recent innovation in the evolutionary history of flies – the strategy becomes potentially fatally futile.

Garry TretheweyArkaroola, South Australia

Yes. The strategy is “head towards the light”. That has worked for them for millions of years, sans windows. Now, it doesn’t.

How do fish recognise others of their own species? Part 2

New Scientist July 22, 2026

The positions of most fishes’ eyes mean they cannot see their own body. So, how do they recognise others of their own species? (cont.)

Shelby TempleUniversity of Bristol, UK

Humans, and most animals for that matter, have eyes fixed in their heads in a manner that doesn’t allow them to see their whole self. Snails and animals whose eyes are on stalks might be the exception. Therefore, the same question applies to us.

Advertisement

Some of it will be innate and some of it will be learned, just like how a baby human sees the face of its parents and learns to recognise them. We also know that, for some species, this imprinting can be tricked: this is how Konrad Lorenz, the “father of ethology”, became the imprinted parent of newly hatched ducks and geese.

Fish are probably no different and can learn to remember people and faces for various benefits. My own archerfish learned to differentiate me from my wife and other guests, because I was the only one who fed them. So, I think the ability to see yourself isn’t really a prerequisite to recognising your own species.

Given the importance of staying in schools for some species of fish, I suspect they use a variety of inputs, including visual and olfactory, plus learned experiences of safety versus danger. Then there’s innate recognition, which must play a role in some species of fish that are so sparsely distributed that, when a male meets a mate, they attach to them and never let go, for example deep-sea anglerfishes.

I doubt a male deep-sea anglerfish in this situation has ever seen itself or even another individual of its species before, but it still seems to know to attach itself to a female.

In this case, it is almost certainly down to an olfactory cue, but there will be many other interesting and bizarre examples in the world of fish.

Is it true that fresh air heats up faster than stale air? If so, why?

New Scientist July 22, 2026

Simon LeeSchool of earth and environmental sciences, University of St Andrews, UK

Air usually seems “stale” if it contains elevated levels of carbon dioxide (from human respiration) and odour, neither of which affects how quickly it heats up.

However, stale indoor air is often (though not always) more humid than fresh, outside air. Humid air has a slightly higher heat capacity than dry air, so it requires marginally more energy to warm. In practice, though, the difference is too small to notice, especially as the difference in humidity between indoor and outdoor air is often modest.

Advertisement

Ventilation can improve air circulation, helping heat from a radiator spread more evenly. If condensation has formed in the room, much of the heat supplied initially goes into evaporating this moisture, rather than raising the air temperature.

Ventilating with drier outside air helps the room dry more quickly, so subsequentheating becomes more effective.

“When soils are dry, less of the sun’s energy is used to evaporate water, leaving more available to heat the ground and air”

A similar process occurs during heatwaves: when soils are dry, less of the sun’s energy is used to evaporate water, leaving more available to heat the ground and air.

Robin MaguireHobart, Tasmania, AustraliaWe might define stale air as air that has been extensively breathed by people. In that case, it contains a higher proportion of carbon dioxide and water vapour than fresh air.

We can see what this means by comparing the molar specific heat capacities of the relevant molecules at constant pressure – that is, the amount of energy required to increase the temperature of a particular volume by 1 unit. Nitrogen and oxygen (which make up over 99 per cent of fresh, dry air) each have a specific heat capacity of a little over 29 joules per kelvin per mole. The equivalents for carbon dioxide and water vapour (at normal temperature and pressure) are higher, around 37 and35 J/mol. K respectively. So, the overall heat capacity of stale air is rather higher than for fresh air and therefore fresh air will indeed heat up more quickly than stale air, assuming a fixed rate of energy input.

However, the effect is likely to be small. If the overall quality of some fresh air was degraded to the equivalent of a typical exhaled breath (which sounds fairly stale to me), this would result in the air composition changing by the addition of about 5 per cent CO₂ and perhaps a couple of per cent water vapour (depending on the initial humidity). This would imply an increase in overall heat capacity of only 1 to 2 per cent. Specific heat capacity increases slightly with temperature, more so for more complex molecules – CO₂ relative to nitrogen, for example. As a result, the difference in heat capacity between fresh and stale air will increase slightly as temperature rises. If the ambient temperature changed from 0 to 30°C (32 to 86°F), the heat capacity differential would increase by about one-tenth – not enough to affect matters greatly.

Sunshine can help with some serious health problems, argues a new book

New Scientist July 22, 2026

BookIn Defense of SunlightRowan Jacobsen, Scribner (UK, US)

About a hundred years ago, doctors actively encouraged sunbathing. Soldiers’ wounds, first world war surgeons had noticed, healed a lot faster when exposed to solar rays; people with arthritis felt their pain retreating, while those with bronchitis and lung infections found their coughs subsiding. Blood pressure in hypertensive patients dropped.

The Lancet went so far as to declare it “one of nature’s greatest aids to maintaining and acquiring proper health”, and even called for more spaces to strip off in public.

Advertisement

“On first consideration, the idea of a community of people deliberately practising nudity, especially with municipal encouragement, strikes the average person as somewhat ridiculous,” reads one article from 1932. “But the discovery that the rays of the sun on the skin exert a beneficent effect on health has done something to undermine these prejudices… as long as they are done for the sake of health and… the sexes are segregated.”

Today, we’re far more cautious. We are told to cover up and apply generous volumes of sunscreen to protect us from the harmful UV rays, even in the winter. But has this advice gone too far?

That’s the argument of a fascinating new book, In Defense of Sunlight: The surprising science of sun exposure by journalist Rowan Jacobsen. He says he was inspired by the finding that sun exposure can trigger mood-boosting endorphins. “Like most people, I’d had it drilled into me since childhood that the sun was… the primary cause of skin cancer, and that the only acceptable amount of its rays that should be allowed to touch my unprotected skin was zero,” he writes. “But if we’re wired to seek out sunlight, there must be a reason.”

Studies found that exposure to UV light releases nitric oxide in our skin, which reduces blood pressure

Despite this slightly shaky premise (the brain’s pleasure system can prime us to seek out much that is unhealthy for us, including drugs, alcohol and sugar) Jacobsen builds a thoroughly convincing argument, as he documents the many surprising ways that moderate sun exposure can revitalise our bodies.

The most famous benefits of sunlight once appeared to revolve around its role in the body’s production of vitamin D. Correlational studies suggested that high levels of the chemical seem to reduce the risk of many health problems, including obesity, diabetes, osteoporosis, heart attack, stroke, depression, respiratory infections and colorectal cancer. Yet Jacobsen notes that dietary supplements of the vitamin have largely failed to make an impact on any of these problems, except when someone has a severe deficiency. This leaves the intriguing possibility that measurements of people’s natural vitamin D levels were simply acting as a proxy of their overall sun exposure, which had been protecting the body through multiple other mechanisms.

One likely pathway is nitric oxide, a chemical that causes our blood vessels to dilate. Scientists have recently started to conclude that nitric oxide deficiency is a major driver of hypertension, and – quite remarkably – a series of studies has found that exposure to UV light releases this tiny chemical in our skin, which then reduces blood pressure.

The finding, Jacobsen suggests, may offer one more reason why people in Mediterranean countries tend to have such good health. The leafy veg of the region’s famous diet, he points out, contain lots of nitrates, but plentiful sunlight in those areas helps people’s bodies to convert this into nitric oxide, relaxing their cardiovascular system. Just adopting a Mediterranean diet has been shown to lower blood pressure, but not as much as also increasing sun exposure, writes Jacobsen: “It’s the combination of the two that does the trick and should be the foundation of a true Mediterranean diet.”

Elsewhere, he points to evidence that moderate exposure to sunlight releases chemicals in the skin that help rein in an overactive immune system, which may explain why it appears to soothe conditions like multiple sclerosis – independently of vitamin D production– and type 1 diabetes. There is even evidence that the infrared wavelengths in sunlight, which can penetrate deep into our bodies, can stimulate our mitochondria, improving our metabolism.

The dark cloud hanging over all this is, of course, the heightened risk of skin cancer that comes with sun exposure. Here, Jacobsen points out that most skin cancers are basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, which don’t often spread to other parts of the body and are typically treatable with surgery. Melanoma is more dangerous, but it is relatively rare and still has a very high survival rate compared with other cancers.

“Yes, sunlight is the major alterable risk factor for skin cancer, but deaths from heart disease are a hundred times higher than deaths from skin cancer,” Jacobsen writes. “And I think we need to find the risk-benefit ratio.” To support this, he points to an influential study of 30,000 Swedish women, which found that sun exposure was associated with a far lower risk of mortality: over a 20-year period, “sun avoiders” were about twice as likely to die as sun lovers.

Clearly, we shouldn’t take this new-found appreciation of “heliotherapy” to extremes; The Lancet is unlikely to resurrect its campaign for nude sunbathing anytime soon. The balance of risks will depend on a huge number of factors, including skin tone, the season and the latitude, which makes it very hard to make general recommendations for optimum levels of sun exposure.

In the end, Jacobsen’s advice is quite close to that of health services in the UK. Make the most of the mornings and evenings when the UV component is lower, he suggests, but cover up and find shade during the hottest times of day. He is a little ambivalent on the daily use of sunscreen outside of the riskiest periods, but agrees it is advisable whenever there is the possibility of burning. Even short periods of exposure, he says, may be enough to glean the benefits.

For all the cutting-edge research this thought-provoking book describes, its message is remarkably simple. “Get sun. Not too much. Go outside.” It’s time we all saw the light.

Life Time: The new science of the body clock, and how it can revolutionize your sleep and health by Russell Foster

Many of us extend our days far into the night. Russell Foster’s guide to human circadian rhythms shows why this is a poor idea. Using his research, he urges us to harness them to enhance sleep, mood and mental focus.

The Remarkable Life of the Skin: An intimate journey across our surface by Monty Lyman

The skin is our largest, fastest growing and least understood organ. It is also, of course, the principal recipient of the sun’s rays. Doctor and research fellow Monty Lyman explores the organ’s major role in our health.

Chasing the Sun: The new science of sunlight and how it shapes our bodies and minds by Linda Geddes

Former New Scientist staffer Linda Geddes offers an in-depth exploration of the sun’s role in our lives across history and cultures – and exactly what we lose when we end up spending so much of our time indoors.

David Robson is a science writer specialising in the human brain, body and behaviour. His latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life

This twisty sci-fi thriller is a fantastic debut from Isabel J. Kim

New Scientist July 22, 2026

SublimationIsabel J. Kim, Picador (UK, US)

In Sublimation, Isabel J. Kim imagines a world where someone attempting to cross an international border may end up splitting into two separate beings.

So, for example, if you were leaving your home country for pastures new but were torn about whether you were making the right decision, you might find yourself splitting into two at the airport. One “instance” of you would leave, and another would stay behind.

Advertisement

The instances are identical at the moment of cleaving, but after that, their memories and lives are their own… unless they happen to touch, flesh to flesh, in which case they may reintegrate, their two selves smashing together again.

It is undoubtedly a complicated premise, but don’t be put off. The execution is light and graceful, and the intricacies of the set-up prove both moving and thought-provoking. Kim makes the cleaving of a human in two feel very natural – the way the world has always been. She also uses an unusual second-person point of view. Two sample sentences: “You shake your head.” And: “You scratch the black cuff on your wrist.”

In less-sure hands, this might be confusing. Here, it is intimate and interesting. Our heroine is Soyoung, a young woman in Seoul. We first meet her as she mulls over whether reintegrating with your instance against their will amounts to murder: a gun on the wall if there ever was one.

Sublimation‘s premise is complicated, but don’t be put off. The execution is light and graceful

Soyoung has an instance she has never spoken to living in New York; that version of herself now calls herself Rose. Meanwhile, Soyoung’s best friend is a man named Yujin, and he also happens to have an instance living in New York. Yujin is very close to his instance, named YJ, and the pair are working together towards shared goals. They intend to reintegrate when they hit 30. Or at least, that was the original plan, but it has been a long time since they were one, so perhaps all is not what it seems.

When Rose returns to South Korea after the death of the grandfather she shares with Soyoung, she and Soyoung meet for the first time. It is an awkward meeting, because the two women don’t trust each other, and with good reason. Their reunion triggers dramatic events that will soon draw Yujin and his instance, YJ, into a high-stakes chain of events.

This is a taut psychological thriller, full of unexpected twists. It is fantastically well written and well constructed. I could have done without the more routine action thriller aspects, involving big tech and baddies being exposed. I’m not sure the book needed it with so much going on between our pairs of instances. But that’s a smallish gripe. This is tip-top stuff; a fantastic debut.

And a second recommendation this week, for those who like their sci-fi very cosy. Moss’d in Space by Rebecca Thorne is about an alien starship covered with intelligent… moss. Yes, Moss’d in Space is about moss. Or specifically, a moss organism called Moss. I thought the title was dreadful until I got into the book, at which point I decided it was genius.

Cosy fiction is absolutely not my thing, and this is marshmallow sweet, but I finished it because quality tells and this is quality. Thorne has the gift of being very funny, with the book’s humour elegantly wrought from the gulf between Moss’s idea of itself – as a delightful and easy-to-get-on-with person – and the reality of Moss’s sneaky, intransigent, easy-to-upset character. This is the first in a series, and it deserves to do well.

BookTime to BurnEllery Lloyd, Macmillan

Another new release this month, featuring journeys back in time to the London Blitz. This twisty time-travel thriller, which you can easily imagine going straight to film, is enjoyable and clever; in short, a romp

Emily H. Wilson is the author of the Sumerians series (Inanna, Gilgamesh and Ninshubar, all published by Titan) and she is currently working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of New Scientist and you can follow her on Instagram @emilyhwilson1

Why do fictional geologists keep getting killed off in movies?

New Scientist July 22, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

When you start watching a film, there are some characters you can confidently predict will die. A minor character joining two major characters for an action sequence? Dead to illustrate the stakes. Wise old mentor in an epic fantasy? Sure to die at the end of act two.

Feedback knows these cliches and more, but it hadn’t previously occurred to us to consider geologists as being at risk. Nevertheless, it turns out they have a life expectancy only marginally better than characters played by Sean Bean.

Advertisement

We learned this from a delightful analysis in Geology Today. Geologist Erik Sturkell at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and his colleagues have amused themselves over the past decade or so by compiling examples of geologists in films: who are they, how are they portrayed and what tends to happen to them?

Sturkell’s team has now documented “141 movies, spanning the period 1919–2023 and starring 202 geologists”. It turns out geologists mostly appear in films centred on adventure, drama, action and science fiction. “Geologist movies are rarely comedic,” write the researchers. Only 11 per cent of movie geologists are female, though this has apparently picked up a bit since the 1990s. Furthermore, cinematic geologists are, if not consistently heroic, “at least not guilty of any professional misconduct”.

And yet they are frequently rubbed out. “Geologists die at an alarming rate in the movies, often very early on,” the authors write. Depending on the decade, the death rate varies between 31.6 and 35.7 per cent. Of the 202 geologists, 69 die, 30 by murder. The authors cite the 1967 film The Money Jungle, which Feedback hasn’t seen, but which involves multiple oil companies scheming for control of a rich field. During this unseemly squabble, five geologists are murdered, mostly by creative means, “such as being electrocuted by a golf cart, poisoned when taking medicine, gassed by the fireplace and killed when his toy train explodes”. This, the authors note, is “the worst serial slaughter of geologists in any movie”.

Across the years, a further 12 geologists died of “work related” causes, such as “being hit by a volcanic bomb, falling into a crater or an opening fault, drowning in quicksand or lahar, and incineration in an oil pit”. Equally common are deaths involving extraterrestrials, such as the geologist in Prometheus who is assimilated by aliens and “consequently killed by former colleagues”.

This is all fascinating, but Feedback finds ourselves consumed by follow-up questions. What are the cinematic death rates for other branches of science? We can’t help but suspect that palaeontologists must be absolutely getting it in the neck, because they only show up in stories where extinct creatures come back to life and start eating people. On the other hand, movie solid-state physicists are probably having a pretty chill time.

Can anyone point us to a dataset?

Feedback is alarmed to learn that the lyrics of pop music have become significantly more self-centred over the past few decades.

This is true in the US and Germany, according to a study in PLoS One, which looked at the 10 most popular songs each year from 1970 to 2019. The analysis revealed an increase in the use of first-person singular words like “I”, “me” and “mine”, compared with first-person plural words like “we” and “ours”. Curiously, this didn’t occur in Japan and Hong Kong, which the study describes as “more collectivist”.

The paper treats this in near-apocalyptic terms, noting that “contemporary societies are increasingly self-focused, as reflected in levels of greed, narcissism, and social disconnection”.

Feedback certainly isn’t going to mount a “greed is good” defence, but we do have questions. For starters, how much of the trend is driven by the highly entrepreneurial US, as opposed to the more moderately capitalistic Germany? Second, how much of the increase in “me” words can be explained by the rise of solo artists and the total collapse of bands? Do K-pop groups – at this point basically the only remaining successful bands – also exhibit this egotistical trend?

Last month, New Scientist reviewed the book We Are Not Machines: The fight for the future of work, which argues that artificial intelligence is not exactly coming for our jobs, but rather that our jobs are being contorted to fit AI (20 June). The result is that jobs that were once interesting are becoming boring and companies’ products and services are getting worse.

Readers Ian Williams and Erik Foxcroft both got in touch to flag the spooky near-coincidence that the book’s author, a journalist at the Financial Times, is named Sarah O’Connor. “O, how close to perfection,” says Erik.

Having a name that is almost but not quite that of the lead human character in The Terminator has previously caused ripples. In 2015, O’Connor was the FT‘s employment correspondent and tweeted: “A robot has killed a worker in a VW plant in Germany.” The combination of seeming cyborg-murderer news and O’Connor’s name went viral. The irony was that she had never seen the film and didn’t get the reference. Feedback assumes she has since watched it, and hopes she concluded her book with a three-word promise of a sequel.

Got a story for Feedback?

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist. com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

Why open-source software can be both good and bad

New Scientist July 22, 2026

A problem shared is a problem halved, or so the saying goes. That is the philosophy of the open-source software movement, which sees volunteers coming together to code, patch and improve software tools.

The approach has been a huge success: most computing devices, including closed commercial machines like Windows PCs or Apple iPhones, use some open-source software. But while openness has benefits – having many eyes on code makes it easier to find and fix bugs – there are risks, too.

Open-source software intended to pilot consumer drones is now being used to guide a cheap Ukrainian cruise missile. Traditionally, military tech is custom-built, restricted and expensive. Ukraine has shown this needn’t be the case in the war with Russia: as New Scientist has reported, cheap consumer drone technology is helping Ukraine hold back the invasion.

Advertisement

But while many readers may cheer on Ukraine’s fight, the fact that anyone can now download a cruise-missile guidance system should give us a moment’s pause.

Open-source models have fewer guardrails and the ones that exist are easier to remove

Open source is also key to another war, though this time a commercial one. In the US, AIs like ChatGPT use mostly private codebases, with access sold for a monthly fee. In China, however, open-source models lead the way. These are generally a few months behind the US models in capability – but anyone with the necessary hardware can download and run them for free.

While the closed US models generally come with guardrails to prevent chatbots from spewing out harmful material, open-source models have fewer such limits and the ones that exist are easier to remove.

That creates headaches for attempts to regulate AI models, such as testing them for national security risks before release, as was recently suggested by Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis. But it also offers the opportunity for more people to find ways of using AI models that US tech firms may not have thought of.

Open source means problems can be shared – it’s just that some will get easier to solve, while others get much harder.

New Zealand Herald July 22, 2026

In the past five years there have been nearly 30 serious incidents involving drivers on specialised school transport assistance (SESTA) contracts.

School van drivers have been investigated for “sexually touching”, hitting, and forgetting vulnerable, high-needs children during drop-off, harm incident records reveal.

The Ministry of Education says there have been nearly 30 documented serious incidents involving driver behaviour on specialised school transport assistance (SESTA) contracts in the past five years. In some instances police have been involved, others have resulted in drivers being sacked or quitting their jobs.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Data provided to the Herald under the Official Information Act (OIA) shows 29 reported incidents resulting in physical, verbal and/or emotional harm to students from April 2021 to June this year.

In one case a driver was stood down and a police investigation launched after “alleged sexual touching” in November last year.

A driver who bought a “student gifts and asked the parents to take [them] out”, was stood down in 2021. The van’s camera was “obscured” and the incident escalated to police.

The father of a boy who lost his son in May after he escaped from a school van unnoticed and drowned, said his trust in SESTA had been “completely broken”.

“I’m really shocked. These children should all have been kept safe.

“There needs to be change.”

Another driver was also stood down but later reinstated, after tying a seatbelt around a student’s arm to restrain them in early February 2025.

Incidents investigated also included seven cases of children either being left in vans, forgotten or dropped off at the wrong location.

In those instances drivers were either given training, stood down or quit their jobs.

There were also seven complaints of alleged physical or sexual assault and aggressive behaviour.

Other incidents included two cases of drivers failing alcohol breath tests at police checkpoints during drop-off; both drivers lost their jobs.

In each of the cases, drivers were either provided further training or stood down.

As part of the OIA response, education ministry officials said it “took the safety of students on school transport seriously”.

School transport drivers must carry a special “passenger endorsement” licence to allow them to carry passengers, go through “fit and proper person” checks and undergo safety checks aligned to the Children’s Act 2014.

“The Ministry monitors compliance with all contractual, and safety requirements, and any non-compliance is treated seriously.”

The OIA noted if a serious breach has occurred, contractors would “generally stand down or terminate the driver in accordance with their employment obligations and internal processes”.

The above incidents have all been closed and the locations and names of contractors were not provided.

In May 8-year-old autistic, non-verbal Gurshabad Singh drowned after escaping a school Ritchies van unnoticed.

Gurshabad’s death has sparked a review by an independent Steering Group, under the Ministry of Disabled People, into SESTA safety and care standards, expected to be released in coming weeks.

An investigation by police and the coroner was also launched.

A ministry spokesperson earlier told the Herald the review team would speak with key stakeholders to identify systematic improvements.

“The work will focus on service delivery, communication, and clear roles and responsibilities.”

The parents of an 11-year-old North Shore boy locked alone in a van for hours have demanded answers from police after learning the transport company’s CCTV footage was corrupted last week.

Six weeks on from the incident, Ritchies has confirmed efforts to recover video from the in-vehicle camera have failed.

Conventions at Te Pae Christchurch Convention Centre generated almost $74 million for the local economy over the past year, according to a new economic impact assessment.

More than $60m of that flowed directly into Canterbury, with the convention centre hosting 56 conventions that supported an estimated 827 jobs across the region.

The Infometrics assessment also found Te Pae hosted another 133 events in the year to June, including exhibitions, banquets, live events and meetings, attracting more than 125,000 attendees.

The figures come as Te Pae marks four years since opening, having hosted more than 865 events attended by more than 422,000 visitors since May 2022.

John Hagen, chief executive of Crown Infrastructure Delivery, which built and owns Te Pae Christchurch, said the results demonstrated the ongoing value of the Crown’s investment in the convention centre.

“The Crown backed Te Pae to help drive the regeneration of central Christchurch by attracting more visitors, investment and activity. These results show it is delivering on that vision in a very tangible way.”

General manager at Te Pae Christchurch Ross Steele said the significant economic impact underscored the venue’s growing national and international reputation as part of a region-wide renaissance of business and events tourism.

“We’re very proud of Te Pae Christchurch’s reputation as one of Australasia’s leading convention centres, helping position Christchurch and Canterbury as a premier business events destination.”

Steele said the success reflected both the work of the Te Pae Christchurch team and the strength of the wider Canterbury events sector.

“That success reflects the dedication of the Te Pae Christchurch team and the strength of our manaaki o Te Pae approach, which places hospitality at the heart of every guest experience.

“It also highlights the importance of an integrated regional effort, bringing together Christchurch City Council, ChristchurchNZ, Christchurch Airport, accommodation and hospitality providers, local food and beverage suppliers, and the many talented entertainers, designers and performers who all play a part in delivering a unique and memorable experience of our region.”

Over the past year, landmark events have highlighted the versatility of the centre and its growing international appeal, including Adaptation Futures 2025, the International Society of Arboriculture Conference, and the 10th IWA-ASPIRE + Water New Zealand Conference and Expo.

Te Pae also played a key role in supporting domestic visitor activity during the city’s shoulder season, with The Art of Banksy exhibition drawing more than 38,000 visitors over summer.

The venue’s reputation has also been reflected in a growing number of industry accolades.

During the past year, Te Pae was recognised as Oceania’s Leading Meetings and Conference Centre at the World Travel Awards 2025 and was named among the Top 50 Convention Centres Worldwide (TTW 2026).

Steele said the international events industry had evolved rapidly in the post-Covid era, with changing expectations around community, culture, sustainability and visitor experience.

“Organisations increasingly want events that deliver meaningful outcomes for delegates while aligning with their environmental and social values. Te Pae Christchurch continues to be recognised internationally for helping set new benchmarks for sustainable convention delivery, which not only provides a key advantage in the global business events industry, but also strongly connects to the values of the Christchurch community.”

The organisation has reduced its greenhouse gas emissions by 20% since 2022 and was recently re-certified by Toitū Envirocare as Net Carbon Zero and Enviromark Gold. Te Pae also retained its Qualmark Gold certification along with ISO 9001 and ISO 22000.

“It’s important to recognise that this year’s success has been built on a foundation Christchurch has been developing for many years. Increasingly, international conference and business event organisers are choosing Christchurch for its safe, welcoming and walkable city centre, strong connection to culture and heritage, and spectacular natural environment.”

Steele said Te Pae had a strong pipeline of conventions and events confirmed for 2026 and beyond, supported by the city’s growing accommodation sector and new visitor attractions.

Stuart Nash has confirmed he has resigned as a New Zealand First candidate, after backlash over his comments had become “a significant distraction”.

It comes after Nash accused National’s Napier MP Katie Nimon of being “lazy” for taking maternity leave. Nash is a former Labour MP and minister and has a string of controversies to his name.

In a late-night social media post, Nash said he did not want the distraction to cost NZ First or the people of Napier, where he was to run against Nimon.

“As a husband and a father of four (including two strong, independent daughters), I have real respect for any working parent, and I regret that my words were open to an interpretation I never intended,” he wrote.

He claimed he was trying to say Napier needed an MP who fought hard for the region, but admitted he could have made the point “far better”.

He was not commenting this morning.

At their Napier home, his wife and public relations specialist Sarah Nash said the couple were “regrouping” and needed to “catch our breath a little bit”.

In a social media post late on Wednesday, NZ First leader Winston Peters said, “Stuart Nash has offered his resignation as a candidate, and we have accepted.”

Earlier, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said Nash would not serve in any government he might lead after November’s election.

Nash did not respond to the Herald’s requests for comment.

This morning, Nimon said Nash’s comments over her maternity leave were an “unnecessary distraction”.

She told Ryan Bridge TODAY that she and Nash “just have different views”.

“You don’t have to be fighting or aggressive to be a good representative and actually doing this job with empathy ... that is what people want, especially in 2026.

“I think he may have an out-of-touch view of what people want in their representative.”

She said she spent six months away from Wellington but had only 10 weeks off work.

“Families have to make all sorts of decisions. I think all power to women that choose to have children and raise their families and do that by sacrificing their time off work.

“It’s an absolute joy, I’m so happy to have my son Lochie.”

She had not heard from Nash.

Luxon’s intervention came via a post to social media in which he said, “Whether reports of Stuart Nash’s resignation as a NZ First candidate are true or not, I am making clear he will not serve as a minister in my government.

“After several instances of poor behaviour, some politicians will claim he has changed. His lack of contrition after comments about one of my MPs’ maternity leave this evening shows he hasn’t,” Luxon said.

The post may draw comparisons to former Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, who, as Labour leader, said Greens co-leader Metiria Turei would not serve in any government she led.

That intervention was one of the main factors that led to the end of Turei’s career.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins called Nash’s comments “sexist and wrong”.

“He has once again highlighted why I was right to remove him from Cabinet. He does not have the judgment or temperament to be a Minister. It is an indictment on both Winston Peters and Christopher Luxon that up until yesterday they thought he did.

“Christopher Luxon is very selective in the way he seems to approach standards of ministerial conduct.

“He’s right that Stuart Nash’s recent outburst was unacceptable, but so was Shane Jones’ insinuations about him performing oral sex on a visiting foreign leader, Winston Peters making masturbation jibes live on TV and Shane Jones’ outright racism towards Indians, yet the Prime Minister did absolutely nothing about any of that.

“Yesterday’s events were a stark reminder that a vote for any of the three parties currently in government is a vote for more of the same.”

Hipkins was referring to remarks made by Jones over the weekend, when he said New Zealand politicians should “take off [their] kneepads” the next time a foreign dignitary visited.

Jones denied the remarks referred to oral sex, saying the remarks were about bowing. Peters took umbrage at a question from Ryan Bridge on Ryan Bridge TODAY, describing it as a “wanker question“.

Nash’s latest scandal began after remarks made on a podcast hosted by former Labour leader Phil Goff and former National minister Chris Finlayson called Cross Party Lines. Finlayson quoted a text message he said he had received from Nash.

Finlayson had been speaking positively about Nimon on a previous episode, saying “had a very good future”. Nash responded, “Comments like yours motivate and drive me harder,” Finlayson read.

“Katie took nine months off on full pay, went back for a week, then took another month off,” the message continued.

“Laziest MP I have ever come across. Nice woman, but ill-suited to the rigours of being an electorate MP.”

Nimon’s son Lochie was born on May 22, 2025 – that year’s Budget Day. She returned to Parliament on December 8.

She said she had 10 weeks off in that time and, as an MP, she was not eligible for maternity leave.

“I was kindly granted parliamentary leave, so I took six months away from being in Wellington, but I was away from work for about 10 weeks.”

Although she was away from Wellington during that time, she was working as a local MP in her electorate in various capacities, taking her baby “with me everywhere”.

Connectivity failure behind Waikato Hospital IT outage

New Zealand Herald July 22, 2026

The outage began at 10.44am and was fixed by Wednesday evening. Photo / Mike Scott

By RNZ

A connectivity failure at Waikato Hospital meant staff had to revert to pen and paper after a widespread IT outage.

Health NZ said late on Wednesday evening that the problem – which began at 10.44am – had been fixed, but it was continuing to monitor the situation.

Te Whatu Ora/Health NZ chief information technology officer Darren Douglass said there had been an issue with its main data centre which meant users weren’t able to connect.

Thames, Te Kūiti, Tokoroa and Taumarunui hospitals were also affected, which resulted in longer waiting times in the Emergency Department, some delayed surgeries, and forced staff to revert to paper systems.

Douglass told Morning Report the outage was because of a network connectivity issue.

“The connectivity between our network that our users use to access systems in our main data centre failed, so effectively the systems in our data centre – though they were running okay – none of the users could access them.”

Both the equipment providing connectivity as well as secondary equipment in place as a “fail over” had not worked, he said.

Urgent care and emergency services were prioritised, but some non-urgent appointments were diverted.

Douglass was unable to clarify whether ambulances needed to be diverted significant distances away.

Staff had told RNZ patient history was limited to paper reports and any recent AI transcribed reports could not be accessed.

Health NZ said it delivered safe patient care throughout the day, prioritising urgent care with “additional resource in place”. It said it would contact patients whose planned appointments were postponed for rescheduling.

The Public Service Association has been warning hospital IT outages would keep happening because of cuts to Health NZ’s digital team.

Douglass did not believe that the outage was an example of resulting impacts of these cuts.

“When we went through our restructure process one of the things we were very clear about is that we were prioritising operational support for these critical systems.”

He did say that they were dealing with a complicated system that had been under-invested for decades.

“We are running a really complex environment with a lot of ageing technology and a lot of district variation as well, so it’s very difficult.”

Douglass said the 10-year plan they had in place, with some additional funding now coming in, would help – but there was no “silver bullet”.

The University of Auckland is preparing to unveil a new Department of Cancer Sciences tonight, with its inaugural head revealing his vision for a purpose-built centre for conducting research and providing clinical care.

Dr Ben Lawrence has been named the first head of the new department, which will operate under the university’s Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences.

He will present the plan in full at an official launch event tonight.

Lawrence stepped down from his position as clinical lead of oncology at Auckland Hospital to take on the new leadership role, but will continue to work two days a week there.

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY that tonight’s launch is the university’s “first step towards a comprehensive cancer centre” that has been nearly a decade in the works.

It intends to provide clinical care for people with cancer in the same space where research is undertaken, the latter of which the university will fund and provide resources for.

“We know that clinical care is better in places that do research,” Lawrence said.

“It’s hard to know exactly what it is, but it’s probably because people are ... on the cutting edge.

“They have some hope that they can change the future, and the patients feel that.”

Veteran broadcaster Paul Henry expressed support for the idea when announcing his Act candidacy last week, saying he would love to build a “world-class cancer hospital” that would treat both Kiwis and foreigners and arguing the case for similar investments.

While Henry estimated the cost for his vision would be in the billions, Lawrence said the university’s centre will be “a lot less than that”.

“We know that there is a cancer building, for example, at Auckland Hospital which is past its use-by date, and Health New Zealand is planning to replace that,” Lawrence said.

“That would be a great time to add research into that building.”

Lawrence said planning the dedicated cancer centre required a lot of time, care and collaboration as they look to bring health professionals, researchers and cancer patients under one roof.

“You don’t really want everybody driving into the middle of Auckland every day to get their cancer care.

“You want to have a mothership which runs that, which is a cancer centre.”

New Zealand has one of the highest rates of cancer incidence globally, ranking second only behind Australia.

Having spent time overseas at Yale University and elsewhere, Lawrence said there were things he noticed New Zealand falling behind on in cancer care and research.

“I think in life, it’s never one thing, and in cancer care and cancer research, it’s never one thing.

“We need to bring population health, lab scientists, drug discovery, clinical trials all together. And that’s what other centres can do overseas.“

Lawrence said there were roughly 30 comprehensive cancer centres worldwide, and hundreds more whose fields operate separately but in tandem with each other.

New Zealand increased cure rates by 10% between 2000 and 2020, which Lawrence attributed mostly to new knowledge from research and healthcare improvements.

“You can’t beat being in the same place, bumping into the same people when you come out of clinic and you’ve got a problem that you can’t solve, and the scientist is there and you can talk to them about it, and then they can go away and try to solve those problems,” he said.

“That’s the ... heart of a comprehensive cancer centre; better care, better understanding of cancer, put them together and you get better outcomes for patients.”

Hundreds of Wellington students reported skipping meals in recent times according to “quite shocking” new data.

The cost of food and public transport is among various factors driving students to skip both meals and classes, the data showed.

The Victoria University Student Association’s (VUWSA) latest State of the Student survey found 38% of the 1238 respondents have recently missed a meal, while 60% said the cost of groceries has made fresh fruit and vegetables less accessible.

For VUWSA academic vice-president and survey lead Ethan Rogacion, the statistic was “quite shocking”.

“[It] really says quite a lot about how directly the cost of living is impacting our students’ ability to go about their daily lives, to put kai on the table, and to get on with their lives alongside study.”

Infometrics’ principal economist Brad Olsen believed it was hard to be a student without some form of income over and above what one might get from Government support.

“Realistically for most students, the fees component of what they have to pay is not the biggest bit, it’s their living costs,” he said.

More than 20% of students surveyed said it had been more than three days since last having a piece of fresh fruit or a fresh vegetable.

It’s a concerning outlook for VUWSA who feared there were students who were eating less healthily than they’d like to.

It has caused a “massive increase” in the number of students making use of the community pantry available on campus.

“It signals that students are struggling to make ends meet, to put food on the table, and not only that, they’re also struggling to put nutritious food on the table,” said Rogacion.

Olsen said it was a bit of a surprise, seeing as fruit and vegetables weren’t considered the most expensive part of a supermarket shop.

He said the price of vegetables had fallen 0.7% on last year, and while the price of fresh fruit is up 6%, “the likes of meat prices have gone up quite a lot more.

“We’d expect probably to see more students that are having to make more difficult choices around the likes of how they’re getting their protein” said Olsen.

The survey found almost half of those using public transport said the cost made them consider other means of getting to university, while 38% said the cost had driven them to skip classes altogether.

Public transport is costing $20 or more per week for 29% of students.

Of those not using public transport, 72% said it was because of the infrequency of services, with over 170 students saying the reliability of services has impacted their decision to not use public transport.

Transport provider Metlink currently runs a bus service from the central train station to Kelburn Campus every 10 minutes during peak times, and its performance report from December last year cited 99.5% of bus services were delivered.

About 60% of students are working as well as studying, with the majority in either the hospitality or retail sector.

Of students not working, 66% felt unhopeful about finding work in the capital in the next six months, while over half were actively looking for work.

VUWSA believes although one of the biggest worries for students is employability after university, a big part is having a part-time job alongside study to “help you pay rent, and help do all of the awesome and fun things that students love to do on a weekend”.

The capital’s current job market came down to “high competition” with unemployment figures leaving people to search for “literally any role” said Olsen.

“We know looking at Seek data over the last year or so that there are sometimes two to three times the number of applications per job than there would have been back in 2019,″ he said.

Wellington has had a 3% drop in 15-24 year olds currently in jobs, and a similar drop in the number of 25-35 year old group, meaning there were “job cutbacks and a pullback in employment” all while there was “high competition for the remaining roles,” Olsen said.

Rogacion said the increasing competition for decreasing amount of work spoke to a lot of the reasons students were looking abroad for options.

Thousands of Victoria University students appear to already have plans to leave New Zealand, with 70% reporting thinking about moving overseas to find work and opportunities after graduating.

While the vast majority were intending to pursue opportunities relating to their study, only 33% felt hopeful about finding opportunities in their field domestically.

For Rogacion, it said a lot about the lack of hope that students felt about the economy and “students’ prospects post study”.

“It’s easy to see, when you see really attractive high wages and lower cost of living overseas compared to what our students are telling us they’re dealing with right now.”

Of the students who flat, more than 40% are paying between $200-$250 per week on individual rents, while well over half cite the quality of both the flat and flatmates as positive.

The condition of homes, as well as the landlords’ responsiveness is seen as relatively satisfactory by the majority of students.

It came as a “surprise” for Rogacion and the VUWSA team, who said it was a “turnaround from the stories we saw on the front pages just a few years back as the housing market in Wellington shifts towards one that’s a bit friendlier for renters”.

Tobias Macintosh is a Newstalk ZB Multimedia Journalist, based in Wellington. He joined NZME in June 2025, after obtaining a Bachelor of Broadcasting Communications at the New Zealand Broadcasting School in Christchurch. Putting a spotlight on all things happening in and around the capital, he also has a keen eye on local politics, crime and justice, and foreign affairs.
