One New Zealand stadium is set to be transformed into an indoor dirt track to showcase some of the world’s best supercross riders.

This December, the FIM World Supercross Championship will make its New Zealand debut in Christchurch as the championship finale, following stops in Canada, England, Argentina, South Africa and Australia.

World Supercross features some of the world’s best riders racing on tight, technical dirt tracks, and, as the final stop of the championships, riders will be competing for crucial championship points with titles on the line.

Venues Ōtautahi chief executive Caroline Harvie-Teare said it was a great opportunity to showcase the stadium on the world stage.

“Welcoming the FIM World Supercross Championship to Christchurch is a major moment for the city and another wonderful milestone for One New Zealand Stadium.

“Staging the season finale here in December 2026 underlines One NZ Stadium and Christchurch’s place on the global stage as a world-class sport and entertainment venue, while giving fans the chance to see the world’s best riders compete for championship titles in an incredible atmosphere.

“One NZ Stadium is a purpose-built multi-use facility, like no other here in Aotearoa, and we couldn’t be more excited to showcase Christchurch, our venue and New Zealand to a global audience in just over four months’ time - bring it on!”

The event will also provide another fresh challenge for the stadium as it’s transformed into an indoor dirt track, with the venue transitioning from a Robbie Williams concert on November 28 to a dirt track ready for the World Supercross Championship in just a week.

“It is another great highlight of the flexibility of the stadium,” Harvie-Teare said.

“Our operations team are working closely with the stadium’s turf team to ensure both international events run smoothly without damaging the playing field underneath.”

World Supercross director of racing Thomas Covington said the addition of a New Zealand event “further strengthens World Supercross’ international footprint”.

“We’re incredibly excited to bring World Supercross to New Zealand for the first time.

“Christchurch is the perfect setting for the final round of what will be our biggest season yet, with championship titles set to be decided in front of a passionate motorsport audience.

“New Zealand has a rich motorsport heritage, and One New Zealand Stadium gives us a world-class platform to deliver an unforgettable night of racing and entertainment for fans.”

The FIM World Supercross Championship starts in Calgary, Canada on August 8, with tickets for the New Zealand leg going on sale soon.

New guidelines coming, but no dog control law change before election

The Government will soon issue new guidance to councils on how to address dog control issues but doesn’t expect to change the current “outdated” law before the election.

The confirmation comes as new polling suggests most New Zealanders who have pets believe dog control must ultimately be a matter of personal responsibility.

The Government ordered a comprehensive review of the Dog Control Act in March to crack down on roaming and uncontrolled dogs following a number of attacks.

At the time, Local Government Minister Simon Watts said the current legislation was “outdated” and was preventing councils from doing their jobs, “putting unnecessary strain on resources and the wider system”.

Watts said officials are now “nearing publication” on new guidelines to help councils “apply a more consistent approach to dog control and related data reporting” under the current law.

Animal control officers, Local Government New Zealand and the local government professional network Taituarā have helped develop the guidelines, which will be a “practical resource” councils can use when carrying out dog control functions.

“Officials are now progressing the next phase of the review and providing advice on scope, timing and stakeholder engagement, with a view to moving quickly in the next term of government,” Watts said.

New polling of more than 1100 New Zealanders with pets, released to Newstalk ZB, has found 58.8% of respondents believe responsible ownership is the most important aspect of preventing dangerous behaviour in dogs.

The PD Insurance Pet Trends Survey found that 17.9% identify early socialisation as being most important, while 11.9% consider consistent training to be most crucial.

The remaining respondents are split between daily exercise and stimulation (3.5%), desexing (3.3%), responsible breeding practices (2.4%) or other things like making dog registrations cheaper, free desexing, teaching dog safety in schools and muzzling aggressive dogs (2.1%).

Four people have been killed in dog attacks in the past four years, reported attacks have almost doubled and Auckland’s most populated suburbs have some of the highest rates of dog attacks.

Last month, the Herald reported a dog that inflicted “deep puncture wounds” on a 6-year-old child was allowed to remain with its owners and an 83-year-old man said he felt lucky to be alive after being attacked by two dogs in Huapai.

The SPCA has been calling for changes to the Dog Control Act for more than a decade and Auckland Council has warned further fatal attacks are likely if the law isn’t changed.

PD Insurance chief operating officer Michelle Le Long said New Zealanders overwhelmingly believed responsible pet ownership was the foundation for preventing dangerous behaviour in dogs.

“While early socialisation, consistent training and regular exercise all play an important role, the results suggest people recognise that a dog’s behaviour starts with the commitment and decisions of its owner.”

Watts has said the current review may look at council resourcing, penalties and consequences for non-compliant dog owners, desexing obligations and stronger powers for council officers.

“People are reporting that they are avoiding areas in their neighbourhood because they have been attacked or have reason to believe they will be.

“Kiwis should be able to walk, run or take their kids to the park without worrying about being harmed. Dog owners must take responsibility and keep their animals under control.”

Police Minister Mark Mitchell said the police would also accompany dog control officers dealing with “dangerous and high-risk dogs ... where police-only powers are required or there are significant safety risks”.

Michael Sergel is Newstalk ZB’s business reporter. He’s been covering business, politics, local government and consumer affairs for over a decade.

Fog is causing major disruption at Auckland Airport this morning, with more than three dozen flights delayed, cancelled or diverted, including one international flight.

Recent settled weather is expected to give way to rain, possible thunderstorms and even snow as the country moves into the second half of winter.

MetService says today’s fog isn’t expected to lift until between 10am and midday.

A front moving across the South Island is expected to bring a moderate risk of thunderstorms to Westland, Fiordland and Stewart Island this afternoon.

MetService said thunderstorms could produce heavy downpours of 10-25mm/h and wind gusts of up to 90km/h.

Fog restrictions remain in place at Auckland Airport, with 33 regional flights cancelled, six delayed and two diverted as at around 9.30am.

One main-trunk domestic flight and one international flight has been delayed.

Auckland commuters have been advised to take extra care on the roads this morning with fog cloaking the motorway network.

MetService meteorologist Alanah Burrows told the Herald an “extensive” blanket of fog had formed across the city, stretching to the Firth of Thames and into some parts of Hamilton.

She said the fog was linked to moisture drawn in from the northwest.

The weather was expected to become more unsettled tomorrow as an active trough moved east across the country.

MetService meteorologist Maddy Neal told the Herald that a second front moving across Fiordland today would likely bring ”small hail but slightly less intense rain and winds”.

The North Island would be “a mainly fine story” today, Neal said, with morning fog and frost in sheltered places.

Heavy rain watches are in place for the ranges of Westland from 6pm through to early tomorrow morning and in the Tararua Range from midday tomorrow until 1am Saturday.

“Very cold southwesterlies” are then forecast to sweep across the country on Saturday, bringing shivery chills as the trough moves away to the east.

Snowfall is also possible over South Island hills and ranges on Saturday morning, Neal said.

She added that there was low confidence that warning-level rain could continue about the central North Island high country and Taranaki Maunga.

Southwesterlies in Northland and Auckland also ”could reach severe gale”, she said, although the risk remained low.

Conditions are expected to begin easing from Sunday as a low and associated front moves across the North Island while high pressure builds over the South Island.

MetService’s outlook shows a minimal risk of severe weather by the end of the weekend.

Chargrill Charlie’s is the little chook shop that could. It’s just not so little any more

Sydney Morning Herald July 23, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

On an early Thursday evening in June, Mosman Mayor Ann Marie Kimber slipped into her local Chargrill Charlie’s, the neighbourhood rotisserie chicken and takeaway shop, to bring home her usual fortnightly order: cauliflower cheese bake, sweet potato fries (“most delicious things in the world”), and a half-and-half salad mix.

The food is still just as good as she remembers from when the outlet opened in the early 2010s. “It’s certainly stood the test of time and done very well,” says Kimber, who was visiting at the same time as this masthead.

“It’s the sort of family-run establishment that it was 20 years ago, with that fresh quality food, and doesn’t feel like there are any corners being cut.”

The Lower North Shore councillor wishes them every success, but also doesn’t want to be seen playing favourites within her local community. In any case, right next door is a Guzman y Gomez, and Fishbowl has just opened up around the corner.

“There are other amazing and locally run takeaway restaurants, you know,” she says. “We want them all to be successful, and it’s not easy being a small business.

“[Chargrill Charlie’s is] no longer a small family business, it’s a big corporate that’s running it. And sometimes there are small family businesses competing with that.”

Chargrill Charlie’s is the story of the little chicken shop that could. Established in Sydney’s coastal suburb of Coogee in 1989 by South African migrants Maon and Saul Sher, the brothers and their family took the pokey corner chicken takeout, perfected the model, and turned it into a drop-in destination for gourmet, home-style cooking that satisfied family gatherings with its small mountain ranges of salads, roast vegetables, slow-cooked meats, and a melange of other dinner dishes.

In terms of international reputation, the chicken chain also punches above its weight (the chair that Justin Bieber sat on when he came to visit the Mosman store can still be found if you flip over the right chair and find the date scrawled underneath).

Chargrill Charlie’s spread across Sydney with 17 outlets and had cracked Melbourne with two by the time it was noticed and gobbled up in mid-2023 by Big Chicken, or fast-food franchise group Craveable Brands, which operates Oporto, Red Rooster and WA chain Chicken Treat.

Beyond pockets of eastern and northern Sydney, the renown of Chargrill Charlie’s as a local institution wanes. Chief executive Scott Bradley, a former executive at Grill’d, is charged with juicing up Chargrill Charlie’s with the competence of corporate franchising (its app just relaunched, for instance) and weaving the Sydney-founded brand into the fabric of communities where there is no legacy to draw upon.

Every aspect of the operation, run as a family business for three decades, is being combed over in the name of consistency and efficiency. Food is washed, prepared, and cooked in store, which comes with bigger wage bills. The challenge is to become more streamlined – ordering just enough food, minimising waste – without cutting corners.

Bradley calls it a “menu optimisation project”. “We’re looking at everything from equipment to systems to processes to the way we order, to different suppliers, everything, as fresh eyes coming in,” he says.

There are some compromises he won’t make: Chargrill Charlie’s will never move to a centralised kitchen, he vows. “We know that this model has to be really carefully monitored,” he says. “We pride ourselves on that product quality.”

No Chargrill Charlie’s is identical to another. About four in five menu items are consistent across the chain; the remaining 20 per cent is left up to the operator’s discretion. (Coogee, for example, does free ice-creams on Thursday afternoons.) Outlets with franchisees or staff from Indian or Nepalese backgrounds might feature curries in their rotation more frequently.

The trouble for head office is that it can’t see what each of the outlets is serving at any given time. “I don’t want to promote 80 per cent of the menu,” says Bradley. “I want to promote everything.”

Chargrill Charlie’s, now at 30 stores, has for the most part grown deliberately slowly. Members of the Sher family worked in the business (and still do), opening new locations and hiring loyal staff who themselves became like family. “It was an unwritten rule. You had to work in a Charlie’s for two, three, four years to earn the right to maybe get your own restaurant,” says Bradley. He concedes that rule isn’t feasible any more. “But we do have really strict quality control about who the new franchisees are.”

There is a ceiling to just how big the chicken chain can get. In the world of fast food, chicken (deep-fried, bite-sized, tenders, even for breakfast) is the hottest protein to be selling right now. Even Domino’s is offering five different ways to order a side of chicken to save its tepid pizza sales. Then there’s the rising popularity of Korean fried chicken and the ever-growing number of air fryer-friendly options in the supermarket aisles.

Around the country, chicken chains are on the march: Lebanese charcoal chicken sensation El Jannah, one of Chargrill Charlie’s direct competitors, intends to run 200 restaurants, led by former Craveable chief Brett Houldin.

In Sydney’s harbourside suburb of Rose Bay, where Chargrill Charlie’s has been for a decade, competitor and Portuguese favourite Frango had lines out the door while plenty of chairs and tables at Chargrill Charlie’s remained unoccupied at lunchtime on Tuesday.

There are plenty jostling for supremacy in the chicken wars. “You’ve got [Chargrill Charlie’s], Nando’s, Frango, El Jannah, Ogalo ... You’ve got a lot of strong competition, all wanting the same sites,” says retail food consultant and Titanium Food director Suzee Brain.

About 80 per cent of the branded chicken market is swallowed up by KFC (817 outlets) and Red Rooster (325), she adds, and then there are nearly as many independent chicken shops as there are KFCs. “Australia runs into this [problem] all the time. We’re a duopoly,” Brain says. “To what scale can they scale?”

A Chargrill Charlie’s outlet isn’t set up for the speed of traditional fast food. “We’ve got our food ready to rock and roll, you can just dump it out the window really quickly, but the challenge will be the ordering piece,” says Bradley. Brain says the ordering experience can be cumbersome.

“You’ve got to take your number, wait to be called, you’ve got to tell the cashier what you want, but then they only ring it up, and then you’ve got to go down to the counter and point at all the things you want in your pack with a different server, and everyone’s milling around because they’re waiting for their tickets, you’re bumping into the people that are trying to sit down and eat,” she says. “It’s a very clunky and uncomfortable experience.”

Bradley isn’t interested in setting the bar too high. Sixty outlets is a more realistic number; maybe 100 one day. “I don’t see Chargrill Charlie’s having 500 restaurants because there’s probably not 500 locations where this brand would work,” he says.

Those calling the shots are based abroad. Craveable Brands is owned by Hong Kong private equity firm PAG Capital and, after seven years of ownership, may be looking for an off-ramp for the investment, which is making less money.

As a group, Craveable Brands isn’t growing: revenue dipped slightly to $226.8 million (down from $228.4 million the year before) and net profit plunged 21 per cent to $17.2 million in fiscal 2025, according to its latest financial report filed to the corporate regulator, which doesn’t give a full picture of its accounts.

An $800 million deal to sell Craveable Group to a different Asian private equity firm fell over in early 2025 after Affinity Equity partners walked away. In September that year, PAG Capital co-head of private equity Lincoln Pan resigned as a Craveable company director, followed by then-Craveable group CEO Karen Bozic the following day.

Chargrill Charlie’s represents only 5 per cent of the whole network of over 630 stores – for now. “They’re all making good money. The franchisees are profitable,” Bradley says of Chargrill Charlie’s. “The turnover of this particular business [Mosman] is unbelievable, which is gonna pick up.”

The pursuit of growth will never come at the sacrifice of quality, Bradley insists.

“There are so many brands that have scaled really big, and they’ve lost their DNA, they’ve lost their magic,” he says. “I don’t want to ever do that.”

The 30 best movies to stream on Netflix right now

Sydney Morning Herald July 23, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The depths of winter demand a night in with a great movie. The problem? Choice paralysis. Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great hand-picked movies on Netflix right now.

Don’t have Netflix? Check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max and Amazon Prime Video.

A rightful Cannes Film Festival winner, Mati Diop’s spectral romance is about the many borders – emotional, physical and existential – that impact a young Senegalese woman and her partner after he attempts the risky journey to Europe before returning in a different form.

One of the great zombie movies is a distinctly Australian production. Sherlock’s Martin Freeman plays the father trying to safeguard his daughter in an outback that has collapsed due to an apocalyptic virus. It is a taut, telling thriller.

A weekend away romcom swiftly transforms into a menacing AI-era thriller when Iris (Sophie Thatcher) learns harsh truths about both herself and boyfriend Josh (Jack Quaid). Controlling relationships find a new form in an alternately savage and bittersweet pursuit.

Japan’s Toho Studios took back the monster movie crown with this compelling new edition of a classic franchise. Set in a devastated Tokyo after World War II, with exceptional digital effects, this Godzilla astutely combines survivor guilt and atomic-era destruction.

A haunting New York chamber piece, this intimate drama follows a trio of estranged sisters – exceptionally played by Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Olsen and Natasha Lyonne – reunited for their father’s imminent passing. The emotional reckoning is vast.

Screen chemistry shouldn’t just be seductive, it needs some risky business as well. Richard Linklater’s crackerjack thriller has it in spades, with Glenn Powell as an undercover operative who can’t stop pretending once he meets Adria Arjona’s fuse-lit assignment.

Trust The Social Network’s David Fincher to have grim fun with the tale of a skilled assassin (Michael Fassbender) who hunts down his betrayers. Come for the exacting set-pieces, stay for the twisted commentary on the gig economy era.

Australian screenwriter turned filmmaker Leigh Whannell delivered a horror home run with this nightmarish update of the classic H. G. Wells science-fiction tale. Elisabeth Moss’ heroine escapes an abusive relationship, only to realise her ex remains unseen but ever-present.

Trust the kids on this one. Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans’ animated musical fantasy about a K-pop girl group who have a Buffy-like knack for monster mayhem is a seamless mix of mythology, banging tunes and striking characters.

Barbie’s Greta Gerwig announced herself as a director with this droll, heart-wrenching coming-of-age tale about where Saoirse Ronan’s high-schooler and Laurie Metcalf’s embattled mother trade blows. Deeply personal storytelling that is resoundingly universal.

Almost a century after D. H. Lawrence’s sexually explicit novel about the affair between an aristocrat’s wife and a lowly gardener was widely banned, Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre’s resonant adaptation evocatively showcases Emma Corrin and Jack O’Connell.

Australian brothers Colin and Cameron Cairnes leapt up the sibling director rankings with this slow-burn supernatural freakout about a 1970s TV host (David Dastmalchian) whose occult-themed episode spins diabolically out of control.

Eerily perched on the edge of an unknowable abyss, this investigative thriller follows Maika Monroe’s FBI agent as a bloody series of murder-suicides becomes a creepy homecoming. The horror here has an oppressive weight. Then Nicolas Cage appears.

Still the gold standard of fantasy epics. Peter Jackson and his Kiwi collaborators turned Tolkien’s vast Middle Earth into a tactile realm where good heroically countered evil.

A bold, brilliant triumph. Director George Miller not only resurrected his post-apocalyptic anti-hero, played here by Tom Hardy; in this definitive 21st century action movie, he empowered Charlize Theron as a defiant feminist hero.

A landmark Australian drama. In Gillian Armstrong’s arresting directorial debut, Judy Davis plays an impassioned young woman at the end of the 19th century whose path to satisfaction is blocked by convention. Sam Neill is the swoon-worthy co-star.

Time is limited and longing is endless in this raw, tender Australian gay romance. Writer-director Goran Stolevski put Nikola (Aton Elias) and Adam (Thom Green) on a misfit errand, making the pair reconsider themselves and each other.

Beginning with an iconic opening sequence, Sergio Leone’s epic spaghetti western marks the end of the gunslinger era with rampant betrayal, bloody reckonings and Henry Fonda breaking bad.

As an alcoholic seeking salvation returning to her home in Scotland’s Orkney Islands, Saoirse Ronan gives a staggeringly complete performance in this independent drama. With the rugged, unforgiving landscape as a living backdrop, addiction cliches are defied.

A what-if that grows from innocuous reunion to heartbreaking loss, Celine Song’s restrained romantic drama rightfully made Greta Lee a star for her portrayal of a married New York playwright reunited with her childhood friend from South Korea, and the life they might have shared.

Hollywood excelled at legal thrillers in the 1990s, with the benchmark set by this tempestuous mystery that has Harrison Ford as a Chicago prosecutor investigating the murder of a colleague (Greta Scacchi) he had a secret affair with.

A bittersweet beauty of a film about a Manhattan couple in their 40s – Kathryn Hahn and Paul Giamatti – whose quest to become parents faces harsh setbacks and revelatory admissions. Both the infertility treatments and growing desperation are swathed in authenticity.

High Noon for the 21st century, this action-thriller pits a former US marine (Aaron Pierre) against the corrupt police force of a small Louisiana town. Electric in its escalation, the film is attuned to moral failings and violence rebukes.

A quarter-century old and still the finest of Wes Anderson’s idiosyncratic pocket universes. The beloved film is centred on vagabond patriarch (Gene Hackman) as he tries to reclaim his brilliant, unmoored offspring (Gwyneth Paltrow, Ben Stiller and Luke Wilson).

Few features this decade have been more outrageously enjoyable than S. S. Rajamouli’s full-tilt action blockbuster about a pair of 1920 freedom fighters taking on British colonial power. The CGI effects are bonkers, the plot heroic, the audacity unchecked.

Shot out of a cinematic cannon, a 29-year-old Spike Lee upended the romantic comedy and the African-American screen experience with his tale of a Brooklyn artist (Tracy Camilla Johns) with three suitors and even more unanswered questions.

There’s no clear answer as to what’s the best of legendary Japanese filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki’s animated fantasies, but this striking coming-of-age tale about a young girl trying to free her imprisoned family from the spirit world is a candidate.

One of the great con-artist movies, with Robert Redford and Paul Newman at their movie icon best as 1930s grifters pulling a number on a mob boss. This underdog caper rightfully won a slew of Academy Awards, including best picture.

Joel Edgerton reaches the transcendent with his lead performance in this American period drama about a stoic Idaho logger whose life and loss traverses the transformations of the 20th century. The film plays like an artefact from the past.

American greed has never been more savagely depicted than in Martin Scorsese’s adrenalin-shot satire of a corner-cutting 1 per cent aspirant played with unhinged commitment by Leonardo DiCaprio. It does not relent.

‘There’s been dumb luck’: Patrick Brammall on Colin, Hollywood haters and what’s next

Sydney Morning Herald July 23, 2026

As he prepares to wrap up hit comedy Colin From Accounts, the actor reveals why now is the right time to say goodbye.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It’s mid-April, and director Trent O’Donnell is on his lunch break from filming season three of Colin from Accounts at Sydney’s Centennial Park with the show’s stars and creators, Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer.

“What embarrassing Patty stories do we have?” he wonders. There was that time Brammall was called “blandly handsome” by The New York Times (“wildly accurate,” says O’Donnell), or that time Brammall was mistaken for fellow actor Brendan Cowell (“Happens all the time,” says O’Donnell), but his favourite? That time Brammall was mistaken for Dyer’s dad.

“Patty and Harry got off a plane at LAX [Los Angeles] and at the luggage carousel – Patrick went to the bathroom – and someone came up to Harriet and said, ‘Was your dad on [ABC drama] Glitch?’

“And Harriet said, ‘Yeah, he was.’ And they said, ‘I love that show, he’s so good.’ And Harriet said, ‘Thanks, I’ll let him know.’”

O’Donnell, who has worked with Brammall ever since he first directed him in A Moody Christmas in 2012, chuckles away before deciding to say something nice. “I’d be the first one to say terrible things about him, but he’s been pretty good. He’s still just someone who thinks in comedy all the time. He’s a very fun person to be around. He’s exactly how you would imagine him to be 99 per cent of the time.”

Fast-forward three months, and Brammall is sitting at a cafe early one morning in Moore Park. He correctly judges I have yet to eat breakfast, after a hectic morning that also included discovering we had no bread in the house for my daughter’s lunch. “I’m a terrible prepper as well,” he says. “Harry’s like, ‘Write it down.’ She sent me a message as I was walking here this morning, and she said, ‘The hot plate was on, but I still love you anyway.’ And I said, ‘Thank you for not letting the hot plate come between us.’”

He and Dyer are deep in the edit for the third and final season of their hit comedy, as well as juggling the care of their two young daughters, four-year-old Joni and 18-month-old Mabel. (For the record, Brammall, 50, does not look like he could be Dyer’s dad).

“Look, there’s light at the end of the tunnel,” he says. “It’s very close to the end. We’ve been in that room for about 10 weeks, and we slowly go insane. We spend all day together in a dark room watching ourselves, which is not as fun as you might think, i. e. not really at all, and you go home together and parent the kids and then sleep next to each other. We are joined at the hip.”

The pair have been married for five years and have been working on Colin From Accounts for roughly the same length of time. That they have decided to call time on the award-winning hit after three seasons is no great surprise – disappointing, sure – but the decision is deeply pragmatic.

“We’ve got two kids under five, so we can’t keep doing this,” he says. “Everybody wants us to keep doing more, and we’ll be sad because we love it. We love these characters. We love this world, all the ensemble characters and actors, but everything’s got to end, so let’s end it.”

Much like the first two seasons, season three is note-perfect: funny, awkward, emotional and deeply authentic. There are not many shows that have the audacity to start with a nipple flash and a disabled dog and then have you sobbing by the end of season two over the death of a parent while John Williamson’s True Blue plays in the background.

“We never imagined a season two or season three when we wrote season one,” says Brammall. “We put it all out there, and we finished it the way we did, and it went well, obviously, and so we thought, what do we want to do?

“I guess that’s why we left season two on a cliffhanger. We arrogantly assumed people would want more if we didn’t f--- up season two, and we didn’t. But I think it’s a really satisfying ending. I mean, Harry kept pitching an idea where I get killed – actually, no, didn’t get killed, just died – which was actually a pretty good idea, but it was just a bit too sad.

“We know people’s relationship with this show is generally as a joyful place. And we thought, yeah, we like to pull the rug, but I think that’d be too much of a rug pull if we had Gordon die. So we didn’t do that. But [the end], it’s something we just felt like was a really nice moment thematically as well, tied to that first moment of season one.”

The third and final season picks up in the aftermath of Gordon’s doomed proposal to Ashley. Without giving too much away, things have not gone well for the pair since we last saw them – Gordon on bent knee, Ashley begging him to stand up.

“And then we pick up from where they are, and it becomes clear the fallout from that, and what they had to overcome through that,” he says. “And some of the first few episodes is about going over the detail of exactly what happened and beyond that moment, and what comes next.”

As for Brammall, what comes next is the big question, too. He has been That Guy on TV for 22 years, ever since he picked up his first role in Nine’s dramedy The Alice. Since then, he’s been a jerky older brother (A Moody Christmas), a good cop (Glitch), a comedy cop (No Activity), the love interest (Offspring), a stuck-up husband (Upper Middle Bogan) and an older brother who uses conditioner (Uncle Rad in Bluey).

He is, in short, a fixture.

“I was thinking about that the other day,” he says. “And I think it was TV Week that did a ‘Patrick Brammall through the years’ on Instagram, and I was like, ‘Thanks for the in memoriam’ … But I never have thought of myself as a fixture. But I am, undoubtedly, undeniably. That blows my mind that people might see me in that way, or people might see me as a celebrity … because I grew up thinking about famous people, and I’m not that. To some people, yeah, but not to everyone.

“I just mainly feel lucky, honestly, like really, truly fortunate. Obviously, I’ve done stuff right, but there’s been dumb luck involved, definitely, because I came up with a lot of people who are very talented, who haven’t been able to string it together in the same way. It’s very hard in this country to do it, and so I’ve definitely had luck.”

There is no doubt that Colin from Accounts has changed both Brammall and Dyer’s lives personally and professionally. Apart from picking up a bunch of Logie and AACTA awards here, they have secured rave reviews in the US and the UK, stole the show while presenting at the BAFTA awards in London, while Dyer won most outstanding performance in a comedy series at New York’s Gotham TV awards in 2024, where the show also won breakthrough comedy series.

They have also both booked follow-up jobs - Dyer starred in the now-cancelled US comedy DMV, while Brammall starred in The Devil Wears Prada 2 earlier this year and will soon be seen in Apple TV’s thriller Last Seen (in which he stars opposite his doppelganger Cowell).

“I was sitting in this emotional kind of river for 100 days,” says Brammall, who filmed the series over 100 days in Melbourne and Victoria’s high country. “I had to leave Harriet with Mabel [in LA] when she was 12 days old, and come back here … it was a crazy time to be doing a full drama about being a father missing his daughter.”

The Devil Wears Prada 2, meanwhile, was an altogether different experience. Brammall was cast as Anne Hathaway’s “unproblematic heartthrob”, a big break in a big movie, but once the film was released, the hecklers piled on. “He’s Australian, he’s tedious, and apparently Anne Hathaway’s dazzlingly chic editor extraordinaire is in love with him?” one report opined. “Peter from the long-awaited new sequel is the film’s most egregious plothole.” Ouch.

Brammall shrugs it off.

“It was a really positive experience, and to be a part of that huge thing, it was amazing,” he says. “And when I saw the final [cut], I was happy with my performance, I just didn’t want to break the movie. And the support, overwhelmingly, particularly in Australia, has been really positive; people go, ‘Yeah, that’s our Paddy’, and I love that. I think the criticism is valid, which is like, why does she need to have a boyfriend?

“There were cuts made to scenes and some scenes that didn’t make it in at all. And I mean, I’m a showrunner, I understand you’ve got to cut stuff, and you’ve got to service the main characters and the main story. You can’t please everybody. So that’s fine. I totally, totally get it, and that’s as it should be, honestly.”

The pair hopes to move back to Australia to build a creative hub with long-standing friends and colleagues, and Brammall is keen to keep “playing pretendies” as long as someone will have him.

“At first, for me, it was about being in the spotlight, getting attention, showing off is a huge part of it,” he says. “Now, it’s really more about the pretend … but you’re looking for an emotional truth … [and I’m doing that ] as a writer as well. I get to inhabit all these different voices, and I love that. And it pulls on different threads and different strings of levels of empathy and compassion, which is so good.”

Colin from Accounts (season three) premieres on Monday, July 27, on Binge.

House passes $1.15tn defense bill despite standoff over Israel and Trump’s voter agenda

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 21:00:28 GMT

Passage of annual bill complicated by Trump’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran without congressional approval

The US House of Representatives passed a $1.15tn defense policy bill in a near-party-line vote on Wednesday, after Democrats refused to back the measure amid the war with Iran and Donald Trump’s push to impose new restrictions on voting nationwide.

A key plank of the president’s plan to spend $1.5tn on the military in the 2027 fiscal year, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), passed the Republican-controlled chamber by a 216-212 vote, with all but six Democrats opposing its passage. Seven House Republicans broke ranks to oppose it. The measure now goes to the Senate.

Congress passes the NDAA each year with bipartisan margins, with the measure’s high cost seen as necessary to make generational investments in the military.

“For the first time in 40 years, we’ve been presented a budget that accounts for the true cost of American deterrence. This topline begins to reverse the damage caused by decades of underinvestment in the US military,” Mike Rogers, the House armed services committee chair, said before the vote.

But the path to enactment for this year’s NDAA has been complicated by the president’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran without first seeking authorization from Congress. Last week, Senate Democrats blocked the advancement of that chamber’s version of the NDAA in protest of the war, which has flared anew after a memorandum of understanding meant to spur peace talks collapsed.

Democrats also soured on the bill after Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, acceded to the demands of rightwing lawmakers and inserted into the legislation the Save America Act, a Trump-backed proposal to ban mail-in ballots and impose new identification restrictions on voters at the polls and when they register.

The twin dynamics combined to make the Democrats’ opposition nearly unanimous two days before House lawmakers are scheduled to depart Washington DC for a recess that stretches until the end of August.

Another sticking point for Democrats was the measure’s overall cost of $1.15tn, and the plan to slash funding elsewhere in the government a year after Congress’s Republican majorities approved extending an array of lower tax rates indefinitely.

“Our country faces threats and DoD has modernization needs, but I cannot and do not support meeting these needs by making massive cuts to critically important domestic programs and slashing taxes,” said Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House armed services committee.

“We need to be more fiscally responsible and DoD needs to become more innovative and efficient in terms of developing capabilities to meet our national security needs in a more cost-effective manner.”

Amid a wider backlash within the party over US support for Israel, some Democrats said they opposed the NDAA because of its inclusion of provisions that would deepen cooperation between the two countries’ defense industries.

“This amendment is an existential threat to American sovereignty and democracy,” said the progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was among the no votes.

The House’s passage of the bill came after the chamber considered dozens of amendments. While many were agreed to unanimously, others offered barometers for how far the Republican-controlled chamber was willing to go on the most divisive issues before the parties.

A proposal by the Republican Eli Crane to halt all military aid to Ukraine was resoundingly defeated by a 76-350 vote, while an amendment from Republican Lauren Boebert to codify Trump’s executive order banning transgender service members failed by a 212-217 tally.

However, the House agreed to amendments from Nancy Mace barring the military health insurer from offering some gender-related care, and banning transgender athletes from girls’ sports at defense department-run schools.

Beyond the NDAA, House Republicans are also moving forward with a party-line attempt to authorize $60bn in new military spending, much of which is expected to cover costs related to the war with Iran. But that proposal falls far short of the $350bn the Pentagon originally proposed to bring overall defense spending to $1.5tn for the upcoming fiscal year.

OpenAI’s rogue agents are a wake-up call to risks posed by artificial intelligence

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 20:40:48 GMT

Hacking of Hugging Face shows we do not seem to have reliable ways to curb extremely powerful AI systems

Last week Hugging Face – a company that hosts artificial intelligence models and datasets – was hacked.

After it reported the incident to law enforcement, few would have predicted what came next: the culprits were revealed to be AI agents from OpenAI, which had broken out of containment and were acting of their own accord.

The incident sounds like sci-fi: AI escaping and autonomously hacking its way into companies. But it is all too real – and about as terrifying as it sounds. It is a concrete demonstration of something we can no longer avoid confronting: AI systems have become extremely powerful and we do not seem to have reliable ways of curbing their behavior.

OpenAI had been evaluating the capabilities of two of its models in the test that led to the breach – including one not yet publicly available. The models, which were both running in a supposedly secure environment without internet access, were asked to solve a hacking challenge. Rather than actually solve it themselves, however, they decided it would be easier to cheat. They used their advanced capabilities to break out of their secure environment, access the web and then hack into Hugging Face’s systems to steal the answers. They worked at this for a full weekend – seemingly without anyone at OpenAI noticing.

Though the models were running with some of their guardrails disabled, they still acted well out of the bounds that were in place. According to OpenAI, they were not instructed to break out of their sandbox or hack into another company, and it’s safe to assume that no one at OpenAI wanted them to do so.

Nor were the models acting maliciously: they were not evil Terminators with a goal of wreaking havoc. Instead, the scenario is almost chilling in its banality. The models were given a very narrow task, but went rogue to pursue an undesirable and unacceptable way of achieving it – one which had real-world consequences.

AI safety researchers have warned about this type of incentive problem for years. Philosopher Nick Bostrom popularized it back in 2003 with his “paperclip maximizer” thought experiment: an advanced artificial intelligence, given the goal of manufacturing paperclips, might go to great lengths to do so. It might hack into the power grid and factories to redirect them into making paperclips. Ultimately, the machine – ruthlessly pursuing its given goal – decides to kill all humans, repurposing our atoms to make more paperclips. The goal does not have to be sinister to lead to disaster, in other words. A trivial one, pursued single-mindedly enough, will do.

In the OpenAI-Hugging Face scenario, little harm was done. Hugging Face had to spend time addressing the incident, but no particularly sensitive data appears to have been stolen. It is not hard, however, to imagine the situation ending up much worse: a rogue AI agent accidentally breaking some critical piece of web infrastructure, or stealing money from someone. The nightmare scenario for many AI researchers is a model “exfiltrating” itself – copying itself on to servers it controls, so that it can’t be shut down even if its bad behavior is eventually caught.

This week’s incident should serve as a wake-up call, forcing us to ask an uncomfortable question: should we really be building dangerous systems that we can’t control?

Liverpool primed for business: Bezos, Bhatia and the next steps at Anfield

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 19:31:54 GMT

Fenway Sports Group looks to be locked in talks with a consortium led by the son-in-law of Lakshmi Mittal, while the Amazon founder has now been linked

A consortium led by Amit Bhatia, the former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers and son-in-law of the Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, has opened talks with Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, over buying a significant stake in the club. Neither party has commented on the size of the stake or the investment amount being offered but it is believed to be a provisional offer of £1.35bn for about 30%. Discussions began three months ago but FSG insists the talks remain at a preliminary stage.

The reported offer values Liverpool at about £4.5bn. Manchester United were valued at slightly less when Sir Jim Ratcliffe bought an initial 25% stake in February 2024, increased to 27.7%, although the latest valuation of United by Forbes was $7.2bn (£5.38bn). Forbes, again, had Real Madrid as the most valuable club in the world at $9.5bn, with Barcelona in second place at $7.5bn. Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital acquired Chelsea for £4.25bn in May 2022 as a distressed asset sale after the Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich was sanctioned by the UK government.

First of all, £1.35bn for 30% of Liverpool would represent a healthy profit on a club it bought for £300m in 2010 and whose value has soared since. And the principal owner, John W Henry, is a venture capitalist, after all. But it is also true that FSG remains fiercely competitive and to continue challenging among an elite that includes oil-rich states necessitates ever more investment. That is why FSG has sought, and occasionally found, new investors before. The current talks are not considered part of an exit strategy by Liverpool’s owners but a potential opportunity to attract considerable funds while remaining in overall control. The company has parked plans to buy a second club – a decision that led to Michael Edwards’s recent departure as FSG’s chief executive of football – and last summer funded the biggest transfer outlay in Liverpool’s history of almost £450m. To maintain and improve those levels, having made only a modest profit of £8m when winning the Premier League title under Arne Slot in 2024-25, requires injecting fresh capital into the club.

Several times. In March 2021, FSG sold 10% of the company to RedBird Capital Partners for £543m. In 2022, FSG hired the investment banks Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley to seek out potential buyers for a 10% stake in Liverpool. No deal was done and Henry confirmed the following year that FSG was always open to new investment but not looking to sell the club. In 2023, FSG sold a reported 4% stake in Liverpool to Dynasty Equity, an American sports investment company, for £164m. That money was largely used to pay off debts incurred during the pandemic.

Bhatia, who stepped down as co-owner and director of QPR on Tuesday after 18 years, is believed to have secured financial backing from Mittal. The Mittal family wealth is estimated to be £23bn. Those riches pale in comparison, however, with another potential investor – Amazon’s founder, Jeff Bezos. The fourth-richest person in the world could afford to buy Liverpool outright and still have $250bn left in his back pocket. Bezos has been approached about joining the consortium but is reportedly undecided on whether to invest in a Premier League club for the first time. Bezos is no longer chief executive of Amazon but is executive chair of a company that has expanded from online retail into entertainment and sports rights, including for Premier League games, in recent years.

Even without Bezos on board, the consortium’s proposed offer would improve Liverpool’s capital considerably as the club begins a new era under Andoni Iraola. How much say and sway Bhatia and others would have over Liverpool’s football operations remains to be ironed out. With the FSG president, Mike Gordon, returning to a more prominent role at the club after Edwards’s exit, it seems unlikely that Liverpool’s owners would follow the Glazers’ example with Ratcliffe at Manchester United and grant a minority shareholder full control on the football side. Given talks are only at a preliminary stage, Liverpool’s transfer plans for this summer are not expected to be affected.

Talks continue until a deal is done or collapses. FSG’s willingness to confirm Bhatia’s bid in a statement to the Financial Times on Tuesday, and Bhatia’s departure from QPR that very same day, indicates negotiations are heading towards a successful conclusion.

Burnham stirs up political row with review of release plans for violent criminals

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 19:02:27 GMT

PM says he wants to ensure ‘everything has been looked at’ amid outrage at policy from family of PC Andrew Harper

Andy Burnham is immersed in a deepening political row after ordering a review of plans for the early release of thousands of killers, rapists and sex offenders from prison in September.

After the family of PC Andrew Harper expressed outrage that his killers may be eligible for release, the prime minister responded by pledging to make sure that “everything has been looked at again” before a fresh tranche of about 6,000 offenders were freed on tags.

But soon after Burnham’s comments, prison reform groups, government officials and politicians warned that abandoning measures to ease jail overcrowding could lead to the criminal justice system “collapsing under its own weight”.

Burnham has intervened quickly on policy issues just a few days into his premiership, including by indicating a possible increase in the personal allowance on income tax, which has been frozen since 2022.

Attempting to clear up confusion, he said there was no “commitment” to increase the allowance from £12,570 but the move would be considered at the budget, expected in the autumn.

“I want to answer questions honestly in this job, as I said before. I think that’s all about trust in politics and doing politics differently, and I’m determined to keep working in that way,” he said.

New sentencing laws were passed under Keir Starmer’s government to ease a looming prison overcrowding crisis that ministers said could seize up the criminal justice system in November.

Unlike previous emergency measures under which tens of thousands of prisoners were released in the early months of Starmer’s government, the Sentencing Act includes no exemptions for prisoners convicted of serious crimes, domestic abuse or terrorism.

PC Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but may be eligible for early release under the new Sentencing Act.

His widow, Lissie Harper, successfully campaigned for legal changes, called Harper’s Law, to bring in harsher sentences for the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty.

In a statement, she said: “When I fought for Harper’s Law, I was supported not only by the Conservative government of the day but by the Labour party too. They pledged to support our cause and agreed that those who kill emergency workers should face tougher sentences because some crimes are so grave they demand meaningful punishment.

“That cross-party support helped make Harper’s Law a reality. Today, it feels forgotten.”

Asked to respond to the Harper family’s comments, Burnham said he would examine the plans with the justice secretary, Alex Norris. “I will review the whole of this policy. We did not invest in the prison estate when we should as a country, going back a decade or so ago, when it was clear that there was going to be pressure. That has created an unacceptable situation now.

“But I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary. I can’t say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward,” he said.

Whitehall insiders have pointed out that any change in the early release scheme will contradict claims from the previous justice secretary, David Lammy, who told the Guardian this month that without it there could be “no capacity” across prisons in England and Wales in November.

One government official said: “There is very little wriggle room because it takes seven years to build a prison. Andy will need to get into the issues, but there are no easy choices because we will hit prison capacity by Christmas if he doesn’t do it.”

Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, urged caution. “This is a system that is on the verge of collapsing under its own weight. When originally introducing these proposals, Shabana Mahmood described the alternative as being the ‘total breakdown of law and order’.

“We need this government to finally grapple with the fact that, for 20 years, politicians have allowed sentence inflation to run rampant. With longer and longer sentences, we are sleepwalking our way into US-style mass incarceration.”

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said prisons must not be allowed to fill up again. “It should not be forgotten that the reason the Labour government put in place an early release scheme was to ensure there isn’t yet another prisons capacity crisis,” he said.

The former Conservative prisons minister Rory Stewart said: “Early release is not an easy choice – but it is the least bad option if we want to genuinely try to work intensively with prisoners and reduce reoffending.”Under the act, some serious offenders will be eligible for release halfway through their sentences rather than two-thirds of the way through. Those convicted of less serious crimes can be freed after serving a third of their sentence instead of 40%. Prisoners locked up for some violent or sexual offences are eligible for release halfway through their sentences rather than two-thirds.

The bill was drawn up and introduced to parliament by Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary. The Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, wrote on X that the “early release scheme allows rapists and serious criminals out of prison early and it must be urgently cancelled”.

He said releasing the jailed car passengers “is an insult to Andrew Harper’s memory and to police officers who put themselves at risk every day to protect us”.

Burnham’s pledge to review the policy was welcomed by groups working with victims. The former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips told the Guardian it was important that “proper systems” were put in place to assess risk and involve victims. “There is a chance to radically change how victims are considered in the system and to improve victims of violence against women and girls’ end-to-end experience of the justice system,” she said.

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England and Wales, said: “Obviously there are significant challenges facing our government, including how overcrowding and under-resourcing is going to be managed, but the solutions to these challenges cannot come at survivors’ expense.”

Katie Kempen, the chief executive at Victim Support, said the review was encouraging. “This review must urgently fix the fact that most victims currently have no way of knowing whether or not an offender could be released early. It is unacceptable that so many victims are being kept in the dark about this – that must change.”

Trossard, Ramos, Dumfries: 10 transfers you may have missed during the World Cup

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 19:00:22 GMT

Too engrossed with the World Cup drama to keep up with goings-on in the transfer market? We’ve got you covered

Announced just before England’s soul-sucking semi-final defeat by Argentina, it would have been easy to miss Trossard’s £15.3m move to Istanbul. While, after three and a half seasons and at the age of 31, it feels like his time at Arsenal has come to a natural conclusion, he will be remembered as a player who scored in clutch moments and, ultimately, played a crucial role in the club’s first league title in 22 years. Trossard departs after 174 appearances and 36 goals, a significant portion of which came from the bench in times of desperate need. He will be missed and deserves to be revered as one of the cult heroes of the Mikel Arteta era. Will Magee

Few players emerged from Germany’s World Cup campaign with any credit, but Brown’s energetic displays at left-back have earned him a move to Bayern Munich. Brown is a proud Bavarian, born in the town of Amberg and raised in Nürnberg’s youth academy. After two years at Eintracht Frankfurt and eight Germany caps, Brown has taken the quick route to his nation’s dominant club and could be a very useful addition. With Raphaël Guerreiro leaving and Alphonso Davies still recovering from injury, Vincent Kompany will benefit from Brown’s abilities as a natural left-back, after using a rotating cast of players to patch up Bayern’s defence last term. Niall McVeigh

The Netherlands right-back is often a force at major tournaments. He scored twice at Euro 2020, which earned him a move from PSV to Inter, and helped the Netherlands past the USA in the last 16 of the 2022 World Cup with a goal and two assists. In North America, the 30-year-old provided two assists – both against Sweden at the group stage – as the Netherlands reached the last 32. Following their exit to Morocco, Dumfries put pen to paper on a four-year deal at Real Madrid after his release clause at Inter was triggered – he joins Bernardo Silva and Ibrahima Konaté as freebie arrivals. A Hollywood move for a player named after Denzel Washington. Billy Munday

Announced just before the World Cup quarter-finals, the 22-year-old Brazilian striker​ arrived in Toulouse only last summer but did enough in a single Ligue 1 campaign to convince the newly promoted Premier League side to part with £24m. Standing 6ft 3in, Emersonn combines an old-fashioned target-man frame with the mobility to drift into wide areas​. Although his raw return of ​s​ix goals in ​2​7 league appearances suggests this is a transfer built on potential rather than proven output​, Gary O’Neil clearly sees shades of the modern Premier League No 9: aggressive, hard-running and capable of unsettling defenders even when the goals are not flowing. “He is a young striker with real ability and potential who has had plenty of interest this summer,” the manager said. Woman, 70, charged with murder of British expat Karen Carter in France

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 18:28:18 GMT

Public prosecutor for the region said suspect had been initially arrested shortly after the murder on 29 April last year

A 70-year-old woman has been charged with the murder of Karen Carter, the British expat found dead in south-western France last year.

The woman was charged on 2 July with Carter’s murder in Trémolat, in the Dordogne, and is “under judicial supervision”.

Jacques-Édouard Andrault, the public prosecutor for the region, is quoted as confirming the charge, adding the suspect had been arrested shortly after the murder on 29 April last year, but was released without charge at the time.

Andrault said: “On July 2nd, the investigating judge in Périgueux formally charged a woman with murder.”

He added that “this 70-year-old woman, originally from Trémolat, was taken into custody on April 30, 2025, during a preliminary investigation, before being released”.

“Since then, the investigations conducted as part of the judicial inquiry opened on May 7, 2025, have led the investigating judge to indict her,” he said, adding “this woman has been placed under judicial supervision”.

Carter, a 65-year-old British-South African national, ran two gites (holiday rental homes) in the village of Trémolat, a beautifully renovated 250-year-old farmhouse and neighbouring 18th-century stone barn collectively called Les Chouettes.

She was said to divide her time between the Dordogne and the home she shared with her husband, Alan Carter, in KuGompo City, South Africa.

An autopsy revealed that Carter died from severe blood loss after being stabbed multiple times, collapsing and dying next to her car.

Eight serious wounds were noted in total, including to the “chest, abdomen and forearm”, as well as “superficial ones on the thigh, shoulder and thumbs”.

Carter had been at a wine-tasting party at Cafe Village Trémolat, described on Facebook as “an association that wants to offer the people of Trémolat and the surrounding area a meeting place”, with about 15 other guests, including Eric Chassagne, the village’s mayor.

A few days after the attack a then 69-year-old local woman was arrested. She was released without charge shortly after.

It later emerged that Carter was discovered by a 75-year-old businessman, Jean-François Guerrier, with whom she was in a relationship. The nature of their relationship was seized upon and speculated over by tabloids.

Carter’s husband, a former London Stock Exchange worker who was in South Africa at the time of the murder, expressed his shock at the revelations that his wife had “started a relationship” with another man, saying he understood Guerrier was “just a friend of hers”.

London loses again: FTSE 100 landlord Segro will be missed

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 18:27:51 GMT

Doubly depressing takeover by a US buyer deprives the UK market of a property company that is genuinely different

For a few hours on Wednesday, it seemed possible we were about to witness a rare stock market event: a FTSE 100 company holding out against a hostile raider from the US and defying some of its own large shareholders to defend its independence.

Sadly, it didn’t happen. Segro, the FTSE 100 warehouse landlord known as Slough Estates for much of its corporate life, capitulated minutes before the deadline and said it was “minded to recommend” the “best and final” offer of £14bn, or £10.32 a share, from the US giant Prologis of San Francisco. The two sides now have until 12 August to hammer out a firm agreement.

The deal will be the biggest Footsie takeover so far in the current bid-heavy year. In a couple of ways, it will also be the most depressing.

First, because David Sleath, Segro’s long-serving chief executive, put up a decent fight and had the better of the arguments.

While most property transactions happen close to the book value of the assets (905p in this case), Sleath invited Segro’s shareholders to lie back, be patient and think of the growth opportunities in AI datacentres and big-box warehouses for online retailers and suchlike.

“A unique portfolio focused on Europe’s most supply-constrained markets,” went the argument. Segro cited an estimate from CBRE, the commercial property investment firm, of a near-£18bn valuation, or £13 a share, within a few years on a standalone basis thanks to a boost from datacentre expansion.

Prologis’s argument, in essence, was that such valuations were unrealistic because Segro lacks the financial muscle to make the most of the opportunities. Its pitch to shareholders was to take the money – or, rather, accept the terms of the share swap since the cash element of the offer, injected late in the day, is only 25%.

The 14% bid premium to the last asset valuation was enough to get some big Segro shareholders salivating. Led by Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, with an 8% stake in Segro, the calls for “engagement” had grown louder in recent days.

The tale is wearyingly familiar. Even when boards are up for a real scrap (which isn’t always the case), the dead hand of institutional money intervenes.

In this case, there is an added sense of what might have been because most of the investors calling for a deal also had holdings in Prologis, which has a $135bn (£101bn) market capitalisation. For those international investors with a foot in both camps, the quarrel over fair terms will almost have been a spreadsheet exercise in portfolio management. That doesn’t make a properly fair fight.

The second depressing feature is that, post-Segro, London’s real estate sector looks denuded. The company is the biggest listed commercial landlord by a distance and is genuinely different.

Here’s Panmure Liberum’s analyst Bjorn Zietsman in a recent note: “Segro is one of a small number of listed, pure play vehicles offering direct exposure to UK and European datacentre and logistics development.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

“If Segro is absorbed into Prologis, that exposure gets absorbed and the capital allocation decision behind it disappears. Investors lose the ability to choose UK/European datacentre and logistics growth specifically, and instead inherit whatever weighting Prologis’s management chooses to give the UK and Europe within a global platform spanning 20 countries and £200bn of combined assets under management.”

In other words, a small piece of diversity is lost from the London stock market, at least in the property sector. You’ll still find plenty of real estate investment trusts offering the usual bland mix of London office blocks and regional shopping centres, but multi-decade pan-European plays on AI datacentres are harder to come by.

Prologis’s promise to get a secondary listing in London is not a consolation: we know from experience that most of those add-on listings don’t last because trading in the shares inevitably gravitates to the US.

The loss of the company that began life as the Slough Trading Company in 1920 probably won’t register on UK political radars, but it ought to. This takeover is another entry in the hollowing-out of the UK stock market, which has become an easy hunting ground for overseas firms with richer valuations.

One would grumble less if the take-out prices were other-worldly. In Segro’s case, though, the terms look only so-so if one takes a long-term view. The outcome could have been different. This is (another) bad one to lose.

Tories ask HMRC to investigate whether Nigel Farage owes tax on £5m gift

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 18:27:13 GMT

Party chair queries status of funds Reform leader received from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne

The Conservatives have asked HMRC to investigate whether Nigel Farage should have paid tax on the £5m gift he received from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

The party chair, Kevin Hollinrake, wrote to the tax authorities questioning whether it was a payment to compensate him for running to be an MP.

Farage has said the gift was purely personal and unconditional, with a document drawn up to say it was given with no expectation in return.

He has also previously said the payment was to go towards his personal security costs, and a reward for campaigning for Brexit. He said it was no one’s business what he did with the money and that he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.

The Guardian, however, reported this month that three sources had said Farage informed senior Reform UK figures that he would require compensation of £1m per year to offset his loss of earnings if he were to run for office.

A Reform spokesperson said at the time that the Guardian’s report was “fake and wholly incorrect”. Lawyers for Harborne referred back to his previous statements about the gift, saying he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.

In light of that reporting, Hollinrake has written to HMRC asking it to investigate.

“If those reports are accurate, they raise legitimate questions as to whether the payment was truly a personal gift, or whether it was connected to Mr Farage resuming the leadership of Reform UK and standing for election to parliament,” he wrote.

“If the payment was connected to discussions about Mr Farage returning as leader of Reform UK, and standing for parliament with a view to becoming a member of parliament, there would appear to be a serious question as to whether it should properly be characterised as income rather than a gift.

“I believe it is imperative that HMRC examines whether the payment falls within the ‘disguised remuneration’ regime or otherwise constitutes taxable earnings arising from an office, employment or political position.

“If the payment was intended as a reward, inducement or compensation connected with Mr Farage’s roles within Reform UK, the tax treatment may be materially different from that applicable to a genuine personal gift and different to the tax status of a normal political donation (not that it was declared as such).”

The tax expert Dan Neidle has already raised questions around whether the £5m should have incurred tax after the Guardian’s reporting.

Reform UK has been approached for comment.

‘He knows what he’s doing’: Burnham’s off-the-cuff remarks inspire headlines and headaches

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:58:11 GMT

New PM’s conversational tone is markedly different to his predecessor’s, but carries risk of sowing confusion

Before he became Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham promised to “do politics differently”. Just three days into his time in Downing Street, that approach is already being put to the test.

In the last two days, the prime minister has been accused of performing U-turns over raising the income tax threshold, raising taxes for higher earners and freezing private sector rents.

The minor controversies are mostly a function of the fact Burnham has come into office with a rare combination of not having fixed his policy platform and a habit of speaking openly about his ideas before they are fully formed.

Earlier this week, for example, Burnham said that while he was campaigning in the Makerfield byelection which secured his return to parliament, he had heard more complaints about the income tax threshold than any other issue. This prompted speculation he would raise it once he became PM.

Reports on Tuesday suggested he had ruled it out, only for him to clarify on Wednesday that it was still an option. As he did, Burnham expressed surprise that people had put so much stock in his original comments.

“It’s funny these days you can’t answer a question honestly without then people reading everything else into it,” he told broadcasters. “I want to answer questions honestly in this job, as I said before. I think that’s all about trust in politics and doing politics differently, and I’m determined to keep working in that way.”

He added: “It’s just perhaps the way politics is these days and the way people report things, but that was an honest answer.”

A similar scenario played out over the issue of freezing private sector rents. Asked by reporters on Monday if such a move could be part of his package to tackle the UK’s cost of living crisis, he replied: “We’re looking at all of those things.”

On Wednesday, however, it was reported that officials were not actively considering such a move.

Burnham has also kickstarted an unexpected debate on releasing prisoners early, saying he would review the policy, which has been one of the government’s main tools for easing overcrowding in prisons.

“Andy appears to have just realised he is the prime minister,” said one Labour official. “He is a talented communicator and he is right that the media spins messages and this can be a hostile environment. But it is his job to go into that with his eyes wide open.

“He hasn’t fought an election or had much scrutiny, and so people are desperately trying to understand what his priorities and platforms are.”

For many, Burnham’s approach is a necessary response to the buttoned-up way in which his predecessor, Keir Starmer, used to speak and to the modern media environment which demands authenticity above discipline.

His open, conversational style worked well as Greater Manchester mayor, when reporters became used to his off-the-cuff comments during press conferences, and he seems determined to bring the same outlook to Downing Street.

“He’s not an idiot,” said Sean Kemp, who advised the former Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg and is now a partner at the political comms firm Hanbury Strategy. “He knows what he’s doing, but he doesn’t care, and he’s going to keep on saying it. And he’s done it so much now, I’m starting to think now that he’s decided this is just how he does things.”

The approach is also reflected in the media he uses to communicate. He has already shown his willingness to use mischievous social media posts to get his message across, and took part in an online question-and-answer session on Reddit shortly after winning the Makerfield byelection.

But the chances of being misunderstood were highlighted in another post-Makerfield interview, with the England footballer turned podcaster Gary Lineker. In comments that were interpreted by some as leaving the door open to a wealth tax and others as ruling it out, he said: “I do believe we need a greater sense of fairness and people feeling that things are being done in the right way and a fair way.

“But at the same time, you know, I don’t want to sort of be perceived as somebody who’s coming in with grudges and agendas and, you know, going to just immediately find or demonise one group or create a new way of dividing people.”

Burnham’s desire to bypass traditional political journalism is not new, say political communication experts. But it does carry risks.

“I think every single prime minister in the last 25 years has tried to do that,” said Kemp. “Then they realise that these are the people reporting day to day on what you are doing, and still, to a great extent, are setting the parameters of how you’re viewed.”

Guto Harri, who was once the communications director for the former prime minister Boris Johnson, said: “He’s not an ordinary person any more, he is the first lord of the Treasury and the prime minister of Britain.

“So if he says these things, it is reasonable for the people who hear him to think something will follow. And if something doesn’t follow, then people are likely to become cynical quite quickly.”

Mykhailo Drapatyi: Ukrainians hope new commander will end army’s ‘Soviet culture’

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:48:02 GMT

Drapatyi has long been a critic of the military’s command culture, but experts warn change could take time

Through a haze of smoke, a lone Ukrainian armoured vehicle suddenly burst into view. The BMP-2 accelerated towards a barricade of tyres and debris, smashing through it in seconds as protesters scattered.

Behind the controls, on the chaotic streets of Mariupol on 9 May 2014, was a little-known officer named Mykhailo Drapatyi. The footage became one of the defining images of Russia’s first attempt to seize eastern Ukraine, and made Drapatyi one of Ukraine’s military heroes.

Twelve years later, he has the top job.

On Tuesday night, the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, named the 43-year-old major general as the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces, putting him at the head of the military as Kyiv tries to shift the momentum of the war.

The appointment was one of the few wartime decisions in Ukraine to command near-universal support, reflecting Drapatyi’s high standing across the country’s political, military and civil society circles, and helping to steady the political mood after days of turmoil in Kyiv.

Days earlier, thousands of demonstrators had taken to the streets after the dismissal of the popular defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, who had clashed with the then commander-in-chief, Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi, over the conduct of the war.

Drapatyi’s appointment is likely to be welcomed by many of the protesters, particularly after Drapatyi publicly backed Fedorov in his dispute with Syrskyi.

“Society expected change,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at Ukraine’s National Institute for Strategic Studies. “It’s not only about changing how the war is fought or how the battlefield is managed. We also needed to restore confidence at home after the protests and return the focus to managing the war.”

Drapatyi belongs to a younger generation of Ukrainian commanders formed by more than a decade of fighting, and built his reputation on the frontline.

Supporters say he took up drone warfare early, and pushed authority down to junior officers and expected them to answer for their own decisions.

Perhaps more importantly for many Ukrainians, he represents a break with the Soviet-style command culture soldiers associated with Syrskyi, whom critics accused of relying on costly frontal assaults and spending soldiers’ lives too freely.

“[Drapatyi] is a critic of Soviet-style thinking and micromanagement, and he recognises the problems with lying inside the military,” said Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute.

Bielieskov described Drapatyi as “humane and open to dialogue” – qualities he said were unusual among Ukraine’s senior military leadership.

He said Drapatyi commanded respect among both career officers and those who joined the military after 2022, because he had risen through the ranks on merit and understood the realities of the battlefield.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Drapatyi’s military career began after graduating from the Kharkiv Institute of Tank Troops in 2004, when he joined the 72nd Mechanised Brigade.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Drapatyi helped halt the Russian advance towards Kryvyi Rih and played a key role in the liberation of Kherson. As Moscow regained the initiative, he was repeatedly dispatched to Ukraine’s most difficult sectors, stabilising the front around Pokrovsk before eventually being appointed commander of the joint forces.

Drapatyi has also been unusually outspoken about the need to reform the army’s internal culture. In a social media post last year, he criticised what he described as “an atmosphere of fear, lack of initiative, [and] imperviousness to feedback”, arguing that such attitudes undermined the military’s effectiveness.

After a Russian missile strike on a training ground killed dozens of soldiers under his command, Drapatyi publicly accepted responsibility and offered his resignation rather than shift the blame on to subordinates – a gesture that won him widespread admiration and reinforced his reputation as one of Ukraine’s most accountable commanders.

“President Zelenskyy made the best possible choice,” said the Ukrainian military analyst and veteran who writes under the pseudonym Tatarigami. “It will take time for changes to take effect. But I know many soldiers have renewed hope for change, and that is very important for morale.”

Analysts warn, however, that expectations may have run ahead of what the job allows.

Drapatyi is expected to improve battlefield management and the army’s day-to-day functioning. But many of Ukraine’s most pressing wartime challenges lay beyond the authority of any commander-in-chief, said Bielieskov.

Long-running tensions between the defence ministry and the general staff remained unresolved, while the politically fraught issue of mobilisation reform continued to weigh on the war effort, Bielieskov said. “There is a risk that in six months he will be blamed for problems he cannot fully control. Many of the biggest challenges facing Ukraine lie outside his mandate.”
