Anti-doping chiefs reject claims of Paul Seixas favouritism as Tour rivals cry foul

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:45:23 GMT

Home rider Seixas yet to be tested at night, unlike some rivals

Authorities deny French doping agency plays role in who is tested

Anti-doping authorities at the Tour de France have rejected accusations of preferential treatment towards Paul Seixas, the teenage French rider and home favourite who is placed fourth overall.

Seixas and his Decathlon CMA CGM team were tested, with the rest of the peloton, on Monday evening as part of the biological passport testing programme, but the 19-year-old has not yet been subjected to the nocturnal test that both the race leader Tadej Pogacar and the now-withdrawn Jonas Vingegaard underwent.

The Slovenian Matej Mohoric, who rides for the Bahrain Victorious team and was among those visited at 5am, said: “It would be good to guarantee equal treatment for everyone. After all, we know that this French rider [Seixas], who is well placed in the general classification, didn’t undergo that [night-time] test.”

The International Testing Agency denied suggestions of bias, saying: “The ITA is responsible for the strategy of the anti-doping programme for the Tour de France, not the AFLD [the French anti-doping agency]. We have our own sample collection personnel for the doping controls.

“AFLD might occasionally support the ITA with additional sample collection personnel, if needed, for instance during the testing mission on Monday evening but the decision who is tested when remains with the ITA.”

The ITA said: “Our decisions are based on facts, risk assessments, performances, scientific results and insights, intelligence and investigations, as well as data analysis. This approach enables us to act as precisely and impartially as possible, independently of any external influence, political interest or opinion.”

Professional cycling’s governing body, the UCI, has now fully endorsed the ITA’s night-time testing regime, but insists: “Carrying out such controls outside normal hours remains an exceptional measure, reserved for limited and justified circumstances.”

Mohoric said:

“I was tested at 5am myself. That’s practically the middle of the night, given that we go to bed around midnight because the stages finish late and we have breakfast around 10am.

“They have to prove they [the tests] are working and ensuring the sport remains clean and fair,” Mohoric said of the ITA. “We are paying the price for cycling’s past.”

On Wednesday afternoon, the UCI said that the ITA’s activities demonstrate that “the fight against doping is an absolute priority”, adding: “The UCI acknowledges that night-time testing can disrupt riders’ rest and recovery [but] these controls serve an overriding interest: the fight against doping.”

On Wednesday a rare breakaway move succeeded as Jasper Philipsen led home a reduced main peloton in the 175-kilometre 17th stage from Chambéry to Voiron.

In a fast and chaotic stage, in which multiple groups formed and reformed, the last man standing Jasper Stuyven was reeled in on the climb to La Commanderie, just 4km from the finish.

That set up a sprint finish and a first win in this year’s race for Philipsen, who was thwarted earlier in the Tour by Tim Merlier, who has now abandoned the race, and the Dutch sprinter Olav Kooij, teammate to Seixas.

But as Philipsen, the winner of the points classification in 2023, celebrated an 11th career Tour stage win, Adam Yates, a key member of the race leader Pogacar’s mountain support, was enduring a stomach bug at the back of the peloton.

The British rider crossed the finish line third from last, looking pale and exhausted, having been sick for the past 48 hours. “He looked terrible,” Pogacar said of his teammate during the time trial on Tuesday.

With three mountain-top finishes now coming, first at Orcières-Merlette and then the dreaded double stage finish at Alpe d’Huez, on Friday and Saturday, Yates would be expected to play a key role in the champion’s title defence.

“Today he looked much better, and was eating good,” Pogacar said, “but when you have a bad day like yesterday, you pay a day later. I hope he didn’t go too deep into the hole and he will be better tomorrow.”

Man killed in ICE ‘encounter’ was on vacation in US with tourist visa – reports

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:40:21 GMT

Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán ran into traffic and killed by semi after federal officials approached him at Florida gas station

The Mexican man who was hit and killed by a semi-truck in Florida when running away from federal immigration officials was vacationing in the US with a tourist visa, according to news reports this week.

The 28-year-old, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, was killed on 14 July after an “encounter” with federal officials, including those with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a state highway patrol spokesperson said last week.

After federal officials approached him and a group of four men at a gas station that Tuesday morning, they all took off running. The Florida highway patrol spokesperson said Coronilla ran into traffic and was hit by a semi-truck.

Coronilla’s death is one of the four ICE-related deaths that took place in less than one week. Two people, one in Texas and one in Maine, were shot and killed by ICE officers. And a fourth person died in ICE custody, while being transferred to an immigration detention center in Georgia. The four deaths have led to renewed calls by the public and lawmakers to rein in ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), as they carry out the Trump administration’s aggressive “mass deportation” campaign promise.

According to the Miami Herald, Coronilla, from the Mexican state of Guanajuato, had only been in Florida for two days when he died, having arrived in the US only three weeks prior. Coronilla had traveled to Atlanta at first to see family and friends and went to Florida to enjoy the beaches.

Coronilla’s wife, who flew to the US last week to make arrangements, had not heard from her husband and found out about his death while watching the news, a local immigrant rights group told the Miami Herald. She then contacted the group, Colectivo Arbol, to ask for help. The group said Coronilla left behind a seven-year-old son and seven-month-old daughter.

DHS has not publicly identified Coronilla, but the Associated Press confirmed his identity with a Mexican government official.

Although the Florida highway patrol’s statement said it was an ICE operation, a homeland security source familiar with the case told the Guardian last week that border patrol agents were involved in the incident.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and devolution: it takes a powerful centre to decentralise power

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:30:20 GMT

When it comes to driving an agenda from No 10, the prime minister seems to have learned important lessons from his predecessor’s failure

Before entering Downing Street, Andy Burnham cited the overcentralisation of power as a cause of Britain’s social and economic malaise. In his first week, the new prime minister has signalled his intent to bolster No 10 as an organ of executive power. The apparent contradiction – fortifying the centre to pursue an agenda of decentralisation – arises from a perversity in the way the British state works or, rather, fails to work.

The prime minister is right that too much policy has historically been directed from Whitehall. Reforms in recent years have created institutions with varying degrees of local autonomy – elected mayoralties like the one in Manchester that afforded Mr Burnham a platform for national prominence. But genuine control, especially when it comes to fiscal policy, has not matched the rhetoric of devolution. The Treasury is wary of facilitating profligacy in lower tiers of government. Heads of devolved administrations are also adept at claiming credit when things go well and, when they go badly, diverting the blame on to national government.

Meanwhile, the prime minister’s office is thinly resourced in comparison to equivalent institutions in similar democracies. Vital functions depend on a small number of special advisers, who are often too buffeted by crises to focus on strategic direction. A lack of focus in No 10 allows chancellors to monopolise economic policymaking.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, those systemic weaknesses were aggravated by his failure to set clear priorities. His Downing Street operation was directionless and ineffective. Mr Burnham looks reassuringly determined to correct that mistake. A notable appointment in his new cabinet is the elevation of Louise Haigh, a close ally, to the role of first secretary of state with responsibility for government coordination. She will be running the Cabinet Office as a department for enacting the will of the prime minister.

Ms Haigh has spoken of the need for a “proper beefed-up economic unit” in No 10, suggesting a rebalancing of power away from the Treasury. John Healey, the new chancellor, is a Whitehall veteran and no pushover when it comes to departmental turf wars, as his resignation as defence secretary from Sir Keir’s cabinet showed. But he is not a big beast of the species likely to build a power base to rival Mr Burnham.

The new prime minister has already asserted personal authority over economic policymaking by choosing a VAT cut on energy bills as his first emblematic act in office. His declared longer‑term intention to reconfigure Britain’s national political and economic model – an epoch-defining redistribution of power – will require a level of interdepartmental coordination for which there is not much recent precedent. The same applies to his ambition to build a “preventive state”, making smart strategic interventions early to avoid “paying for failure” down the line.

An early test will be whether Mr Burnham’s mooted No 10 North looks like a significant institutional innovation – a shift in the centre of national political gravity, not just a gesture of compensation for generations of southern bias. Mr Burnham will need to marshal the full authority of his office to drive change through systems that are prone to inertia, but the new prime minister seems to understand this challenge. He knows the paradox of devolution: that it takes a confident assertion of central power to give real power away.

The Guardian view on Chinese workers picking up the pen: poetry in motion

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:25:20 GMT

A food delivery rider has won the country’s highest literary award. It is part of a growing trend for writing by labourers

The hundreds of millions who have built modern China from the ground up – sweeping its streets, labouring in its factories and ferrying its goods – are often overlooked. But they refuse to go unheard. Last week, a food delivery rider won China’s top literary award. Wang Jibing, 56, first caught attention when a poem about his experiences went viral in 2022. The following year, Hu Anyan’s memoir, I Deliver Parcels in Beijing, became a bestseller.

In the early 20th century, Chinese intellectuals sought to capture the harsh realities of working-class lives. But it was under Mao Zedong that the idea of writing by as well as about the masses became reality, with labourers encouraged to take up the pen. In an era when the party tried to govern the language even of diaries and personal letters, the parameters of style and content were strict, and this enthusiasm swiftly diminished after Mao. But workers’ writing has seen a revival in the 21st century. This time, it is bottom-up rather than directed from above.

Maoist literature was meant to educate and mobilise the masses. Heavy labour was portrayed as offering a kind of transcendence, with workers becoming almost superhuman in their efforts. Contrast that with the testimony of the poet Xiao Hai, whose memoir, Adrift in the South, was published in English in May. Forced by family poverty to work on assembly lines from the age of 15, he writes of his “bitterness and regret … when I realise I let the best decade of my life slip away from me on the factory floor”.

The individual scrabble to get by has replaced paeans to collective toil, and the sense of hope has given way to numbness or despair. The image of the screw once represented workers’ pride in their small contribution to a greater cause. But in the poetry of Xu Lizhi, a Foxconn worker who killed himself in 2014, it reflects their insignificance and replaceability.

These accounts of exploitation and dangers, of bodies and souls ground down, may seem unsparing. But the Communist party has little tolerance for work that touches on topics such as the role of corrupt officials or collective organisation. Many grassroots writers post online, where their work can easily be deleted. The well‑known poet Zheng Xiaoqiong collected the stories of fellow labourers in Woman Worker, but it has never been issued in full because publishers demanded extensive changes.

The work of this new generation has drawn wider attention in the last few years. Fan Yusu’s essay on life as a migrant worker made her a literary sensation in 2017. In the pandemic, some began to notice the low-paid workers who were keeping the country running. A growing sense of precarity among the middle classes may have contributed. Labourers have been at the sharpest end of China’s breakneck development, but others share their concerns about the country’s path – and fear what happens if their status slips.

These narratives resonate with readers outside China too. They delineate the unsavoury underpinnings of the globalised economy and speak to the unease that many feel with it. I Deliver Parcels in Beijing has been sold to 16 countries; an English edition came out last year. In many places, there are still more books about workers than by them. Where is the English-language bestseller by an Amazon warehouse operative, or the viral poetry about care work on a zero-hours contract?

London Spirit’s new look, new squad and new ambition for the Hundred

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 17:09:21 GMT

When Jamie Overton reported to Lord’s last Friday for the start of the new Hundred season, he experienced something that, even in the often head-spinning world of franchise cricket, was extraordinary, potentially unique. Returning to a team he played for in 2025, he would have looked around the dressing room and seen none of his former teammates. He is the only survivor of the men’s squad from last year, part of a team that will be led by a new head coach, assisted by new coaches for batting, fielding, spin and pace bowling.

“It definitely does feel like a different competition this year, because every team is effectively different,” he says. “Oval Invincibles were the best side over the last three or four years, but that’s spread out a little bit now and every side you look at them and go: ‘Oh yeah, they’ve got a good team.’

“It’s going to be a tough competition, and I’m going to be biased, but I’m backing this squad. We’ve got a lot of firepower, a lot of wicket-taking potential and we’ve got a hell of a lot of experience. We’ve just got to go out and perform well.”

The Spirit women’s squad is twice as settled, in that among the playing group they have two veterans of 2025: Charlie Dean, who has taken over as permanent captain having stood in for the injured Heather Knight (now the general manager) in 2025; and Grace Harris. “It’s a little bit weird, but it’s not that bad,” Harris says.

“It’s only bad if you miss friends. I really enjoyed playing with Sarah Glenn [now at Southern Brave] and with Dani Gibson [now captaining Sunrisers Leeds]. I enjoyed playing with a few of the London Spirit girls that were around last season, but it’s not like they’ve completely gone missing. They’re going to be playing for other teams so we’ll still see them around.”

London Spirit are not one of the three Hundred sides who come into this season with a new name, but they do have a new logo, a new sponsor and a new kit made by a new kit producer. They have relatively new co-owners in the Tech Titans, the consortium of entrepreneurs who paid £144m for a 49% stake, a deal announced in January 2025 and completed last July, making them the competition’s most valuable franchise.

Andy Flower, the new men’s coach, says they will bring “renewed energy and perhaps a bit of pizzazz”, and also new ambitions: the women’s team has reached (and won) one of the five previous finals, but the men have come last or second-last in four years out of five and never been in the top two.

There is no reason, though, for them to be defined by results obtained by different people in a different era and Flower has won the Hundred, with Trent Rockets in 2022, as well as the past two Indian Premier League titles with Royal Challengers Bengaluru. He summarises his role, now that the squad has been assembled, as “looking to get people feeling as confident and clear as possible … to make them feel confident and clear and free to go and make decisions for themselves”.

As a young player Overton worked with Flower when he was the England Lions coach and the pair reunited more recently at Gulf Giants in the ILT20. “I’ve known him quite a long time and I know how he works,” Overton says.

“He’s very different now than he was, but franchise cricket is very different to younger players trying to play for England. You’re on a journey in that phase of your life, whereas in franchise cricket you probably know where you want to be.

“He’s developed, like all good people do. But he’s very direct in how he wants to play the game. He’ll do all the one percenters, find the small margins.”

SFA punishment means ban for start of new season

Derek McInnes, the new Rangers manager, is poised to begin the season in the stands after being handed a four-match ban for his comments on Celtic’s controversial penalty at Motherwell last season.

The then-Hearts manager described the VAR decision to give Celtic a stoppage-time spot-kick – which proved crucial in the Scottish Premiership title race – as “disgusting”. On Wednesday the Scottish Football Association announced McInnes would receive a four-match ban, with one game suspended until the end of the season.

McInnes watched Hearts beat Falkirk 3-0 in the penultimate game of the league season, which looked like they would have had to avoid a three-goal defeat at Parkhead on the final day to win the title for the first time since 1960. However, the scenario changed later that night when Celtic were awarded a penalty by the referee John Beaton – after an interjection by VAR Andrew Dallas – deep into added time at Fir Park.

Kelechi Iheanacho scored to secure a 3-2 win that meant Martin O’Neill’s side needed any victory at all on the final day to keep the title in the east end of Glasgow for the fifth successive time, which the Hoops clinched with another late winner.

Asked for his view of the penalty decision after beating Falkirk, McInnes described it as “disgusting” and he was charged with breaking rule 72 of the SFA disciplinary guidelines and issued with an official notice of complaint. A hearing at Hampden on Wednesday found the charge proven and McInnes was given a four-match suspension, with one match suspended until the end of the 2026-27 season.

Rangers begin their league season with an away game against Dundee United on Friday week. The suspension would mean McInnes is banned from the touchline for that game, as well as home matches against Hibernian and St Mirren.

Ex-Southern Water boss to face trial over allegedly manipulating sewage testing

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:54:09 GMT

Former CEO Matthew Wright and three other ex-employees named in criminal proceedings by Environment Agency

The former chief executive of Southern Water is being prosecuted for conspiracy to defraud along with three other former employees, over allegations they manipulated sewage wastewater testing results to avoid tens of millions of pounds in fines.

Matthew Wright is the first water industry boss to face a criminal charge over sewage discharges. He and three others are charged with conspiracy to defraud the Environment Agency and ​the water regulator, Ofwat, between 2012 and 2017 by ⁠creating artificial “no-flow” ​events ​at wastewater treatment ​works to ​influence ‌compliance checks.

The case focuses on operator self-monitoring, which was introduced to cut regulatory costs in 2009. The other former employees are Philip Barker, Clive Massey and Mark Gregory.

Operator self-monitoring allows water companies to monitor and test discharges from their wastewater treatment works, rather than the testing being carried out by an independent regulator.

Strict rules govern how samples must be taken to ensure their independence and accuracy. It is an offence if there is evidence that flows or data have been deliberately manipulated to avoid compliance checks.

Southern Water, which has more than 4 million customers, is also being charged with breaching environmental permits linked to the same conduct. Three further individuals are also being charged linked to failure to comply with environmental permits.

The charges come after a long investigation by the agency. An attempt by the defendants to remain anonymous was overruled by the high court.

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “We can confirm that we are taking criminal proceedings against Southern Water Services Ltd and a number of former employees.

“We take our responsibility to protect the environment very seriously and will always pursue and prosecute those alleged to have committed serious offending against the environment.”

In a judgment published on Wednesday, the ​high court rejected Wright’s argument that the EA lacked the power to prosecute him for conspiracy to defraud.

The ruling clears the way for the Environment Agency’s prosecution to proceed ahead of a criminal trial due to begin in September.

According to the judgment, the EA alleges that by the company’s own assessment, the scheme allowed it to avoid penalties of about £45m, but the regulator’s assessment put the figure higher.

Conspiracy to defraud carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment. The case will now proceed at Medway magistrates court.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said: “The public are rightly sick of environmental pollution and attempting to cover it up is outrageous. Anyone found guilty of this crime will face the full force of the law.

“This government will always back tough enforcement action to protect our rivers, lakes and seas. We have already committed to ending the practice of operator self-monitoring to ensure this cannot happen again in the future.”

The Falklands-Malvinas and fundamental rights

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:51:19 GMT

Jack Ford of the Falkland Islands legislative assembly says the Falkland Islands are British because that is the wish of the people who live there, in response to an article by Simon Jenkins. Plus letters from Marcelo Alberto Albarenque and Lucian Comoy

For several years, Simon Jenkins has written articles on the Falkland Islands and his view that it is inevitable that one day the sovereignty of the islands will be transferred to Argentina. His latest article is no different (‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’? Not quite – but the Falklands cannot remain British for ever, 16 July).

Jenkins’ arguments misrepresent our modern relationship with the UK – one that is based on self-determination, which is a fundamental right enjoyed by all people and enshrined in the UN charter. This has been the position of successive UK governments, including the present one, and enjoys strong cross-party support.

The Falkland Islands are British not because anyone in Whitehall says they are, but because that is the wish of the people who live on the islands, many of whom can trace their roots in the islands back 10 generations.

The islands are British for as long as Falkland Islanders wish, and in 2013, islanders made their position very clear when 99.8%, on a turnout of 92%, voted in favour of remaining a UK overseas territory.

If Jenkins were to visit the islands, he would see new houses, facilities and commercial premises being built. Critically, he would see a proud and confident people with their democratically elected government investing in the future – a growing population and a growing economy that is self-sufficient in all areas except defence, with resources being invested in protecting our unique environment.

To portray our relationship with the UK as one-sided and transactional could not be further from the truth. We enjoy a mutually beneficial relationship.

New economic developments in the Falklands are creating thousands of jobs and billions of pounds of investment in the UK, and the UK’s military presence in the islands is about far more than just defending the Falklands. It also provides a valuable training ground and protects wider UK interests in the region. Jack FordChair, Falkland Islands legislative assembly

As an Argentinian reader, having just finished Simon Jenkins’ piece, I welcome confirmation of something we already knew on this side of the Atlantic: there is good sense and goodwill on both sides of the ocean.

Mr Jenkins’ account of the 1970s leaseback talks is a useful reminder that real progress was made in a fruitful dialogue, before 1982 froze everything. Sadly, our own institutions allowed a dictator who had seized power by force to take a cause sacred to every Argentinian, regardless of age or politics, and sully it with a war that cost the blood of brave men from both our nations.

That freeze carries a cost that the UK rarely reckons with: it stops our two countries from building on the historic ties that bind us, alongside the differences that are just as historic. Consider the benefits we could reap together in investment, tourism, cultural exchange, scientific research, and food and energy security.

Argentina was, and is, home to Welsh, English, Scottish and Irish immigrant communities woven into our history. Indeed, there are more Argentinians of British descent on the mainland than there are people living in the Falklands-Malvinas. Our constitution guarantees the benefits of liberty “to all the men of the world who wish to dwell on Argentine soil”, and we are proud of that.

As Mr Jenkins rightly says: “Argentina’s claims are not going away.” Never. It is in our DNA. Marcelo Alberto AlbarenqueMaría Grande, Entre Ríos, Argentina

Thank goodness for a voice of reason. Of course, now that blood has been shed, it would be political suicide for any British politician even to hint at discussing sovereignty for a number of years yet. Both sides have been at fault with the islands, unscrupulously exploiting the issue to gain political capital. Until 1982, the islands and Patagonia were closely integrated. Of course Argentina was at fault for invading, but Britain’s vow to protect the islanders cost what it may stinks of self-righteousness: after all, it had considered ceding the islands prior to the invasion.

I have a foot in both camps – my wife is Argentinian – and I know that while the notion of Argentinian sovereignty is hammered home in the schools, the vast majority of the population couldn’t much care either way and would be happy to see this become a non-event, resolved in one way or another.

In Argentina, vox populi declares that the islands should be Argentinian, but that it is fully understandable the islanders should not wish to be governed in any way by whatever self-serving government head happens to be living in the Casa Rosada. They also suspect that the only reason Britain is being so stubborn over these faraway, windswept rocks is for money: there is oil there is fish. Lucian ComoySgonico, Trieste, Italy

Target ultra-processed food to reduce obesity in Britain

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:51:07 GMT

James Capon responds to an editorial on the health select committee’s call for radical action to regulate food markets

The MPs’ report mentioned in your editorial is welcome and overdue (The Guardian view on obesity: put public health before food industry pressure, 15 July). The health select committee is right to clarify that obesity is an engineered outcome, not a failure of willpower. But there’s a flaw running through decades of British food policy that risks being repeated: the “high in fat, salt or sugar” framework itself.

“High in fat, salt or sugar” combines three nutrients as though they carry equivalent blame. However, the evidence on weight gain and type 2 diabetes points to sugar and refined carbohydrates as the primary drivers, not fat. Salt matters, chiefly when combined with sugar, but the body needs salt to function. Fat matters because without it many fat-soluble vitamins will just pass through our bodies. We need no sugar at all.

The low-fat, calorie-controlled orthodoxy inherited from flawed nutritional science still shapes labelling, reformulation targets and public understanding, encouraging manufacturers to strip out fat and replace it with sweet-tasting substitutes, while ticking the “healthier” box.

To hold supermarkets and manufacturers to account, the target must be sharpened. The culprit is the ultra-processed food model itself: products engineered for shelf life, craveability and margin, using cheap sugar and refined starch as primary ingredients. Ice-cream or potato crisps sold on rare occasions are fine, but the food system that has made them the cheapest, most heavily advertised, most convenient choice is the problem.

We shouldn’t need to romanticise the Greggs sausage roll as some kind of national treasure. Consider it a treat, not a staple. That’s the shift in our relationship with ultra-processed food that this report should be pushing for – one built on carbohydrate and sugar reduction, not a blunt fat-and-salt panic that has already failed us. James CaponWaterloo, Belgium

AI agent went rogue and hacked startup by itself, OpenAI reveals

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:34:23 GMT

Company behind ChatGPT says agent ‘cheated’ an evaluation by attacking a Hugging Face database

OpenAI has revealed that an autonomous AI agent powered by its technology went rogue during a test, accessed the open web and hacked a prominent startup by itself in an “unprecedented incident”.

The company behind ChatGPT said the startup Hugging Face had detected and contained the agent – an AI tool designed to carry out tasks without human assistance – which had entered its systems.

“We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” OpenAI said.

The company said it expected this type of incident to become more commonplace as models – the technology that underpins AI tools such as chatbots and agents – become more capable. OpenAI said the hack occurred via an agent powered by a combination of its latest publicly available model, called GPT-5.6 Sol, and an even more capable model that was yet to be released.

While being tested internally on their hacking capabilities in an enclosed digital laboratory known as a sandbox, the models gained open internet access – effectively an escape route – by locating a vulnerability that had not been discovered before.

The agent then hacked Hugging Face, which is a database of AI models, to locate technology that would help it pass the hacking evaluation, having “inferred” that Hugging Face might have the models, datasets and solutions for passing the test. OpenAI said the models “successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation”. The attack ended when Hugging Face’s security team and its own AI agents spotted and stopped the rogue activity.

Hugging Face’s chief executive, Clément Delangue, said the attack was “mind-blowing” but believed there was “no malicious intent” from OpenAI.

“We suspected last week’s cyber-attack might have come from a frontier lab, given the sophistication of the agent,” he wrote on X.

When Hugging Face disclosed the hack last week it did not know OpenAI’s role in the incident, but said at the time that it had turned to a freely available Chinese AI model to analyse what had happened because the safety guardrails on commercial high-end models would not allow it to do so.

The term for an unknown IT flaw is a zero-day vulnerability because developers have zero minutes to fix the problem. In April OpenAI’s close rival Anthropic said its Mythos model had found thousands of these flaws.

The revelation of Mythos’s ability to locate and exploit zero-days led to the US government restricting exports of Mythos and its sister model, Fable 5, although it has since lifted the ban. GPT-5.6 Sol had similar restrictions but has since been rolled out worldwide.

METR, a non-profit organisation that measures AI performance, said last month that Sol’s cheating rate was higher than any public model it had evaluated before. It has also recorded 44 incidents in which AI agents “deliberately acted against their users’ intentions”.

The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISA) revealed in a blog post this week that one AI model it was evaluating, developed by an undisclosed tech firm, also went rogue and attempted to hack its testing systems. AISI said no damage had been done and it has since taken steps to make its systems more secure. It said models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic had all attempted to “cheat” during tests.

AISI warned that even more capable models may find cheating methods that are harder to detect and more damaging if they succeed, particularly in areas such as cybersecurity.

One cybersecurity expert said the Hugging Face incident showed the OpenAI agent had acted “like an actual real hacker” by, for instance, seeking out zero-day vulnerabilities and using stolen credentials to access Hugging Face’s systems.

“The AI thought that maybe Hugging Face would have important information around how to achieve its goal, which is a better score in a cybersecurity benchmark. In that sense, it acted like a real hacker,” said Nathaniel Jones, vice-president of security and AI strategy at the cybersecurity firm Darktrace. . “It had a goal put in front of it and it went to accomplish that goal.”

Greg Casar, a Democratic US congressman who has called for greater control of the AI sector, described the incident as alarming.

“AI is developing extremely fast with no real regulations to keep us safe,” he said in a statement calling for mandatory independent safety testing, mandatory disclosure of security incidents, and international cooperation “to keep people safe from absolute disaster”.

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:14:57 GMT

Up to 25 tonnes of nurdles, the raw material for plastic manufacturing, have spread further than initially feared

Approximately a billion tiny plastic nurdles have entered the River Tyne after a “devastating spill”, with the pellets thought to have spread much further than first thought.

Nurdles, which are usually 1mm-5mm in size, act as the raw material to manufacture most plastic products.

On Sunday, the Wind Orca ship collided with the berthed container ship BG Orange at the Port of Tyne, causing damage to a dockside crane and injuring one person.

The collision caused up to 25 tonnes of nurdles – about a billion in total, according to environmental charity Fidra – to enter the water, said South Tyneside council.

After nurdles were found washed up on South Shields beach, the council warned residents to avoid handling the pellets and to keep dogs on leads. The pellets themselves are not toxic. But once in the environment, they are almost impossible to remove and can absorb toxins present in the water.

Animals can easily mistake the nurdles for food. They have been found in the stomachs and digestive tracts of a variety of species, from seabirds in the North Sea and Australia to green turtles and fish off the coasts of Brazil.

The spill is less than 3 miles (4.8km) away from Marsden Bay, which is home to one of England’s most important seabird colonies.

One person who lives locally, Alistair Leadbetter, told the Guardian he was “really shocked” at how many nurdles he saw and said they covered the whole stretch of the South Shields beach. He said he saw children playing on the beach among the pellets.

Once nurdles are lost to the environment they can easily be washed, swept or blown vast distances and can accumulate on beaches worldwide. Last year, Fidra found plastic nurdles at 84% of UK sites of special scientific interest.

Fidra’s nurdle map, which tracks global nurdle pollution, indicates the pellets may have already spread much further than first thought, with sightings reported as far south as Sunderland, about 7 miles from South Shields.

HM Coastguard said it is supporting local authorities in the initial response to the pollution along the North Tyneside coastline, including at Tynemouth Longsands, Cullercoats and King Edward’s Bay.

Heather McFarlane, senior project manager at Fidra, said it is “devastating to see another plastic pellet spill”. She said most pellet pollution can be prevented with simple measures such as better packaging and safer stowage.

A spokesperson for South Tyneside council said it is now assessing the extent of the contamination and supporting efforts to remove pellets from affected areas where appropriate. “The council will look to recover the costs of the clean-up from the insurers of those responsible,” they said.

An Environment Agency spokesperson said its officers are “working with local authorities and other partners, providing expert advice to support in the early stages of the clean-up operation”.

The human fridge: is this really the best way to cool down in a ‘cruelly hot’ climate?

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:11:53 GMT

A ‘personal cooling booth’ that promises to chill you out in 10 minutes has launched in Japan, with its makers claiming it beats air-conditioning or a fan

Name: The human fridge.

Age: Brand new.

Appearance: A 2.1 metre-high (7ft) stainless-steel fridge for humans.

Aren’t all fridges for humans? I guess that’s right, but this one is to put humans into.

Oh, like a refrigerated mortuary cabinet? Yes, just like that, except you don’t have to be declared dead to use it.

It still sounds grim. Don’t knock it until you have tried it. The Do Hiemon “personal cooling booth” has launched in Japan and promises to chill your body completely in just 10 minutes.

How? You climb into it, it cools you down and then you leave.

Why does this thing exist? Why do you think? The world is on fire. We have spent this summer being pummelled by heatwave after heatwave. Records have been broken across Europe, and this week Japan logged its first “cruelly hot” (above 40C) day of the year.

What’s to be done? Well, we have two options. We can devote ourselves to achieving net zero as quickly as possible, because all the scientific evidence suggests that the longer we continue adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, the hotter the planet will become.

And the other option? Build a big fridge and hop inside.

It’s a compelling point. And a medically useful one too. The inside of the fridge is cooled to 15C, and a 5C jet of air is blown on to your head, neck, shoulders and back. The makers claim that it can ease the symptoms of heat exhaustion faster than air conditioning or a fan.

It sounds expensive and wasteful though. The fridge is said to cost just 7p an hour to run, which is about three times less than a toaster. But then it does sell for about £6,900 (1.5m yen).

I knew there would be a catch. But if you operate a warehouse or a factory where workers are routinely exposed to punishing heat, or you put one in a public place – like a vending machine for people who feel unwell – then it might save lives. Admit it, you want to try it.

I’m still not sold. It’s such a big investment. I’ll just stick to using the budget option – hiding between the milk trolleys in the supermarket. Your loss.

Do say: “They have built a fridge for humans.”

Don’t say: “Ooh, do a salad spinner for humans next.”

Commonwealth Games organisers will hope for a late surge in ticket sales as Glasgow prepares to stage the opening ceremony on Thursday night, with seats still available across a number of events at the four competition venues despite the significantly reduced scale.

The opening ceremony at the OVO Hydro still had adult tickets available on Wednesday, with prices ranging from £45 to £95. The 13,000-capacity arena will host live music, the parade of nations and the arrival of all 74 Commonwealth batons. The six-time Olympic cycling champion Sir Chris Hoy, who revealed in 2024 that he has stage-four cancer, will also take part.

Glasgow 2026 is a very different proposition from the city’s widely praised 2014 Games. The opening ceremony 12 years ago was at Celtic Park, where more than 40,000 people watched Queen Elizabeth II officially declare the Games open. This year’s event has been scaled back after the Australian state of Victoria withdrew as hosts over rising costs.

Only 500,000 tickets have been made available for the Games, less than half the 1.2 million for Glasgow 2014. Organisers have faced questions over demand, with reports suggesting ticket sales have been slower than expected and public interest more subdued than during the previous edition held in the city. Prices vary considerably across the programme: adult tickets for bowls and para bowls start from £10, while Friday’s swimming session featuring the three-time Olympic gold medallist Adam Peaty carries a starting price of £90.

This month, members of Scotland’s Tartan Army supporters’ club were offered free tickets for selected sessions, including athletics, para powerlifting, netball and 3x3 basketball. Organisers said the promotion was a gesture of thanks to fans who supported Scotland at the football World Cup.

Scotland will be led into the opening ceremony by the veteran lawn bowler Alex Marshall and the double Commonwealth judo champion Sarah Adlington. Marshall, 59, is Scotland’s most decorated Commonwealth athlete with five gold medals, plus a silver, while Adlington won gold on home soil in 2014 and at Birmingham 2022.

England’s flag bearers will be the lawn bowler Sian Honnor and the swimmer Luke Greenbank. The latter won relay gold in 2022, while the former claimed Commonwealth titles in Glasgow and Birmingham.

Cutting down on ultra-processed foods isn’t easy. Here are eight tips that worked for my family

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 16:00:19 GMT

Experts say reducing ultra-processed foods can be challenging in a world built around convenience, but these strategies can help make it more manageable

I have been trying to eat fewer ultra-processed foods with my family for five years, and it has been challenging.

Many experts agree that ultra-processed foods (UPF) pose health risks, whether because of unhealthy ingredients, links to disease and environmental impacts, or replacing more nutritious foods. Thus, some consumers – including me – are interested in removing them from their daily diet.

Getting here took time, effort and consistency, but we have had some success. Here are some strategies we used in our family.

Plant foods are some of the easiest, most plentiful substitutes for UPF. Most obvious are fruits and vegetables, but nuts, seeds, popcorn and roasted seaweed are other tasty, nutritious options.

When it comes to introducing fruits and vegetables, the six to 12-month age is crucial, says Kary Rappaport, pediatric occupational therapist and the executive director of Solid Starts, an organization that supports parents with feeding their children: “It is an exceedingly important window of time, when most babies are most developmentally open to a wide variety of foods and flavors.”

Introducing new foods to older children is similar: use small tastes, different preparations and a child’s natural curiosity, she says. Focus on describing the food, rather than whether the child likes it – for example, encourage them to lick or take a bite and notice qualities like sweetness or temperature. “It’s not a value judgment on the food,” she says.

Additionally, timing matters. “We are all more motivated to try and like things when we’re a little bit hungry,” says Rappaport. Try “putting out a tray of raw veggies with hummus while you’re cooking dinner, during that window where kids are looking to snack”, she suggests. On the other hand, don’t try to force a hangry child to try new veggies.

“Even when you don’t have great options that are fully non-UPF, incorporate vegetables and fruits and raw products as much as possible,” says Julia Wolfson, an associate professor in public health at Johns Hopkins University.

At our local farmers’ market, there is a stall selling fantastic apples. When in season, they are consistently crisp, sweet and apple-y. This is true for much of the food at the market.

“Whatever they have in your farmers’ market is what is seasonal, and what is seasonal is going to be better,” says chef Penny Stankiewicz. “If you go to a standard American grocery store and you buy a perfectly round, somewhat red tomato, it’s going to have absolutely no flavor in January. But in August, when it’s prime tomato season, you don’t have to even do anything to that tomato to make it amazing.”

Produce is typically more expensive at a farmer’s market, and not everyone has access to one. But the flavor payoff can be huge. Otherwise, try the produce at different grocery stores; additionally, frozen and canned produce is usually preserved at its peak. After you source your produce, learn the best ways to store it so it lasts as long as possible.

Part of my motivation to minimize UPF was not wanting to support powerful corporations that exploited workers, mistreated animals and harmed ecosystems. The more I learned about food systems, the less I wanted to participate in them as a consumer.

Teaching children where food comes from and how to prepare it builds appreciation and understanding. Rappaport also suggests discussing how foods make their bodies feel: for instance, “if I eat too many gummy worms or I only eat a bag of Flamin’ Hot Cheetos on our car trip, I’m going to feel bad. It’s not gonna sit well in my belly.”

Familiarize yourself and your family with the definition of UPF, so that you can identify one by looking at an ingredient list, says Wolfson.

I already knew how to cook, but I studied the science of cooking as we embarked on this project. Now, my from-scratch meals taste better than before, sometimes more so than UPF alternatives.

Often the barriers to cooking are systemic: insufficient time and energy to cook. People may also lack confidence in their kitchen skills. “We need to make it easier for people to cook healthy meals from scratch, and that means making those scratch ingredients more available and affordable, and building those skills from a young age so that people have the confidence and self-efficacy,” says Wolfson.

Stankiewicz offers the following tips for newer home cooks:

Learn techniques: “Once you know how to saute, it doesn’t matter what you put in the pan.”

Develop knife skills: “If people want to get more comfortable in the kitchen, they should take a knife skills class. Those skills are a massive upscale for confidence in the kitchen.”

Know your taste: “Know what you like, then create that, because that’s the starting place. Don’t start by making miso brownies when the core is to make a really good brownie that you like, because then you’ll do it again.”

Wolfson found in her research that “when people cook more at home, they consume fewer ultra-processed foods.” She notes that even when people are cooking frequently, the majority of their calories often still come from UPF. Try not to feel defeated if you notice something similar; this speaks to the ubiquity of UPF, she says: “If you picture a typical American grocery store, almost 70% of the foods in the store are ultra processed … that’s what’s mostly available to us.”

after newsletter promotion

In terms of replacing UPF, replacing desserts and snacks was an easy sell. I wasn’t replacing cookies with carrot sticks; I was replacing them with cookies – sometimes better ones.

Stankiewicz says to approach baking with fearlessness. “Messing up is part of it and is really how you learn,” she says, telling me that brownies were created by accident when a baker didn’t add enough flour to the cake.

The next step is to find trusted recipe sources. Start with recipes that are not overly intimidating or complicated. Read the recipe through before beginning, then gather the ingredients. Organize the ingredients (mise-en-place) – and then just do it!

Consuming UPF is easy. It takes very little time and mental capacity to, say, unwrap and heat something. Try to make cooking and baking at home similarly easy.

First, master a few dishes. “Find a handful of recipes or techniques that are accessible in terms of ingredients, cost, number of ingredients, and how long they’re going to take to make. Then just get really good at those,” says Stankiewicz.

Second, build a pantry. Keep a stock of frequently used ingredients. My husband and I maintain a shared shopping list, and if we notice something running low, we update the list.

Third, make more than you need. Leftovers are great. Even better are meals that can be frozen and reheated because your past self did all the work.

We have a rule at the table: no phones or toys during mealtimes. We have conversations instead (often mundane and not terribly deep). Our meals aren’t long; they usually take 20 minutes from when we sit down to when my youngest is done.

“The research is really clear that family meals, where people are eating together, have a huge positive impact on child development across many different areas in terms of school performance, mental health and social engagement,” says Rappaport.

It can be difficult when schedules are varied. Rappaport has older children and strives to fit in three dinners together each week around work and extracurriculars. It’s less about “having a Norman Rockwell meal at the dinner table” than finding opportunities to engage, she says. “It can be burritos that we got for takeout while we’re all sitting at the park waiting for practice to start. I can still find those same benefits, which are that I’m asking about their day. I’m showing interest in them. We are connecting around the food.”

We have not completely eliminated UPF. But for the most part, I try to cook, choose whole food items and purchase better-quality ingredients. Over five years and thousands of decisions, our palates have shifted to prefer non-UPF foods. Cooking and baking have become routine. When you reach the stage where UPF is no longer desirable taste-wise, and regular cooking is as habitual as brushing your teeth, opting out of UPF becomes less daunting.

Without fail, every expert I spoke with emphasized the structural factors that make it difficult for consumers to reduce UPF consumption. Their prevalence, coupled with time and cost pressures mean that UPF often makes the most sense. There will be unexpected work emergencies or illnesses that make cooking from scratch impossible. Some days are full of extracurriculars and social events, and you won’t have time to bake or cook. You may attend catered events, meetings or functions where you have no control over the food.

The vast majority of us will eat at least some UPF. Your children will eat UPF – especially at birthday parties and play dates. But that’s not failure, just reality. Being realistic about your options can help you stay consistent instead of giving up entirely, and that’s ultimately what got me and my family to this point. When it comes to UPF consumption, don’t let perfect become the enemy of good.

Funding bus fare cap from aid budget will hit world’s poorest, Burnham told

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 15:47:10 GMT

Proposal ‘throws global south countries under the bus’, says ActionAid UK director

Burnham announces bus fares to be capped at £2

The world’s most vulnerable people will be put at risk by Andy Burnham’s decision to use the aid budget to pay for cheaper bus fares in England, charities have said.

The prime minister announced on Wednesday that he would reduce the fare cap from £3 a journey to £2 next year, funded mainly by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

The switch allows the government to borrow more against those loans without violating its borrowing rules. But some experts say it will also leave people in the poorest parts of the world more vulnerable to the effects of the climate crisis.

It comes after the government indicated the new aid minister, Kirsty McNeill, would not attend cabinet as her immediate predecessors had done, causing concerns it was downgrading its commitment to international development.

Joanne O’Neill, the co-director of advocacy at ActionAid UK, said: “The prime minister’s fare cap scheme is a welcome initiative but his funding proposal throws global south countries under the bus, penalising those most impacted by a climate crisis they did not create.”

She added: “Delivering international climate finance as loans instead of grants pushes countries deeper into debt and forces them to divert funding away from essential public services such as education, health and social protection – which disproportionately impacts women and girls.”

Monica Harding, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for international development, said Burnham’s decision would “further undermine the UK’s standing as a reliable global partner”. She said: “Swapping crucial climate grants for loans will ultimately fall on the backs of the world’s poorest, racking developing nations with more destabilising debt. This will only harm Britain’s security in the long run, fuelling more migration and instability abroad.”

Romilly Greenhill, the chief executive of Bond, which represents aid organisations, said: “It is disappointing that the new prime minister is picking up where the previous one left off, by continuing to raid the diminished UK aid budget to prop up much-needed funding for the cost of living crisis here in the UK.

“The cost of living crisis in the UK needs to be urgently addressed, but robbing Peter to pay Paul is not the answer and pitches marginalised communities here in the UK against marginalised communities in lower income and climate-vulnerable countries.”

Other analysts disagree, pointing out that a number of major donors use loans to track climate finance, ensure it is well spent, and develop an ongoing relationship with the recipient country. Many multilateral organisations, including the World Bank, already provide the vast majority of climate finance as loans rather than grants.

Burnham made the bus fare cap his second major policy announcement in office, a day after he said he would cut VAT on electricity bills.

During a visit to Bath, the prime minister said the move would “really help people with the cost of living pressures they’re facing”. He added: “It’s there for the whole of 2027, and I think it will put money in people’s pockets.”

Downing Street said on Wednesday the cap would cost more than £500m next year, £400m of it funded by switching international climate investment to loans.

Officials said the switch would enable the money to go to international financing schemes such as the Tropical Forests Forever Facility, an anti-deforestation initiative set up last year by the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Changing donations to loans, however, means money is likely to go to countries that can repay them – which are more likely to be middle-income countries such as India or Brazil than some of the world’s poorest.

The switch could reduce the amount of money the UK gives as international aid, which the previous government promised would stay at 0.3% of national income after cutting it in half to pay for more defence spending.

Though loans can count towards overseas development spending, that will depend on the terms on which they are given. Only loans given at a significant discount to market rates will count.

Experts say some of the money is likely to have been allocated already, leaving ministers having to renege on agreed donations.

Development strategy experts criticised the government’s decision to bar the new aid minister from attending cabinet.

Andrew Mitchell, the former Conservative development secretary, said: “It’s a blow to the sector that the PM has not seen fit to put Kirsty McNeill – who knows a great deal about international development – into the cabinet, let alone attending cabinet.

“As I well know from having done the job as a full member of the cabinet and as a member attending cabinet, it would give her more clout at home in Whitehall battles and overseas.”

Sam Rushworth, a Labour MP and member of the international development committee, said: “I hope Andy Burnham will consider bringing this role back into cabinet, where it used to be, to give it the prominence it deserves and ensure cross-ministry working.”

A government spokesperson said: “We are committed to spending 0.3% GNI on official development assistance. International climate finance supports a range of projects such as protecting forests and development of clean power.

“Switching a small proportion of that spending from grants to loans give us more flexible ways to tackle the climate crisis while making the best use of taxpayers’ money.”

Lobbying giant filmed offering reporter payment for flattering client coverage in national press

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 15:42:55 GMT

Exclusive: Guardian investigation of CT Group uncovers practice that appears to seek hidden influence over public opinion

A political lobbying firm founded by the former electoral strategist for David Cameron and Boris Johnson secretly pays journalists to write pieces for British newspapers that are favourable to its clients, a Guardian investigation can reveal.

In a practice that appears to create a backdoor for private companies to influence public opinion, lobbyists for CT Group – co-founded by the campaign strategist Lynton Crosby – told an undercover reporter they had paid journalists to place apparently independent stories in newspapers.

They offered hundreds of pounds in cash incentives to do so for a property industry client and said the deal would grant the lobbying firm increased editorial control.

The Guardian began investigating the arrangements after Gavin Stollar, the head of CT’s real estate division, approached a freelance journalist and offered to pay him to pitch a piece to a British national newspaper about problems caused for the housebuilding industry by the Building Safety Regulator, set up in the wake of the Grenfell Tower fire that killed 72 people.

Stollar hoped the journalist would write about the human consequences of the UK’s housing shortage and suggest the regulator was making the situation worse. Stollar, a Liberal Democrat activist who was awarded an OBE in 2024, said CT Group would help with research and provide human case studies of people affected by the housing shortage.

Stollar led the journalist to understand that while they would be paid by the newspaper for apparently independent reporting, they would also be paid by CT Group, which has property industry clients.

Other CT Group staffers then proposed the freelance journalist could be paid to write stories for newspapers as part of its work for a leading property guardianship company, Live-in Guardians. One said: “You can do it either way. We don’t have to pay you, and you just go off and do how you normally do. Or, we can pay you, but we get more control over it.” They then offered him “£100 for every story that is successfully published (national or trade)”.

In meetings with the reporter, the CT Group employees proposed he chair a roundtable for the company for £500 and pitch pieces to national and trade papers that would support the guardianship sector – which sometimes has a reputation for low quality housing with few protections for residents. One suggestion was to write “a call to action from the industry for [Andy] Burnham to be smart about this”.

They said they did not want pieces to appear like advertorials – which are transparently signposted paid-for editorial pieces – “but clearly we’d like you to keep our client’s messaging and overall objective in mind”.

In a statement, CT Group said the events had been “deliberately mischaracterised”. It said it did not engage the undercover journalist to do anything and did not pay him anything.

CT Group is a £40m-a-year turnover lobbying company whose recent clients include Airbus Defence and Space, the tobacco company Philip Morris and the owner of the football club Manchester City. It has a global workforce of 150 staff and describes having achieved results for clients “on corporate issues, general elections, reputational transformation and legislative reform”.

It is part of an industry of public affairs and political consulting firms facing growing scrutiny after Peter Mandelson’s dual role as an owner of the lobbying company Global Counsel while he served as British ambassador to Washington. Last week the Ethics and Integrity Commission demanded new laws to improve transparency after a review ordered by Keir Starmer.

The investigation spanned more than four months and involved discussions in person, on video conference calls, and over email, that touched on placing stories in newspapers including the Financial Times and the Guardian.

When the undercover reporter said he would feel “discomfort” at “being paid to write something with the newspaper not knowing”, one lobbyist said: “I completely understand that, but I also think if you were to tell [the editor] ‘CT has commissioned me to do this’, she would instantly bat it out of the room. She wouldn’t … I think you’d be hard pressed to find an editor who [would].”

During the same meeting the journalist noted he would ordinarily be paid by a publication, asking: “Is there a sort of financial arrangement with CT Group as well?”

“Yeah,” a CT manager replied. “Historically, yeah.”

In a subsequent call, another lobbyist said CT Group had since worked with a journalist “where I paid her to do a certain piece, a certain national piece”, but the journalist “never discloses to editors where she gets her sources from”. They described the financial arrangement with this unnamed journalist as “a retainer”.

In a statement, CT Group said: “We do not comment publicly on work we do for clients and we therefore cannot respond to the specific allegations you have made.” It said the events had been “deliberately mischaracterised” and said it did not engage the undercover journalist to do anything and did not pay him anything. It said the journalist was looking for work and “chased us relentlessly over a period of more than six months”.

“We are happy to confirm, however, that we never ask journalists to behave otherwise than in accordance with their professional and ethical standards, and we trust journalists to conduct themselves by reference to those standards,” it said. “We note it is commonplace for journalists to chair or participate in roundtable and similar events, and to provide other media services to their clients, and we support the right of journalists to do so.”

The lobbyists delegated to speak to the journalist did not always seem comfortable with paying to place stories. One, who had recently joined, said it seemed “a bit weird to me”, but she said if a payment was made, CT Group would need to see the story before it was submitted to a national newspaper “because you’re paying them to achieve an outcome of a piece”.

Asked about the input CT Group would have over his story, another said: “The commercial relationship very much varies, there’s no sort of set formula about it. It’s not like this is how we always operate … it’s a project by project, piece by piece, sort of system.”

Referring to the payment offer, he said “we can 100% take that off the table”. They said: “I can understand you being like, no, I don’t want to work in that way. That’s completely fair. And so happy for this to be a sort of much more traditional relationship.”

CT Group publishes a code of conduct that states that “ethical and professional behaviour is at the heart of CT Group’s business, and those values should be followed at all times”. It says “we never do anything we cannot justify publicly”.

The Guardian’s code of practice requires journalists to tell a senior editor of “any attempts to induce favourable editorial treatment through the offer of gifts or favours”, while the FT’s code of conduct states that “no one at the FT should abuse their position for personal profit”.

In a discussion about how he would pitch a piece to the FT or the Guardian, the undercover journalist asked if he would tell the newspaper he was working with CT Group or pitch it as his own story. “I think you’d pitch it in like that,” one of the CT staff members replied.

“So they wouldn’t necessarily know that it kind of had a CT group angle?” the reporter asked.

“No, I don’t think so,” they said. “No, I don’t think they need to. We can help you flesh out the angle and stuff to take to the editor and make sure you’ve got the case studies and stuff. But I don’t think, no, I don’t think … we kind of sit behind that.”

Live-in Guardians was approached for comment.

Austria opens police station at Hitler birthplace to deter neo-Nazi tourists

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 15:05:04 GMT

It is hoped opening of unit tackling narcotics trafficking will deter people from visiting it as pilgrimage site

Austria has opened a police station in the birthplace of Adolf Hitler in an attempt to “neutralise” its toxic legacy, after years of debate over how to stop neo-Nazis visiting it as a pilgrimage site.

Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in a rented flat in the centre of Braunau am Inn and spent the first weeks of his life there.

Now the building will be the workplace of a police unit specialised in tackling narcotics trafficking, with the new occupants meant to put off Nazi displays, which are illegal under Austrian law.

Given the community’s proximity to the German border, it is on a key drugs running route, according to district police commander Stefan Haslberger.

The conversion, whose estimated cost reached €20m, followed an intense public discussion about how to deter today’s fascists from using the site as a shrine.

News agency APA reported that even construction rubble from the remodelling had been disposed of in a secret location to avoid it becoming a gathering place for Hitler devotees.

At the opening ceremony, the Austrian interior minister, Gerhard Karner, called it a “new chapter” in which the building would be a “place of democracy, the rule of law, security”. At the same time, he said, “memory will not disappear”.

In recent years skinheads laid roses and wreaths for the Nazi leader’s birthday before the elegant building’s ochre facade, while extremists and drunken revellers posed for pictures doing the straight-armed Hitler salute.

Local people, fed up with such stunts, often call the former residence the “house of evil”.

An expert commission tasked with determining a future for the building had recommended a “use for social or charitable, or for official or administrative purposes”.

It said a museum on the site could continue to draw rightwing extremists, especially those whose “blood and soil” ideology particularly reveres birthplaces and gravesites. Demolition, on the other hand, would obfuscate an important chapter of local history.

Polls showed a majority of Austrians preferred it to become a centre for promoting democracy.

The building, parts of which stem from the 1600s, hosted an inn and brewery with flats on the upper floors, one of which was briefly occupied by the Hitler family.

A decade ago, the Austrian government agreed to take over ownership from a private proprietor, who had previously rented it out to the interior ministry, which used it as a care home for people with disabilities.

It stood empty from 2011, with a small memorial stone outside taken from the former Mauthausen concentration camp whose inscription only hinted at its problematic past: “For peace, freedom and democracy. Never again fascism. The millions who died serve as a warning.”

German news magazine Der Spiegel reported recently that hackers had replaced the building’s proper address on Google Maps with the street number 88 – neo-Nazis code for Heil Hitler based on the eighth letter of the alphabet.

The government said it hoped the opening of the police station would foster the “neutralisation of the whole place” and repel Hitler admirers.

Hitler’s private apartment as Nazi leader on Munich’s Prinzregentenplatz has served as a police station since the late 1940s while his official residence in Berlin’s Reichskanzlei was destroyed by bombing during the second world war.

Germany under Hitler annexed Austria in 1938, a fact that historians say led many in the country to long dismiss its shared responsibility for the Holocaust and other Nazi crimes.

The far-right Freedom party (FPÖ), which was founded by former Nazis, won the most votes in an Austrian general election for the first time since the war in September 2024 but was unable to take power because mainstream parties refused to form a coalition with it.

Since then, support for the FPÖ had continued to rise.

From posh egg cups to secondhand lamps: 22 cheap ways to make your home look more expensive

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 14:00:17 GMT

Good taste doesn’t have to cost a fortune. Whether it’s designer-looking cutlery or affordable art, these clever buys start from £2 – but punch well above their price tag

You don’t need the budget of a boutique hotel to make your home look a bit more pulled together. It’s all down to knowing where to look, picking a few well-made objects, choosing good-quality fabrics and materials, and spotting timeless classics (or designs inspired by them) that won’t date too quickly.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Here are some tricks, hidden gems and affordable-but-stylish finds, from egg cups to art, that will elevate your space – and prove good taste and quality needn’t cost the earth.

Easy chair cover

I recently bought an inexpensive Ikea armchair that looked a bit Identikit. So I added a made-to-order cover. This swirly pattern from Bemz spoke to me – and I am now the proud owner of an armchair that looks more Architectural Digest than aisle 78.

Hay Common Oblong rice paper shade

Akari has been following traditional methods since the 1950s to make beautiful rice paper lamps that are rightfully a modern classic. If you can’t afford one, tasteful Danish design brand Hay has some beautiful options, adding serenity to even the most hectic home for a sixth of the price.

Geraniums

Geraniums and pelargoniums exude the sort of taste vibes you’d find in Charleston House. Plus, they’re hardy, perennial, easy to grow (I managed to keep them alive and flowering for an unusually long time), and they look great in any old terracotta plant pot. Just make sure to pop them on a sunny windowsill – according to the RHS they need “full light but shade from scorching midday sun”.

Blue spot bowl

Choose your hero pieces wisely – by which I mean that the things that will be out on display should look nice to you. This 25cm-diameter fruit bowl, from a Polish ceramics shop in Lewes, features an elegant polka-dot design that won’t age – and there are plenty of lovely dishes and custard jugs where that came from.

Steve Camps fine art print

If you’re a fan of the bluey-grey maritime-themed works of Cornish painter Alfred Wallis but can’t afford their £30,000+ price tag, perhaps you could stretch to £46 + postage? Steve Camps, a retired builder from Cornwall, is an artist who sells high-quality prints of his nautical-themed art on Not Another Bill. Your home will look like Kettle’s Yard in no time.

Stainless steel egg cup

These stainless steel egg cups might seem like a piffling little thing, but anything that adds design wattage to a basic is a win. These wouldn’t look out of place at Service Projects, the home of chic tableware and (for me) many lost hours.

Marbled paper

There’s something unnerving about seeing the same affordable art you have on your walls in the backgrounds of numerous other people’s interiors on Instagram. This beautifully marbled handmade paper is an alternative approach – just add a frame, and you have a piece of abstract art that probably isn’t also hanging next door.

Reclaimed Jaisalmer sandstone bowls, each

I hope it doesn’t detract from the craftsmanship of these handmade sandstone bowls to suggest they’d look lovely filled with easy peelers. No two are the same. Available via a reclamation yard based in Herefordshire, but also available online.

Stripe hand towel

The impeccably tasteful Danish company Tekla makes undeniably good-quality striped towels in beautiful colours. But they’re not cheap. So while you’re waiting for your Isa to mature, these designs from John Lewis, especially the dove grey stripe, should elevate your bathroom.

Twisted candles

Wax candles in sweet-shop pastels and quirky patterns have become a major (and often pricey) trend in recent years, but these more muted moss-green twirly ones from Danish chain Søstrene Grene are a more timeless way to add class to your dinner table.

Made in Yorkshire and hand-cut and finished, this cosy blanket wouldn’t look out of place in even the fanciest homes of Harrogate. The fact it’s wool-blend, and not pure wool, keeps the price down, but the look of it transcends its price tag.

Blue leaf dinner set, 12 pieces

If you’re after a dinner set that channels Finland’s heritage ceramics company, Arabia, then look no further. This Habitat design is straight out of Tove Jansson’s summer house, and the whole thing costs far less than a one-way ticket to Helsinki.

Three-tier coffee shelves

I’m seeing a lot of love online for coffee stations – yet another way to glorify your morning cup of joe. But if worktop space is limited, this set of shelves is a great place to house your mugs, beans and other coffee paraphernalia. It’s made in the UK, from reclaimed wood.

Stainless steel cutlery set with resin handles

Made from resin and stainless steel, this cutlery set – more David Mellor than Mango – will instantly zhoosh up your table. I love the emerald green and mustard yellow options.

Vintage alabaster lamp

If an alabaster sculpture doesn’t fit your price tag – or the look of your one-bed – but you like the vibe of the soft, cool stone, secondhand sites offer an Uffizi’s worth of alabaster lamps. Wall-mounted candle sconce

Wall-mounting a candle sconce instantly brings calm to a space (which is a sentence I never thought I’d type). Le Provendi rotating soap holder and soap

I love the idea of a wall-mounted soap, known in France as the porte-savon écolier. The classic design is the work of French company Laboratoire Provendi, which has been making soap since the 1950s, and it keeps soap clean, dry and always on hand. This one, the original French school soap holder, will make your house feel like it’s passed its baccalaureate.

Silver candlestick holder

There’s something sculptural and Scandinavian about this curved candlestick holder, and not just because it’s from Ikea. Its design belies its mass-manufactured origins and with the right candle (see above) could bring a little Nordic minimalism to your home.

Striped Irish linen fabric for napkins

Do you find yourself lusting after the kind of napkins available at fancy shops for £16, but can’t bring yourself to spend that much on something you’re just going to wipe your hands on? Consider buying linen fabric and either knocking some out yourself (this tutorial might help), or seeing if an affordable, local seamster would. It’s an easy enough job, and your dinner table and bank balance will thank you for it.

Red dining chairs, pair

These scarlet dining chairs look a little Josef Frank, but at a fraction of the price. Pair with whatever other chairs you have: there’s nothing wrong with mismatched.

Hand-painted lampshade

Nearly £100 is not nothing for a lampshade, but I’ve been ogling these handmade lampshades by artist Cressida Bell ever since I first set eyes on them. This vivid green oak leaf print with gold highlights has Bloomsbury set written all over it – and there are tropical, topiary-inspired and geometric prints available, too.

Checkered washed cotton tablecloth

Made from 100% cotton, this tablecloth is neutral enough to provide a versatile backdrop for brighter colours via dishes and glasses. Alone, it will also add a touch of Toast-like charm to your kitchen table.
