Tate desperately needs a radical overhaul – but will its new director really be an agent of change?

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 13:32:59 GMT

From over-hyped shows to the woeful Turner prize, this huge institution has been beset by problems – yet new boss Jessica Morgan seems too much like a safe pair of hands to shake things up Jessica Morgan named new Tate director

Even Tate knows it needs to change. This top-heavy montage of four museums really needs to scrutinise itself and ask hard questions about its aims and how it works – including why it often doesn’t. Apparently aware of the crisis, it hails its new director Jessica Morgan as “an agent of change”. Well that’s a relief. But is she really?

Morgan is a highly rated curator of contemporary art, recently leading the Dia Art Foundation in the US to great acclaim and with an earlier track record at Tate Modern itself. Yet these very strengths suggest she will stay within a groove that Tate is all too comfortable with. It’s unlikely she’s going to rush to put on a show about art and the Reformation, for instance.

This capacious institution loves to identify itself with new art but owns a lot of the old kind too. The Tate collection includes British art since 1500, but Tate Britain has become chronologically parched in its exhibitions, rarely going back into the Tudor or Stuart ages and mostly focusing on art since the Victorians. At least Gainsborough gets a show next year, but seriously, Tate needs a proper plan for its older British art. I hope Morgan will give this thought despite her background.

Not that Tate Modern is perfectly fine and dandy. When things go right they can be magnificent, like the current exhibition of Ana Mendieta’s shamanistic, myth-making visions. Yet alongside it is the museum’s disappointing, over-hyped Frida Kahlo show that was obviously problematic from an early stage. The question here is why no one raised the alarm: why there was no pre-mortem before the critics pronounced their postmortems? The same goes for last year’s dire Turbine Hall installation by Máret Ánne Sara. The faults of this installation must have been obvious but, somehow, nobody in Tate Modern seems to have said so.

These unforced errors, which have also happened at Tate Britain with its ludicrously over-attitudinising collection hang, suggest a real problem with self-questioning. Tate seems to have a culture of rigid self-belief and sees all criticism as enmity. This internal complacency or lack of democracy needs fixing fast. And the Tate brand itself needs work. “Brand” – there, I’ve said it. An art gallery should not be a brand. The transformation of Tate into its current form happened at the end of the 1990s in an era of hyper-marketing and PR-massaged cool. Today it’s almost as if Tate’s PR machine and branding determine its values: even the announcement of Morgan’s appointment comes with a long list of endorsements by artists – a totally unnecessary piece of pre-judging.

Morgan has to totally rethink Tate (maybe even allow it to be called “the” Tate). The outlets need serious attention. I like Tate St Ives but it’s arguably a rather cosy sideline. And of course, there’s the annual agony – the moribund Turner prize. Tate is too set in its ways, too dogmatic about championing “groundbreaking” art – and its curators are very confident they know what that looks like. But the idea that a museum should take sides and strike attitudes is wrong.

Tate needs to surprise us. Morgan will bring that fresh eye we are promised, even if she looks like a safe pair of hands who might bring more of the same. I hope she proves to be a revolutionary Trojan horse.

Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: mermaidcore calls for shimmer and shells – just don’t go overboard

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 13:00:15 GMT

What does a grownup mermaid look like? It starts with the silhouette …

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Before wild swimming was even a twinkle in the eye of the culture, and before ice plunging went viral on TikTok, there were mermaids. Mermaids are the original summer It girls. Who doesn’t want hair that looks great when it’s wet and salty, shell jewellery, killer sex appeal and a life of sun, sea and winding up sailors for kicks? These chicks know how to live.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Mermaidcore is this summer’s hottest style vibe. It is beach chic with a hot-sauce dash of brat energy. Every summer has its own off-duty avatar – tomato girl summer, anyone? – and 2026 is all about mermaids. For legal reasons, please note this column is not endorsing the luring of innocents to certain death. The vibe is Daryl Hannah in Splash, not selkies and sirens.

In other words: you need to up your beach cover-up game. Bring on the crochet trousers. Dig out the iridescent sarong. Say yes to coral jewellery. Embrace shell-encrusted flip-flops. Mermaidcore is the romanticisation of summer, a cinematic vision of beach life with you as the main character. It is a new spin on my all-time favourite dress code, which is what Americans call “vacation formal”, and Brits call “going for dinner on holiday”.

What it does not mean is dressing like you are going to a kids’ pirates and mermaids party. Mermaidcore can be sophisticated. Designer Matthieu Blazy’s most recent Chanel show, held on the Atlantic shore of Biarritz, had sea anemone embroidery and seahorse jewellery, and closed with a slithering dress of seafoam sequins. Clothes for sipping rosé with a sea view, not for Ariel cosplay on a bouncy castle.

So what exactly does a grownup mermaid look like? It starts with the silhouette. A certain slinkiness is in order. The switch is from an airy kaftan or maxidress to a narrower dress or long skirt. Or from sporty beach shorts to palazzo pants, snug at the hip and falling wide to the floor.

Long and narrow is not the most practical silhouette, which is probably why you don’t see mermaids playing beach volleyball. This aesthetic is best suited for graceful lounging, but if you insist on exerting yourself (or have young children), fishing-net mesh or crochet work as shorter cover-ups. A shell necklace can bring much-needed glamour to a morning spent wrangling sun cream on to small bodies.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

The line between mermaidcore and fancy dress is restraint. Pile on every pearl and sparkle and you will look as if you’ve fallen into a Sea Life gift shop. The trick is to borrow from the palette and texture of the ocean, not to dress as an actual resident. The most elegant mermaid shades are those washed-out blues and green-tinted turquoises that look artfully faded by salt and sunshine – a slip dress in pale aqua, or a sheer shirt in lagoon blue or seafoam green. You want to channel the spirit of a woman who has spent the afternoon drifting through a secluded cove, not one who just escaped from a kids’ TV show.

Texture matters as much as colour. Crochet, mesh, raffia and anything with a subtle shimmer all evoke the seaside without screaming it. A gauzy skirt catching the breeze has the magical quality of looking different every time the light hits it.

And footwear? Once again, fashion is nudging us toward jelly shoes. These truly amphibious sandals can paddle through rock pools, survive a sea dash – and still take you to lunch. Very on-brand for anyone aspiring to spend their summer moving seamlessly between land and water. Because mermaidcore is all about embracing the dream of a carefree summer. And that’s a fantasy worth diving into.

The Treasury will check Andy Burnham’s ambitions – unless old orthodoxies are challenged

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 12:57:36 GMT

Fifty years ago, another Healey ran the Treasury. Today’s chancellor may find some things haven’t changed

Some things never change. Fifty years ago, Britain was sweltering in the long hot summer of 1976. The Labour government was acutely aware that the financial markets were scrutinising its every move. And a man called Healey was running the Treasury.

On the surface, the challenges facing John Healey are less severe than those Denis Healey had to grapple with half a century ago. Inflation is a lot lower and the City has reacted calmly to Andy Burnham as prime minister. And, while things could turn nasty pretty quickly, they would have to get a lot worse before Healey Mk II felt the need to ask the International Monetary Fund for an emergency loan.

That’s the good news. The bad news is that today’s Healey has big problems of his own to solve, not least how to reconcile his pledge to run a tight ship with the new administration’s aims of rolling back more than 40 years of Thatcherism and reindustrialising Britain. Fine aspirations will eventually run into the quicksands of fiscal orthodoxy.

But so far things have gone as well as Burnham and Healey could have hoped. The message of optimism – a deliberate contrast with the doom and gloom when Keir Starmer arrived in Downing Street – was the right one. The cut in VAT on electricity bills and the cap on bus fares were largely symbolic but symbols matter. Burnham was keen to avoid a repetition of Starmer’s first big economic policy announcement: the means testing of the winter fuel payment for pensioners. That and the purging of the Starmerites from the cabinet are intended to give the impression that the real Labour government starts here.

Other conclusions can be drawn. Burnham clearly sees Reform UK as his biggest threat. That’s evident not just in the makeup of the cabinet – which has a stronger north of England flavour to it – but in the emphasis on the cost of living and rebuilding Britain’s manufacturing base. There is an attempt to reconnect the party with its working-class roots.

Keeping Shabana Mahmood as the home secretary was also significant because it shows that Burnham intends to maintain a tough stance on migration. That has economic consequences since it will force businesses faced with staff shortages to hire and train UK-born employees rather than bring them in from overseas. The days of unlimited cheap labour are over. Burnham’s desire to try a different economic model seems genuine, as does his intention to be heavily involved in the big economic decisions.

Prime ministers come in three types. There are those who enjoy focusing on domestic issues, there are those who get a buzz from foreign policy and there are those who want to do everything. It is not rare for a prime minister to start a term of office with a burning passion to sort out the economy only to find after a while that glad-handing on the global stage is more fun. But, for the moment, Burnham falls squarely into category one, and has plans to create an economic power base for himself at No 10 to act as a counterweight to the Treasury.

That, at least, is the theory. In reality, Burnham’s first 24 hours in office showed just how much power and influence the Treasury holds. Healey said meeting the existing fiscal rules was his top priority, and he now has to find the money for a fully funded defence investment plan that the Treasury denied him when he was defence secretary, precipitating his resignation.

The chancellor may get lucky and be able to pay for higher spending through stronger growth, but with the strait of Hormuz still closed and oil prices creeping up again it would be inadvisable to bank on it. That leaves borrowing more or higher taxes. A bit of extra borrowing may be available while sticking to the fiscal rules, but Burnham and Healey have big ambitions and are wary of upsetting the bond markets, which are already charging the government interest rates of 5% to service its debts. Something has to give.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Healey has floated the idea of war bonds to pay for higher defence spending, but that would be borrowing by a different name. Inevitably, therefore, taxes are going to rise in the autumn budget and the only real questions are: by how much, who pays them and what damage they will cause.

Faced with the prospect of a sluggish economy and tax rises to come, it is a tad hubristic for the seventh occupant of Downing Street in a decade to be serving notice that he will shortly be announcing a 10-year plan for change. Burnham doesn’t have the luxury of 10 years to deliver results. A general election is due within the next three years, leaving little wiggle room if things go seriously wrong – as they did for Denis Healey.

Some things have changed since the long hot summer of 1976. One of the abiding legacies of Britain’s shift to the right in the 1970s was the idea that there was no difference between the government and a household when it comes to spending, with the implication that either can go bust if it lives beyond its means. That notion lives on today, with even the most modest of ministerial spending pledges met with the challenge: how are you going to pay for it? If Burnham is serious about rolling back neoliberalism, he needs to start by challenging this entirely wrong-headed idea.

Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

Three speeches on a single day signaled a dying American democracy

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 12:00:15 GMT

Stephen Miller warned of a leftwing ‘cancer’ threatening civilization. As a critical care doctor, I have a response to his diagnosis

The presumption that US elections are legitimate died last week in Washington. It was 237 years old. It did not die of one wound. It died of three, inflicted in a single day, in daylight, on the record. And the country, running to the loudest of them, never examined the one most likely to kill.

In critical care we distinguish the mechanism of death from its cause. The mechanism was a Thursday. The cause was chronic, progressive and untreated.

The morning belonged to the secretary of state. Before officials of more than 60 countries, he announced that the counterterrorism architecture of the free world, built over a generation against jihadist mass murder, should be rebuilt and aimed at the domestic left. He named a transnational enemy defined by hatred of the west, “a revolt of the worst against the best”. He tied it to Iran and to Cuba and offered no evidence for either link. He said the journalists and thinktanks who might check the claims often agree with the enemy’s goals. The move is old and reliable: discredit the second opinion in advance.

Midday belonged to the White House deputy chief of staff. What he said deserves to be quoted rather than summarized, because summary is a mercy it has not earned. He called “leftwing political terrorism” a “fatal cancer of civilization”. He said that its politics, left to run its course, “always becomes a gulag”. He said antifa demonstrators are “all deformed in some way, in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism”, that “their outer appearance becomes a manifestation of their inner hatred”, and he asked why there is “not one normal-looking person among them”. He said that when the leftist protests that his rights are being violated, those appeals “must fall on deaf ears”. He urged the assembled governments to be “completely unflinching in the pursuit of justice against these enemies of civilization”. And he described the work already under way in six verbs: “disrupt, identify, defund, debank, arrest and prosecute”.

I have been practicing medicine for four decades. Cancer is my vocabulary, not his. And I know what happened the last time a government borrowed it. The Nazi state’s central perversion was the medicalization of killing: the enemy as tumor, as bacillus, the nation as patient, extermination as cure. Robert Jay Lifton called it the biomedical vision. It recruited my profession first, and my profession answered willingly. When a government describes citizens as a cancer, it has written the first line of a treatment plan. On Thursday, the plan was read aloud, from a state department podium, in six verbs.

One disclosure belongs in the chart. My family left Russia in 1917. My relatives left Germany in 1933. In both generations, leaving was called excessive; staying was the reasonable position. But an alarm that was right both times it sounded is not overcaution. On Thursday, it sounded a third time.

The evening belonged to the president. In primetime he called the American election system indefensible, claimed a foreign power held 220 million voter files, declared mail voting inherently corrupt, accused his own intelligence services of concealment, and told Congress that the only reason to oppose his bill is the intent to cheat. That framework converts every future outcome into evidence. Pass the bill and win: the bill worked. Fail and lose: the cheaters blocked it. A presumption of legitimacy cannot survive inside a belief system engineered to be unfalsifiable.

It was just a Thursday. Netflix’s forecast disappointed Wall Street. A rocket aborted on the pad. No sirens sounded, because this is not how they sound. Democracies do not die to soundtracks. They die on ordinary weekdays, between the earnings reports, while the country is at work.

Then came the response, and the response was a triage error. Nearly all of it ran to the evening. The factcheckers parsed the voter files. The law professors graded the bombshells. Real work, spent on the loudest injury. The morning’s remarks, the ones that declared a class of Americans a cancer and read enmity on their bodies, drew the attention of an ordinary news cycle: straight coverage in the mainstream, horror at the margins, and in a portion of the press, open applause. I have watched teams run to the dramatic patient while the quiet one, the one not crying out, exsanguinates behind a curtain. The most dangerous words spoken in Washington on Thursday were not spoken in primetime. They were spoken before lunch, to more than 60 countries. The official transcript records the applause.

The decedent is survived by the federal courts, still open. By 50 secretaries of state, still certifying. By a general election, still on the calendar, 108 days out. And by an electorate that has not yet been asked the only question that matters, which is whether it will accept a count its president has pre-declared corrupt, counted among citizens its government has pre-declared malignant.

In 40 years of intensive care, I have pronounced death many times. The criteria are strict because the declaration is irreversible, and so we are taught to be certain before we speak. I have also, more than once, seen a rhythm return after the room had gone quiet, when someone refused to stop compressions on schedule. This notice is filed in the knowledge that pronouncements can be premature. It is filed in the fear that this one is not.

Robert B Shpiner is a clinical professor of medicine in pulmonary and critical care at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA

‘The magnificent, the magical, the marvellous!’ It’s TV’s happiest endings

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 11:01:42 GMT

Gold dances, the Good Friday agreement and standup superstardom … get ready to blub because here are the most heartwarming denouements in TV history

Warning: this article contains spoilers

What does perfect 50s housewife Midge (Rachel Brosnahan) do after her husband leaves? She gets drunk and flashes her boobs on stage while doing an impromptu comedy set. It’s impossible not to root for her from this moment on. With the help of her unlikely manager, Susie Myers (Alex Borstein), she embarks on a standup career with the odds constantly stacked against her. Finally, Midge makes her breakthrough moment happen on a late-night show.

“I want a big life,” she tells the studio audience, who have just been howling at her jokes. “They say ambition is an unattractive trait in a woman. Maybe. But you know what’s really unattractive? Waiting around for something to happen.” All of her family members – who had been so against this career – are there cheering with pride. Gordon Ford (Reid Scott) then introduces her to the world: “The magnificent, the magical, the marvellous Mrs Maisel.”

But the real gut-punch moment? When Midge looks over to Susie, who has a tear in her eye and her hand on her heart. The final scene jumps to decades later, with the hugely successful pair joking over the phone as they both watch an old episode of Jeopardy. Hollie Richardson

The brilliance of the 30 Rock finale – aired as two episodes back-to-back in 2013 – really begins halfway through the closing series. That’s when Liz Lemon gets married and embarks, via adoption, on motherhood, both milestones at which a traditional sitcom would usually end a show centred on a female protagonist. But not for Lemon, and not for creator Tina Fey, who ends it with TGS (the show within a show) being uncancelled and brought back for one last episode – an appropriately meta end for the show itself – so that everyone else’s storylines can be tied up. Liz is shown to be back at work and realising she needs to have work and not just family in her life or she’ll live on a knife-edge of insanity as much as she did when it was just work.

It gave us callbacks (even unto St Elsewhere), the full gag quotient (plus The Rural Juror song), Kenneth’s ascendance (possibly transcendence), and closure. Even Pete got a brief year of happiness before the epilogue. Above all, it gave us Jack’s lovely speech to Liz from the boat, which she eventually interrupts to tell him she platonically loves him too. Affectionate respect has never been so beautifully captured. See-through dishwasher for all! Lucy Mangan

There was rarely anything tricksy about the narrative of Detectorists – it was based round a set of simple, binary storylines concerning relationships, parenthood and mild discord over metal-detecting territory. All the same, Lance and Andy were deceptively complex characters and the show’s seemingly still emotional waters ran deep. It soon became clear that we were being offered one of the most charming and convincing depictions of friendship in television history.

The show’s conclusion was gently audacious, suggesting continuity as the happiest of endings. Andy and Becky buy a delightful, dilapidated house. Toni is preparing to move in with Lance. Andy and Lance don’t actually need anything they don’t already have. Friends, lovers, a pub nearby, modest roofs over their heads, a shared passion and perhaps most importantly of all, each other. Their gold dance is, at all times, right in front of them. Phil Harrison

“If YES put an X in this square.” The Derry Girls had to grow up sometime, and so it came to pass, after Erin and Orla made it through the wildest 18th birthday/joint first communion party ever – theme: literary monkeys – that they all got to vote on the Good Friday agreement. For a show so consistently hilarious, Lisa McGee’s cracker comedy finally turned on a sixpence into the most beautifully poignant piece of historical analysis. I was weeping with joy from the moment Granda Joe says: “What if no one else has to die? What if all this becomes a ghost story you’ll tell your weans one day. A ghost story they’ll hardly believe.” By the time all of them chose yes, chose hope, chose to end the Troubles that were all they’d ever known, I was a goner. Of course it was soundtracked to the Cranberries – the only possible choice – and of course, in the ultimate cameo, Chelsea Clinton got their letter decades late in the closing seconds! As Michelle said, being a Derry Girl is a fuckin’ state of mind, and I’ll never stop loving them. Sláinte! Kate Abbott

If you’ve watched the finale of Hacks this might be a hard sell. Major spoiler incoming: the final episode of this biting showbiz satire ended with our Joan Rivers-inspired antiheroine Deborah Vance (Jean Smart) revealing a terminal cancer diagnosis, and planning her death by assisted dying. Fans had already noted the morbid foreshadowing all season, but it still felt like a brutal plot twist – not only for Deborah but for Ava (Hannah Einbinder), her protege, surrogate daughter and sometime pretend girlfriend.

Frankly it was all a bit triggering, not just because I lost a parent to cancer, but because Hacks is really funny and this was absolutely the unfunniest thing that could have happened. But in a way – stay with me here – Hacks did have a happy ending. At the 11th hour, Deborah changed her mind and decided to hang on a little longer and write another comedy special, delivering one of the best lines in the whole damn series: “I may not have 30 years – but I think I have another hour.” I was, like most professional journalists, watching the finale from an airport Starbucks, ugly crying. When I heard that line I got instant chills. I stopped sobbing, let out a gasp, then started crying again – but this time it was happy tears. The thought of Deborah writing one final bitchy, tell-all special really made me smile. Hannah J Davies

Like one of Del Boy’s dodgy deals, Only Fools and Horses gave us two happy endings for the price of one. The first was 1996’s iconic fairytale finale: an antique watch makes Del and Rodney millionaires – cue a fever dream montage of the brothers living in the lap of luxury. Yet for the elder Trotter, the giddy euphoria was tinged with wrenching nostalgia for his old life, resulting in a profoundly bittersweet conclusion that cemented the show’s place in the British pop cultural canon. Then came the 2000s reboot: three Christmas specials, widely derided as knock-offs. Still, the eventual denouement – which involves a more modest windfall, some closure for Rodney and a long-awaited baby for him and Cassandra – is actually more uplifting and heartwarming than the original. A less artful ending, undoubtedly, but I’m still glad we said goodbye with a more relatable kind of happiness. Rachel Aroesti

How to end one of TV’s most gleefully daft comedies? With a ludicrously elaborate set-piece episode, featuring the most OTT version ever of the annual event where the characters go all out to double cross each other in a heist – naturally. This double-bill farewell was a glorious exercise in fan-pleasing that packed in a whistlestop tour of the show’s most significant moments (the warehouse where they solved their first case! The interview room behind the best ever skit – where Peralta made suspects sing Backstreet Boys!), joy-inducing returns of fave characters and the heartfelt emotional moment that had been brewing for eight seasons – Captain Holt telling Peralta he’d be proud to have a son like him. It all ended with a quiet, beautiful moment – the lights being turned out on the precinct as they stepped into the lift together for one last time. Then they threw in a bonus scene set a year later with the crew announcing that they’d get back together every year for their annual heist. Cue a last sketch, including bad magic, hammy acting and one final rousing call of the team motto: Nine-Nine! Now that’s how you say goodbye. Alexi Duggins

Things weren’t looking great as Sex and the City careened and Carried its way through its too-long final season. Even Charlotte’s dog was starting to look exhausted. But writer Michael Patrick King and this beautiful cast of women really pulled it out of the Birkin for the two-parter finale in which Carrie has to choose between moving to Paris with a handsome millionaire, or staying in New York with a different handsome millionaire (look, we’ve all been there).

There’s breathy old Hollywood dialogue that somehow works. There’s Sarah Jessica Parker galloping across wet cobbles to moody French hip-hop. And if you didn’t get goosebumps from Miranda gripping Mr Big’s hairy, Rolex-clad forearm and gasping “Go get our girl!” you’re as dead inside as the second movie. Dylan B Jones

Unlike most TV “happy ever afters” which can seem rushed, Parks and Recreation treats us to a two-part finale which jumps forward in time not just once but several times, as it lovingly explores what happens next to Leslie Knope and our favourite gang of Pawnee government employees.

Each character gets their storyline tied up in a way that is entirely befitting of their personality and arc – and of course, it would end with Amy Poehler’s overachieving Knope possibly becoming president of the United States. We also finally get some karmic justice for Jerry/Garry/Larry, the perennial office scapegoat, who becomes a much-beloved mayor of Pawnee and lives to the ripe old age of 100.

The ending is sweet, offbeat and supremely wholesome – all the things we’ve come to expect from Parks and Rec over the years. And this cuddly sitcom couldn’t have ended in a better way – as a tribute to the power of “friends, waffles, work” (Knope’s life priorities), right to the very last credits. Ann Lee

So many classic shows have been led by a monstrous male character we secretly root for – Tony Soprano, Walter White, Doc Martin – and the protagonist in Scott Ryan’s flawless crime drama is up there with the best/worst. Ray Shoesmith has bludgeoned and gouged his way through Sydney’s criminal underworld but, in the final episode, he’s given up killing to become a rural cab driver. When two hoodlums who mean Ray harm get in the car, Ryan makes a brilliant creative decision: the last shot is Ray breaking the fourth wall, eyeballing the camera and grinning. Ray knows what we want. He’s going to horribly murder them! Hoorah! Jack Seale

From the ashes of one of the bleakest television programmes ever made (in a nutshell: 2% of the world’s population goes missing, and those left behind go mad with grief) came a beautifully hopeful ending. A long-separated couple reunite. The woman says she visited an alternative dimension where the missing 2% live happily in peace. It almost certainly isn’t the truth, but the story brought her comfort. The man says he believes her. They cry. They hold hands. They smile. For a show that never had any intention of explaining its central mystery, this ending – an emotional truth landing harder than a logical one – was absolutely perfect. Stuart Heritage

It’s the drama, Mick, I just love it. There’s a reason why the Anglo-Welsh romcom’s finale became Britain’s most-watched scripted show in more than two decades. Five years after Nessa proposed to Smithy, nuptials loomed – except it was boring Sonia who the lovable lummox was marrying, not his love-hate soulmate. What was occurring? After a spine-tingling intervention at the altar, Smithy called it off and dashed to Southampton docks, where Nessa was about to set sail on a cargo ship. Now it was his turn to pop the question. The pair married in Barry while 21m viewers wept with joy into their Quality Street tins. Tidy, cracking and well lush. Michael Hogan

The world is on fire, and who does Trump blame? The Canadians

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 10:00:13 GMT

The US president has been complaining about Canada’s ‘filthy, polluted and unhealthy air’. Maybe he should put all that energy into tackling the climate crisis

Right, that’s it: we’ve got to do something about Canada. The country’s wildfires, which resulted in air quality alerts across more than 20 US states, ruined my weekend. On Friday the air in Philadelphia, where I live, was so unhealthy I couldn’t go outside without my eyes stinging. My kid’s preschool cancelled outdoor time, while the city suspended trash pickup and closed public pools.

You know who did not suspend their regularly scheduled programming because of a bit of toxic smoke? The plot monitoring committee at my allotment. Despite the apocalyptic conditions, they were still busy ensuring the gardening bylaws were strictly adhered to. I realised this on Saturday when I got an official violation for too many weeds. Yes, I’d got a bit carried away with “chaos gardening” (all the rage these days) and I’d meant to clean things up on Friday, until the smoke got in the way. So, thanks for that Canada.

Luckily, Donald Trump is on the case. On Friday he complained on Truth Social that the US had been “invaded” by “filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air”, and the situation was “totally unacceptable”. Then, on Sunday, the president said he’d spoken to the Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and told him “you got to stop these fires from coming in and, you know, poisoning our air”. He added: “Maybe they should pay some damages or something, or we should do some tariffs.” I’m surprised he didn’t order ICE to stamp out the fires.

Carney, for his part, responded to Trump’s comments by referencing the climate crisis, and noting that this was everyone’s responsibility to address. But who wants to talk about an inconvenient fact like the human-caused climate crisis when it’s much easier to just blame Canadians? Maga certainly doesn’t. On Thursday the Republican senator Bernie Moreno from Ohio introduced a new bill that would sanction Canadian officials for wildfire smoke. Meanwhile, the geniuses on Fox News have been busy yelling about Canada while skirting around the root causes of the wildfires.

Poor Canada isn’t just getting a lot of hot air directed at it from Trumpers, it’s now issued its own air quality warnings because of American fires to the south. It turns out that smoke doesn’t recognise border policies. And, as the weather becomes more extreme, things are only going to get worse: the world is literally on fire and the arsonists are fiddling with tariffs as it burns.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Pass the pit diapers! Why are fans wetting themselves to stand front row at concerts?

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 09:39:51 GMT

Olivia Rodrigo, Noah Kahan and Morgan Wallen have all dealt with audience effluence in recent weeks – but that’s only one part of a fearsome subculture that has built up around fandom, endurance and ‘getting barrier’

The front row of a gig is a sacred space. When you love an artist, you want to be as close to them as possible, without a view obscured by someone else’s hairdo. You want the possibility that the artist will pluck you from the crowd, form a deep and enduring connection and end up marrying you. Or at least notice you. Last month, Olivia Rodrigo revealed how acutely she had noticed some of the fans lining the barriers at her shows. “People wear diapers so that they can be front row,” she said, adding, to everyone’s absolute horror: “That’s been an experience as a performer that I have smelled.”

This is no aberration, and while genuine medical needs should be taken into account, situations down the front have clearly got out of control. Also last month, video of a very stoic stadium worker cleaning up human excrement at a Noah Kahan gig went viral and prompted Kahan himself to post on X: “If you have to poop at a show please dear god just go to the bathroom lmao.” This week, a fan of US country star Morgan Wallen complained that he, his brother and his niece were urinated on by another concertgoer, and police are investigating. Must we be subjected to headlines such as “Someone Also Shit Their Pants at a 5 Seconds of Summer Concert”? And in 2024, someone urinated on the floor of the standing section of a Sabrina Carpenter concert, causing a run on a fairly horrifying item called a “pit diaper”, whose mere existence speaks to a wider problem.

Since the pandemic, when music lovers missed out on two years of live shows and young fans were forced to wait for their first gig experiences, those hard-won spots on the front row have become more and more coveted. The cost of VIP pit tickets has rocketed, stan culture has grown ever more feral, and the social media value of scoring clear gig footage is at a premium, partly because surprise celeb cameos – as in Rosalía’s confession booth, Charli xcx’s Apple dance or Sabrina Carpenter’s on-stage “arrests” – are now built into many pop shows. So as well as the adult nappies, today’s barrier culture is a world of strict fan-run queue conventions, cross-venue sprints and specialist hydration systems.

In an effort to find someone who would admit to even considering wearing a nappy, I popped down to Wembley Stadium on night 11 of Harry Styles’ recent 12-night Together Together residency. The dazzlingly sequinned girls I spoke to weathering the heatwave to queue for the final section of floor standing were mostly horrified by the question. “I think that’s a bit ridiculous,” said Eloise, 23, having once queued for 10 hours to get the barrier at Harry’s last run of Wembley shows. What will you do if you need the toilet? I asked Shannon, who was hoping to leg it to the barrier when doors opened: “Hope for the best!”

Nineteen-year-old Keeley, who started queuing at 11am, said that she, “personally”, wouldn’t wear a nappy. “That’s not for me. Especially in this heat. It’d feel really unnatural to wee just in front of everyone.”

But if you’re paying hundreds of pounds for a show and are queuing for hours to be mere metres from Rodrigo or Styles, it does make a warped kind of sense that you might take the nappy route rather than risk missing a song or losing your spot at the front. On TikTok, plenty of Swifties claimed to have worn one to the Eras tour (and with shows of more than three hours, you’d assume even Taylor Swift took a loo break). But it’s hard to track down anyone who will admit to a Guardian journalist that they wore a pit diaper in order to keep their coveted front-row view.

When Katie, a seasoned Swiftie, planned her route to the Eras tour barrier, she forwent pissing herself in a crowd. Instead, she developed a hydration strategy that kept her show-ready but dry as a bone. “I drank loads of water the day before and then as soon as I got up at 4am to queue for the barricade, I had like two pints. I kept drinking until around midday then had a hard cutoff.” Energy gels, glucose tablets and mid-show waters handed by security over the barricade kept her from passing out – a sure-fire way to lose your spot. “No point in getting barricade if you faint during the first era!” she added brightly.

There is a long tradition of people (mostly cis men, let’s be real) pissing into pint-glasses in crowds – and in one particularly horrifying Primavera crowd, directly on to my friend’s leg. Concerts by US psychedelic rockers Phish have become notorious for fans supposedly pooping with gay abandon since an infamous incident in 2015. You can see how it might happen in a boozed-up festival crowd or somewhere drugs are being liberally consumed. And perhaps the Phish experience is so transcendent it elevates the listener outside the workings of their gastrointestinal tract. More desperately, fans could argue they are counterculturally rejecting toileting norms, though this behaviour is actually relatively mainstream: urination was apparently rife as far back as concerts by Frank Sinatra and the Beatles.

If you are minded to just let go, the potential for it to backfire is huge. “I tried this with a sanitary towel and it didn’t work,” confesses one gig-goer, insisting on anonymity for reasons that will become obvious. Let’s call her Fiona. She and a friend had travelled to see Arctic Monkeys in Finsbury Park in 2014. Fiona was a spritely 15-year-old who had got her hands on a bottle of rosé and reached the barrier right in front of where Alex Turner and co were soon to be asking Do I Wanna Know? The answer here is an emphatic: no you don’t.

“I was determined to stay there,” she says, bodily functions be damned. “I had some sanitary towels in my bag so I thought I could discreetly wee into one. But it just overfilled because, unsurprisingly, pads can’t hold a rosé-induced wee’s worth of liquid.” With huge wet patches all down her black skinny jeans, she had to shimmy her piss-soaked way out of the crowd to find a portable toilet to deal with everything. “The worst thing was, when I tried to squeeze back through to my place, no one believed that my friend was waiting for me at the barrier.” It’s hard to believe that really was the worst thing about the situation.

Toilet troubles are one thing; but just “getting barrier” in the first place is a whole other matter. The Harry Styles fans queuing in the heatwave had numbers written in Sharpie on the backs of their hands as part of a fan-run system that is supposed to ensure that whoever queues the longest gets the best spots. It goes pretty far back down the queue, at least to the hundreds. The idea is that no one can push in – or at least that it’s obvious if they do – though no one was clear exactly what anyone would or could do about that.

There are some obvious flaws in this system. I could have written a number on the back of my hand and strolled to the front, and who could deny me? It’s an honour code that some people just don’t abide by, even in England, the spiritual home of queuing. Videos of the walk into the stadiums for Styles’ shows often become popular on socials: the ones from the night I investigated had just as much panicked jostling and yelling as there would have been without the numbers.

Fans of all stripes have always staked out venues to sprint in and nab a space at the front – the forthcoming documentary Metallica Saved My Life shows the every-man-for-himself combo tactic of camping out then legging it in – but the newly regimented, numbered, self-policing approach seems to have stemmed from teenage girls. Anecdotal evidence suggests these “roll calls”, as fans call them, started proliferating in the mid-2010s. “Fans policing the order in which they’re in the queue to get into the venue first has always been a thing,” says Hannah Ewens, author of Fangirls, in which she documents how the teen fangirl queue community has its own microcommunities, complete with influencers. The spirit of the community, infused with a deep love for the artist plus the need for a decent view – teenage girls tend to be among the smallest in any given gig crowd – is all part of the barrier-questing experience.

But while it’s always been about getting to the front, getting a spot on the front row has also become a lot more about clout. “TikTok has made it so much more rewarding,” Ewens adds. “It’s ramped up a sense of competition.” Getting to the barrier could be the difference between your videos of the show going viral or disappearing into the digital ether, and that gives the numbering systems even more perceived weight. “Fandom is about being in a community and being part of something, but it’s also very hierarchical,” Ewens says. “Queuing scratches both those itches for fans.”

Some artists have made it clear that fan-run queue systems will not be entertained. For Bring Me the Horizon’s Manchester gig earlier this month – which had no barrier at all, just free-flowing rockers right up to the stage – the FAQs included a note: “Queueing will begin from 10am on show day … Fan numbering will not be acknowledged. Order of first entry will be selected at random.” The band and promoter would not comment on the decision, and whether or not it had any effect on the toileting habits of the crowd is unclear.

Fandoms are starting to push back against fan-made queuing systems, too. Search Reddit or TikTok for this subject and you will find just as many people rejecting it as participating. Louis Tomlinson brought in randomised wristbands to take away the incentive to queue for hours for his shows earlier this year. Whatever time fans checked in, they were assigned a number to determine the order they could enter the pit. Venues including Wembley Stadium have also banned camping, making the process fairer for people who can’t give up several days to the cause.

But despite the horrors of dirty nappies and enforced fan regimes, the barrier is generally a place of bonhomie. Friendships are made, core memories created. Whenever a member of BTS chucks a worn T-shirt to a specific fan at the barrier, no one around them tries to grab it (much as you know they desperately want to). If fans need help or water, those around them will signal to security to fetch it. And some of the photos and footage coming from front-row fans at this summer’s stadium shows are of professional-level quality. Whatever they did to capture them is between them, God and the nostrils of their favourite pop star. Even Fiona has no regrets: “It was worth it,” she says, 10 years removed from the wet jeans. “And I’m glad I have the story too.”

World Cup 2026 awards: the Guardian team give their final tournament verdicts

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 09:01:34 GMT

The best games, goals and personal highlights – from a magical Azteca to Erling Haaland breaking America

Paraguay 1-1 Germany. There were plenty more games with more goals but none could match the drama of the penalty shootout in this last-32 tie. Germany aren’t supposed to lose in them but they did this time in spectacular fashion. Ed Aarons

Algeria 3-3 Austria was a completely strange fever dream, seeming to exist on a separate plane of reality. I know that sounds grandiose but remember, going into this one the expectation was that it would be a biscotto – a meaningless, pre-arranged kickabout where a draw would see both sides through. For a while in the second half, it looked like that would happen. And finally, in stoppage time, chaos. There were certainly better matches in terms of quality, and maybe a couple that had this beat for drama, but no game was weirder. Alexander Abnos

From the 14 I attended, it has to be Mexico 2-3 England at the awesome Azteca. The buildup seemed to start as soon as the draw was made – fortunately the stars aligned and a grippingly tense game ensued in a venue like no other. It was a high point for England that should cut through despite later disappointments, too. Nick Ames

France 4-6 England was borderline hilarious. Egypt 1-1 Iran in Seattle had plenty of late drama, Iran’s disallowed stoppage-time winner bookended by them twice hitting the woodwork in the final minutes. The draw ultimately proved insufficient for unbeaten Iran, faced with endless hurdles, to progress. Ben Fisher

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The defending champions looked down and out, thinking about their flights home, before a late Lionel Messi-inspired comeback enabled them to claw back a two-goal deficit and win this last-16 match in normal time. Barry Glendenning

The game no one wanted to play. Sid Lowe

Mexico 2-3 England. I have decided that all my answers should relate to things that happened while I was at the tournament and this was one. I mean, I wasn’t there ticking off the “bucket list” of a visit to the Azteca (I think I saw at least half a dozen British hacks claim that), but I did watch it on TV. Besides being like drinking cortisol neat, this was so dramatic, the images so evocative, that even if you are an ardent England fan (as I am) this was pure cinema. Paul MacInnes

I am biased here in the sense I attended it but Cape Verde 2-2 Uruguay in Miami was superb. Cape Verde’s attitude and discipline were a joy. Such fun to watch. Ewan Murray

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. Incredible drama, despite the questionable behaviour of the referee. Osasu Obayiuwana

Tough to pick from over 100 options, but Mexico 2-3 England with Thomas Tuchel’s men surviving the vaunted Azteca and the best first half Mexico could have mustered narrowly takes this category. Jeff Rueter

Bias says Mexico v England, but Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde was incredible, Sidny Lopes Cabral bending it top right. Max Rushden

For improbable wonder there was Argentina v Cape Verde, for sheer unpredictability there was Mexico v England. Often, though, one is drawn to something more predictable, more familiar: England 1-2 Argentina. Jack Snape

Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde. It’s not a debate. Jacob Steinberg

Argentina 3-2 Egypt. The possibility of a shock, a great Messi-inspired turnaround, a couple of great goals, refereeing controversy … what else do you want? Jonathan Wilson

Rodri was the standout player for the best team in a tournament where the big stars came to the party but all ultimately fell short. EA

Kylian Mbappé. Yes, his Golden Boot was padded a bit by that insane third-place game, but the France striker was the best player on what looked to be the best team in the tournament ... at least until that loss to Spain in the semi-final. AA

It’s impossible to look further than Rodri, who looks back to his best and absolutely in his element as the fulcrum of this Spain setup. Otherwise it was good to see a World Cup where the stars largely shone. Jude Bellingham, Erling Haaland, Messi and Mbappé were all one more decisive knockout display away from rising above the rest. NA

Rodri. Michael Olise was majestic, though should have scored a hat-trick against England. Bellingham was equally instrumental for Tuchel’s side – it is crazy to think there were people questioning his inclusion in the squad. BF

Rodri – capitán, líder, leyenda. BG

Lionel Messi. SL

Vozinha. What a man. I think it’s largely because his story is so relatable in these parts – middle-aged man finally receives the plaudits he has always deserved! – but the saves were also top drawer. Add in the pedigree of the teams he either shut out or frustrated, and this was an actual fairytale that didn’t need to be spun by any marketing department. And did you know that he’s 40? PM

Pau Cubarsí. EM

Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper. At 40, and without a club, he was brilliant for the World Cup debutants. OO

While Rodri is an incredibly worthy Golden Ball winner and others made their marks, Erling Haaland leaves this World Cup with the greatest possible souvenirs: a credible if short Golden Boot campaign, a famous first Norwegian foray into the quarter-final stage, and perhaps the biggest boost in star appeal in the lucrative North American market. JR

Hard not to say Rodri although I thought Dani Olmo was great too, and a shout for Pico Lopes. MR

Haaland, Mbappé and Messi have lived up to expectations. But in those moments where a contest teeters – evading pressure with the ball, in transition to defence or staring down a 50-50 – no player has shown his quality more consistently than Rodri. JSn

Rodri. If only England had a player like the Spain captain. JSt

Rodri. As Spain have reverted to a more possession-driven model, their metronome in midfield has been the outstanding figure, setting the tempo and providing control. JW

For sheer drama, it has to be Sidny Lopes Cabral’s brilliant equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina. His reaction was almost as good as the goal itself, clasping his hands to his head before picking out his girlfriend in the crowd to celebrate with. EA

I mean, it’s Sidny Lopes Cabral v Argentina. But I feel that the goal from Uzbekistan’s Eldor Shomurodov against the Democratic Republic of the Congo deserves mention too: an instinctive, oddly satisfying lob from a tight angle. No other goal in the tournament was quite like it. AA

Julián Alvarez had a largely quiet World Cup but his vicious, swerving long-range goal in extra time against Switzerland was a jaw-dropping moment and lit up the cauldron-like stadium in Kansas City. NA

Those seen in the flesh always seem to score more points. A buzz surrounded Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic coming into the tournament and the 18-year-old eliminating a clutch of defenders and blasting in, off balance, from the outside of the box against Qatar only enhanced his reputation. Johan Manzambi’s run and pass in the buildup to Breel Embolo’s opener against Algeria was also a joy. BF

While Morocco’s superior quality would ultimately see them through their group-stage win against Haiti, Wilson Isidor’s breathtaking long-range strike to put the Caribbean nation 2-1 up was as good a goal as any scored in the World Cup. Ever. BG

Sidny Lopes Cabral, of course. SL

I had the privilege of reading the paper by the Seoul Women’s University on the aerodynamic effect known as “drag crisis” which is particularly common when people smack an Adidas Trionda, so as such I thought a lot of the big hits were overrated. I do, however, exempt Sidny Lopes Cabral from that critique. Absolute long-range worldie from the Cape Verde full-back-cum-winger. That it pegged Argentina to parity in extra time of a knockout round only made it more memorable. PM

Harry Kane’s second for England against DRC. EM

Sidny Lopes Cabral of Cape Verde, against Argentina. Magical goal. OO

I will never, in all my years, be able to recreate the sound that left my body as Sidny Lopes Cabral’s audacious effort against Argentina completed its curl between a diving Emi Martínez and his far post. Masterful execution in an unprecedented moment. One of many proud moments for Cape Verde at this tournament. JR

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Beyond Sidny Lopes Cabral – the disallowed Uzbekistan one (was it Uzbekistan?) – someone walloped one into the top left-hand corner and it didn’t count. MR

Erling Haaland’s second against Brazil, placed into the bottom-right corner from outside the box to seal the upset, was a microcosm of his effectiveness at the tournament: precise and powerful with a hint of whimsy. JSn

Sidny Lopes Cabral’s equaliser for Cape Verde against Argentina was a proper jaw-dropping moment. One of the great World Cup goals. JSt

Wilson Isidor v Morocco. There were more consequential goals, but none struck quite as sweetly or quite as accurately. If Haiti have nothing else, they’ll always have that. JW

It was a joy to watch Eloy Room’s performance in goal for Curaçao against Ecuador as he broke the World Cup record for the most saves made in a 90-minute match. While Cape Verde’s veteran Vozinha stole most of the headlines for his heroics, the 37-year-old Room clearly enjoyed his moment in the spotlight. “I think I need a statue in Curaçao now,” he joked. EA

Fifa and the stadium authorities typically guard the natural grass pitches heavily, and with good reason. But after the last games in each venue I went to, I loved watching those pitches get taken over by the people whose names you’ll never know but who actually made this tournament run: stadium workers and low-level Fifa staffers, volunteers, security guards, longtime local club representatives and others. Some used the opportunity to have a little kickabout, take selfies, or just run around. An awesome perk for what were almost certainly very hard, stressful jobs over these last several weeks. AA

My first visit to the Azteca was Mexico’s win over Ecuador and I’ve never heard a noise like it. The place really is as magical and monumental as they say. The celebrations afterwards weren’t conducive to a good night’s sleep but were incredible in scale too. Football-wise I’ll also add Messi’s record-breaking goals against Austria in Dallas, which seem an awfully long time ago now but were such a thrill to witness. Those early Argentina games were essentially mass Messi pilgrimages. One more? The view from Monterrey Stadium. Just go, if you can. NA

Watching Senegalese journalists pass around a pack of malted milks during their anthem before their collapse against Belgium. And playing eight-a-side with Danny Cipriani, who once spent six weeks training at Tottenham, Harry Kane among his teammates, will stick in the memory. BF

Watching my Irish compatriot Roberto “Pico” Lopes excel while repeatedly putting his body on the line for Cape Verde, his father’s homeland. It would be nice to think Pico’s performances will earn him a life-changing move to a more lucrative league in the twilight of his career but his age could stand against him and he may well be content with being a Shamrock Rovers and Cape Verde legend. BG

Explaining to a mariachi in a gigantic sombrero how it could possibly be that a team in third could get through the group and how it might still be Spain turning up at the Azteca. Alas, it wasn’t. Sharing a birthday with Martin Ainstein and Luis de la Fuente and my family. And watching a motorcade with the Spain bus pass from the sixth-floor window where Lee Harvey Oswald shot JFK was pretty surreal. SL

I loved watching both France eviscerate Sweden and the Instagram reels of Americans acting like they thought the Tartan Army had permanently changed their lives. PM

Players running out to warm-up to the tune of Scotland the Brave, via bagpipes, before the game against Haiti in Foxborough. Scotland’s 28-year World Cup wait was over. The less said about all that happened next, the better. EM

Seeing Vozinha’s mum, against all expectations, travelling from Cape Verde to the World Cup to see her son play. OO

Having covered the nation’s third-to-fifth most popular sport for more than a decade and lived through ICE’s heinous occupation of Minnesota this winter, the sheer scale of interest in soccer was overwhelming and so invigorating – a welcome reprieve in the isolationist second Trump era. Impossible to go through a couple of hours in a World Cup host city without some stranger striking up a conversation about the sport. Long may this remain a part of American society. JR

Shouting Paraguay. Number 10. Cover his mouth. Decision is RED CARD. Jonathan Wilson thinking Robbie Williams was Kevin Pietersen. Mark Langdon’s chow mein bridge. The pancakes at Mile End Deli. Doing a live show in Manhattan and legitimately getting to say “HELLO NEW YORK!” MR

Covering Australia, the tournament petered out from an extraordinary high. Twenty-six minutes into the Socceroos’ opening victory against Turkey, goalscorer Nestory Irankunda revived Tim Cahill’s goal celebration in a ceremonial handover to mark a new generation. JSn

Being at the Azteca for Mexico 2-3 England. It did not have the most quality but it was hard to beat as an occasion. An epic night at an iconic stadium. A thunderstorm pushing kick-off back, a brilliant display from Bellingham, everyone exhausted when it was over. Things didn’t end well for England but this was easily their greatest away win. JSt

Standing knee-deep in raging floods in Monterrey waiting for a bus having only gone to the stadium to collect a mislaid iPad that I then lost in Houston a week later anyway. That or the weirdly beautiful flyovers outside Dallas. JW

The level of interest from the American public surprised me and it was fascinating to meet so many who were interested in what was happening in the tournament. Many people in the US definitely caught World Cup fever. Logistically it was a real test of endurance with so much travelling required between venues and that wasn’t helped by so many being miles from the city centre. And it would have been much better to have played the final in Mexico City or Atlanta’s impressive downtown stadium. EA

I felt unfortunate not to make it to any games in Mexico and only one in Canada. But overall I’m happy that the everyday people who populate the US seemed to show visitors their good side throughout the month. This country has plenty of infrastructure issues I’d like to have seen fixed, but the personal impact is arguably more important, and it seems like the US mostly got that right. AA

If first impressions are everything then I refer you to the often troubling weirdness of the Texas Republican party convention in Houston. But more seriously I was very happy, in the US, to find the hoped-for warmth and openness pretty much everywhere – and in bundles. In their different ways, people really did engage with the World Cup. Less welcome was the US administration’s attempt, duly pandered to by Fifa, to bend the course of the tournament with Folarin Balogun’s reprieve. In Mexico I found a fervent, febrile, fascinating football culture that deserved not to be dwarfed by other co-hosts. NA

Americans love a big-ticket event but it was clear they were hooked by Mauricio Pochettino’s side as they progressed. It was a privilege to witness Canada’s first World Cup game on home soil in Toronto, where there was a match-day buzz and an afterglow despite being held to a draw by Bosnia and Herzegovina. BF

While I didn’t meet Donald Trump, the handful of Americans whose acquaintance I did make – hotel staff, a few bartenders and one LA-based reality TV show star – could not have been friendlier. BG

So many people came up to us to say they really hoped we were enjoying this and that we understood that that wasn’t them. We did and they were so nice. SL

I spent two days in Toronto, around Canada Day, and I think they were both welcoming and very keen to hear that they qualified as an actual football nation. People in the US were pleasant, although for travelling fans most experiences will have been complicated by the ubiquitous request for a tip. I did think, though, that sometimes there was an expectation that we should all be delighted to be there. Which we were, but perhaps not for the reasons some wanted. PM

Canada and Mexico? Excellent. US stadiums were first class, as was the extent to which the nation embraced the World Cup. It is just impossible to ignore the stench of the Balogun situation. EM

On an on-field football level? Far from spectacular. The US needs a new player-development architecture to ensure there is a pipeline of high-quality players. They also need a new head coach, with the right vision for the future. Tournament organisation? The fact that Fifa took direct control of it should be a cautionary tale. A local organising committee is always needed. OO

All three co-hosts fared about as well as I had projected, but each may have exceeded my expectations in terms of how they went about it. Canada were thrilling at times – I covered their 6-0 win over Qatar at BC Place – and had plenty of pluck with Jesse Marsch as their coach-cum-hype man. The USA played some of the prettiest soccer ever seen by a US national team of any gender, and will for ever rue a missed opportunity to do something greater against Belgium. Mexico were one of the biggest bandwagon teams as they barnstormed Group A, then outclassed an Ecuador team on the rise and pushed England to the brink until they ran out of ideas in the final half-hour. Jobs well done across the board. JR

I had six weeks in America. All the Americans were lovely. MR

This tournament put the whirled in the World Cup, its scale ensuring it evaded generalisation. Cities such as Vancouver and Seattle – with downtown stadiums and soccer traditions – were fitting hosts, while metropolises such as Dallas and San Francisco accommodated the month-long novelty without embracing it. JSn

The people in Mexico could not have been more welcoming, even when England beat their side. It was the same in Kansas City, England’s base and where I spent most of my time. On the other hand it would have been better if getting around some US cities was easier. Public transport infrastructure isn’t really a thing in some places. Florida especially. The Boston traffic was ridiculous, too. JSt

A wide range depending on venue but broadly friendly, welcoming and enthusiastic. Would benefit from improved public transport and generally lower volume. Wifi hopeless, coffee weak. JW

World Cup 2030 (very early) power rankings: who will challenge Spain at top?

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 09:00:11 GMT

The next men’s World Cup is still four years away, but we take a look at the teams with the firmest foundations who should be primed to contend

The 2026 World Cup provided many an esteemed veteran with what could be their international swansongs, with golden greats Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Luka Modric, Neymar, James Rodríguez and Guillermo Ochoa all making teary exits as their tournament ended. As we turn ahead to the 2030 World Cup, any player 32 or older will be sweating their selection status and changing their daily routines to stay sharp against inevitable aging.

For these power rankings, we’re overvaluing sure things. Teams with plenty of leading players comfortably in their 20s can build for this impending four-year cycle with greater confidence than a team replacing an ageless talisman. Consider these the 10 teams with the firmest foundations and viable reasons to hope to reach a quarter-final in four years’ time.

Mentioned players’ ages on 1 June 2030 listed (in parentheses).

The first defending World Cup champion to host the ensuing installment, Spain will enter 2030 as favorites to run it back. With Luis de la Fuente’s masterful sense of his team’s strengths and universal commitment from his players, this group could develop into a juggernaut.

Unai Simón (32), Joan García (29) and David Raya (34) could repeat as the goalkeeping trio. Marc Pubill (26), Eric García (29), Pedro Porro (30) and Pau Cubarsí (23) are a solid defensive bedrock. Dani Olmo (32), Gavi (25) and Pedri (27) should return in midfield, while Rodri (33) stands a good chance to start at the midfield’s base. Nico Williams (27) and Lamine Yamal (22) will hope to enjoy better fitness but demonstrated their importance in the final stages, and Ferran Torres (30) may be a threat from the bench again.

And, of course, there’s great talent beyond the title-winning 26. Dean Huijsen (25) and Cristhian Mosquera (25) are options to replace Aymeric Laporte (36), while Fermin López (27), Pablo Barrios (26), Javier Guerra (27), Marc Bernal (23) and Jesús Rodríguez (24) have featured under de la Fuente. If Samu Aghehowa (26) or Gonzalo García (26) can become a viable option at striker, Spain could wring even more goals from their possessive machine – a scary thought, indeed.

A fresh touchline voice arrives just in time, with Zinedine Zidane replacing the great Didier Deschamps after decreasing returns across his three World Cups. What lessons can Zizou glean from their stunning semi-final crumble against Spain?

Mike Maignan (34) should have another cycle in his capable gloves, shielded by Dayot Upamecano (31), Ibrahima Konaté (31) and William Saliba (29). The midfield is in good stead with Manu Koné (29) and Aurélien Tchouaméni (30), as well as squad snubs Eduardo Camavinga (27) and Khéphren Thuram (29). Kylian Mbappé (31) will be raring to extend his goalscoring record with Michael Olise (28) and Désiré Doué (24) in support. Talent wasn’t the issue so much as overcoming Spain’s structure, and for all his success with Real Madrid, Zidane impressed more with his squad management than his tactical chops.

The Three Lions showed impressive resolve, outlasting Mexico in an instant classic and coming back against Norway to return to the semi-final. Their timid failures to close out a 2-0 lead over Argentina will haunt many, but the reality is that England are poised for a very strong response at Euro 2028 and the next World Cup – with one glaring asterisk.

Marc Guéhi (29) looked a leading center-back for much of the tournament, with Djed Spence (29) having finished the World Cup in top form. Declan Rice (31), Elliot Anderson (27), Jude Bellingham (26) and Kobbie Mainoo (25) offer plenty of midfield combinations, and Bukayo Saka (28) and Anthony Gordon (29) fared well on the wings. The biggest question is whether Harry Kane can be a 90-minute option at age 36, as England hasn’t yet found an obvious successor to their leading goalscorer. Goalkeeper should also be an open battle, but players who missed Thomas Tuchel’s squad such as Lewis Hall (25), Cole Palmer (28), Adam Wharton (26), Alex Scott (26), Phil Foden (30), Rio Ngumoha (21) and Ayden Heaven (23) reiterate the depth of the pool.

The groundwork is excellent for another of 2030’s primary co-hosts. Back-to-back World Cup quarter-final runs, with one berth in the semis. Legal custody of the Afcon 2025 title. A freshly installed coach who got more verve from his side without sacrificing stability. Can Morocco take things a step or two further in 2030?

Achraf Hakimi (31), Chadi Riad (26), Anass Salah-Eddine (28) and Noussair Mazraoui (32) project to stick around in defense. Ayyoub Bouaddi (22) should be even better after his emergent World Cup, along with his midfield partner Azzedine Ounahi (30). Ismael Saibari (29) was a safe bet to score before his injury, while Bilal El Khannouss (26), Gessime Yassine (24) and Brahim Díaz (30) also challenge any backline.

Morocco won the most recent U-20 World Cup, led by forwards Othmane Maamma (24) and Yassir Zabiri (25) as well as goalkeeper Ibrahim Gomis (25). If goalkeeping hero Yassine Bounou (39) can somehow stay in his usual blistering form, they’ll be a tough draw for anybody.

Argentina’s run to the final reiterated how uniquely vital Messi was to his team, both as the determinant of their attack and the heart every teammate fought hard to protect. He is, by every definition of the word, irreplaceable.

Then again, Argentina were not just a one-man band. Julián Álvarez (30) has grown increasingly comfortable as a leading man, and should again be backed up by lethal Lautaro Martínez (32). Enzo Fernández (33) has a lot of apologies to give after his send-off, but should anchor midfield this cycle. Nahuel Molina (32), Cristian Romero (32) and Lisandro Martínez (32) will be veteran defenders, while Emiliano Martínez (37) should have plenty left to offer. They also were runners-up at the last U-20 World Cup, with standouts including midfielder Milton Delgado (24), left-back Julio Soler (25) and goalkeeper Santino Barbi (24).

Sign up to Soccer Desk: World Cup Edition

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Portugal were left to wonder what could have been with a more natural and mobile line-leader atop an otherwise terrific team. Ronaldo has admitted he won’t play in the 2030 tournament at age 45, and the biggest question will become whether Roberto Martínez squandered this generation’s best chance to win a first World Cup.

Diogo Costa (30) is among the world’s best goalkeepers, with Gonçalo Inácio (28) and Nuno Mendes (27) forming a strong defensive base. António Silva (26) will hope to get his promising career back on track, seemingly with Bournemouth, while João Neves (25) and Vitinha (30) would start in nearly any nation’s midfield. Gonçalo Ramos (28), João Félix (30) and Francisco Conceição (27) return in attack, too. But with the list of aging players including the great Bruno Fernandes (35), Bernardo Silva (35) and Rúben Dias (33), it’s hard not to feel the best opportunity has been missed.

Few will underestimate Norway after their deserved run to the quarter-final, with a culture in and around the team that became the envy of the summer. Many of their men should be back in four years, including the main-est man of all.

Few people seemed to have enjoyed this World Cup as much as Erling Haaland (29), who should still be devastating defenses when the next one comes around. Andreas Schjelderup (26), Antonio Nusa (25) and Oscar Bobb (26) are credible running mates in the final third, while Martin Ødegaard (31) will hope to shirk his injury bugs to pull the strings once again. There will need to be ample rotation in the defensive half and in goal, but as long as Haaland is leading the line, Norway will stand a chance.

The Elephants impressed in a tricky Group E, beating Ecuador and Curaçao before falling to Norway in the last-32. If Emerse Faé is back to lead this team, he’ll enjoy an immense level of talent to work with as (part of) the tournament returns to Africa.

Yahia Fofana (29) is steady in goal, his job made easier by the collective defending of Ousmane Diomande (26), Odilon Kossounou (29) and Wilfried Singo (29). Their forward options pose champagne selection issues: Amad Diallo (27), Oumar Diakité (26), Elye Wahi (27), Yan Diomandé (23), Simon Adingra (28) and Ange-Yoan Bonny (26). Midfield appears to be their only thin area especially if Franck Kessié (33) ages out of starting status. But on paper, and on the back of a first World Cup knockout match and the Afcon 2023 title, they’re a team to watch.

While the legion of club managers making their World Cup debuts in 2026 saw mixed returns, Jürgen Klopp has four years to build his ideal culture and refine a new system for Die Mannschaft. That seems a dream scenario after a trio of disappointing tournaments on the back of 2014’s triumph.

The bigger question is whether Germany have the players. An injury to Lennart Karl (22) on the eve of the World Cup put a damper on preparations, but the Bayern playmaker would be a welcome addition. Kai Havertz (30) should pop up with timely goals, while Florian Wirtz (27) and Jamal Musiala (27) will hope to arrive in better form and fitness. Nathaniel Brown (26) looks to be an ideal wing-back for the next few cycles, and Joshua Kimmich (35) has already dismissed concerns that he may retire before Klopp arrives. That’s a relief given how much turnover will be necessary from this summer’s squad in the defensive half.

The Balogun Affair stripped the sheen off of what had been the US’s most promising men’s World Cup showing to date. Mauricio Pochettino’s status for the next cycle is uncertain. Still, the Americans’ run to the last 16 saw many players of a similar age group step up and project to be mainstays.

Folarin Balogun (28) should be an even more refined forward to follow his three-goal showing this summer, while Malik Tillman (28) offers strong dead-ball service and tidy midfield play. Chris Richards (30), Tyler Adams (31), Weston McKennie (31), Christian Pulisic (31) and Alex Freeman (25) will probably continue to be foundational pieces, while Sebastian Berhalter (29), Gio Reyna (27) and Ricardo Pepi (27) should stick around after capable World Cup showings. A 12th-place finish still indicates a last-16 exit that has become the frustrating norm for the US, but perhaps the lessons of a high-pressure hosting gig will really pay off in four years.
