Here’s how Andy Burnham really could end homelessness

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 09:00:10 GMT

Utilising empty homes, capping rents and fixing the benefits system would all help, but they’d require a serious fight

In January 2017, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham, promised to end rough sleeping in the region by 2020 – a bold, frankly absurd promise that inevitably didn’t materialise. Nearly a decade later, shortly after becoming prime minister, Burnham promised to end rough sleeping again, only this time for the whole of England. So why should we believe him this time around?

I have interviewed Burnham several times over the past decade. At the end of 2019, when it was clear he had not lived up to his promise, I asked him if he regretted making it in the first place. “I wasn’t making what you would call a traditional target,” the mayor said. “I issued my commitment to make it more of a wake-up call to the system. And I think it has had that effect.” Burnham’s advisers had told him to tone down the pledge, but he resisted. “The team here said I should have said: ‘End the need for rough sleeping,’ because you can’t force people into a shelter … In retrospect, if I had said ‘end the need for’, that probably would have been a wiser thing to have done. But I wasn’t in the space of wanting to play semantics with it.”

Official figures showed rough sleeping decreased by two-thirds in Manchester during his first five years as mayor. There are reasons I can quibble with this claim. First of all, it doesn’t pass the eye test. Just walk through the city centre in the early hours, and you’ll find people still bedding down in their dozens. Second, the statistics on rough sleeping are based on single-night snapshots, which involve council representatives walking around counting the people they find rough sleeping. The problem with this is obvious. Third, even those stats, as unreliable as they are, now show that rough sleeping in Manchester is three-quarters of what it was in 2017.

But let’s forget all that, and give the prime minister the benefit of the doubt. Maybe his “promise” was merely a “wake-up call”. He was a metro mayor after all, and for most of his time in office, he depended on the generosity of a Conservative government. He simply didn’t have the resources to end rough sleeping. Let’s also assume that Burnham means what he says. He didn’t have to make his pledge back in 2017, and he certainly didn’t have to make it on the steps of Downing Street on Monday.

The difference is that now he has control of the purse strings, so how does Burnham intend to honour his promise this time around? Initial signs are not encouraging. After Burnham finished his speech, his new government pledged an extra £340m, equivalent to £68m a year over five years, on top of the £3.5bn already allocated, to tackle homelessness. The UK can’t quite agree on how many rough sleepers there are, but I think a sensible estimate is anywhere between 15,000-18,000 unique people over a 12-month period. So, £68m divided among 18,000 people amounts to £3,777 per head. That’s about four months of rent if you’re lucky. It’s less a panacea, more like defending yourself from a tidal wave with a cocktail umbrella.

The government will say it is only targeting 3,000 of the most vulnerable rough sleepers with this cash, and they will receive closer to £22,000 per head. I don’t know how one would qualify for the most-vulnerable list. Just how hopeless do you need to be in the new Burnham era?

If Burnham really wants to live up to his promise, he’ll need to do a lot better than this. He should be aware from the start that rough sleeping represents the very tip of an enormous iceberg, and solving homelessness in this country will demand something close to a revolution. According to Shelter, there are 380,000 homeless people in England, and even that demoralising figure is almost certainly an underestimate. To permanently house those people would require an unprecedented social housebuilding programme that would make the postwar rebuild look like a casual game of Minecraft.

Burnham’s government would also need to reverse 16 years of austerity. This is all quite spendy, and to fund it would require higher taxes, more borrowing and aggressive nationalisation of natural monopolies. An upheaval of the economy of such magnitude is unlikely to happen when so many Labour MPs have their fingernails firmly embedded in the market. If there’s even a suggestion that Burnham intends to depart from turbo capitalism, then he will be out of SW1 faster than you can say Liz Truss.

So, what can Burnham realistically do about homelessness? There are several levers available to him to ease people’s suffering in the short term, and they cost next to nothing in political or real capital.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

His priority should be triggering a nationwide Housing First programme. Housing First, a policy pioneered in Finland that effectively eliminated rough sleeping, gives people a home with no preconditions, then tailors support to their individual needs. We know this works because we did it ourselves, only with a different name. The Everyone In campaign, established during the Covid-19 pandemic, virtually ended rough sleeping overnight by emergency block-booking hotels. Surely we can do the same thing again.

The next thing on the agenda should be removing the stick from the benefits system. Currently, the welfare state resembles a gameshow created by Kafka, where contestants have to complete a series of timed trials to win basic subsistence.

There are about 300,000 long-term empty homes in England. Housing people in some of these dwellings might be a good idea; capping rents at an affordable rate would be another, as would fast-tracking asylum applications and enabling asylum seekers to receive benefits and temporary work visas while their claims are processed.

I’m not confident that Burnham will do any of these things. Not because I think he doesn’t care or lacks the political will, but because government apparatus is smothered in molasses, and most Labour politicians are Tories in all but name.

But let’s see what Burnham does before writing him off as yet another neoliberal metronome with fine words and dry parsnips. Let’s give the man his honeymoon period, but the “king of the north” should keep this in mind: winter is coming, and he must act quickly, not just for his premiership, but for the poor souls he has promised to get off the streets.

Daniel Lavelle writes on mental health, homelessness and social care. He received the Guardian’s Hugo Young award in 2017, and is the author of Down and Out

Why many Black Americans were rooting for Argentina to lose the World Cup

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 09:00:10 GMT

Many Black Americans were not cheering Spain’s complicated history. They were rooting against the racism, politics and silence associated with Argentina

There are moments in sports when you realize people aren’t just watching the score any more. They’re watching values. They’re watching who speaks. They’re watching who stays silent. And they’re watching what those silences say.

I found myself thinking about that throughout this World Cup. On paper, Sunday’s final looked simple. Spain v Argentina. Two footballing giants and countries with glorious soccer histories. Two nations whose pasts are also stained by colonization, oppression and chapters of history that shouldn’t be whitewashed simply because someone can score a goal.

So no, this wasn’t some fairytale of good versus evil. Spain’s colonial legacy is well documented. Nobody who knows history should pretend otherwise.

Yet for many Black Americans, this final wasn’t really about rooting for Spain. It was about rooting against Argentina.

When your fanbase repeatedly becomes associated with racist incidents … when videos circulate of Argentinian fans decked out in Argentina team gear hurling racial epithets toward Black people … when the world watched members of Argentina’s national team sing a racist chant targeting France’s Black players after winning Copa América … when American streamer IShowSpeed was verbally assaulted by fans fully dressed in Argentina team gear … when word spreads across social media that in Argentina, there is a real hamburger business in Llavallol whose official name uses the “-a” version of the N-word: “Big N– Burgers” … when Argentina president Javier Milei openly embraces positions that align very closely with Donald Trump and offers support for Israel in the midst of a genocide, ethnic cleansing and slaughter of Palestinians … when Benjamin Netanyahu is asked on a recent podcast if he was rooting for Messi and says, “No, before Messi, Milei. He’s a superstar” … eventually, the tide of supports shifts. After a while, any accomplishments on the field become overshadowed.

It’s like a college basketball coach who has all the appearances of a great program. He has a great winning percentage and a high graduation rate, and all of his players are disciplined, articulate and present themselves as professionals. But you keep hearing stories of verbal abuse and berating, whispers of a tyrant coach who is actively damaging his players’ mental health. At some point, the results become secondary and people start asking, “What’s going on with the Indiana Hoosiers?”

Argentina kept giving people reasons to ask that question. Which brings us to Lionel Messi.

This is where people get uncomfortable because everybody loves Messi, and for good reason. His brilliance doesn’t require exaggeration. His résumé speaks louder than any sports debate ever could. Whether you think he’s the greatest player ever or merely one of them – shoutout to Pelé – you’re arguing over different shades of greatness.

But greatness on the field has never automatically translated into courage off it.

Muhammad Ali taught us that. Bill Russell taught us that. Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf taught us that. Craig Hodges taught us that. John Carlos and Tommie Smith taught us that. Being extraordinary with a ball, a bat or track shoes isn’t the same thing as being willing to risk comfort for conviction.

To my knowledge, throughout this entire World Cup, Messi never publicly condemned the racist incidents involving sections of Argentina’s fanbase. He did not publicly address the racist chant that drew worldwide criticism after Copa América. Nor has he publicly spoken out after videos of Argentina supporters racially abusing Black people circulated online.

He didn’t even offer the kind of broad, indirect condemnation that many critics argued was insufficient when Caitlin Clark addressed racist abuse coming from some of her supporters. As my co-host Chuck Modi argued on our show The Collision: Where Sports and Politics Collide:

“She has to be more specific. When Alyssa Thomas was getting death threats, she has to say Alyssa Thomas by name, and say directly to her fans that you cannot have death threats going to Alyssa Thomas in my name the same way we as Jewish people say not in my name for Palestinian rights. She needs to use all of her clout and tell her fans this is unacceptable.”

Messi did not even clear that lower bar. He offered no public statement at all addressing the racism carried out by some of his supporters.

As Dr Martin Luther King Jr said in his Beyond Vietnam speech: “A time comes when silence is betrayal.”

Sometimes silence becomes its own statement simply because the loudest voice in the room chose not to use it. Contrast that with the generation coming after Messi.

Lamine Yamal has spoken openly about his family’s sacrifices. He has recalled how his father searched through discarded items that could be repaired or sold so there would be enough money for food. He has said he grew up in a tiny apartment where the kitchen and bedroom were one and the same. Today, he says what makes him happiest is seeing his mother smile and knowing his younger brother can enjoy the childhood he never had.

Nico Williams carries a similarly powerful story. His mother, María, walked nearly 2,000 miles while pregnant, from Ghana toward Spain, in search of a better life. Decades later, her son set up the goal that won Spain the World Cup and then placed his winner’s medal around her neck.

Spain’s triumph was never just about tactics, possession or technical excellence. It was about possibility. It was a team that reflected the modern Spain – diverse, confident and shaped by the journeys of families who crossed borders in pursuit of a better life. That, more than any passing sequence or tactical innovation, was their most powerful statement.

After Spain defeated Argentina on Sunday, one image stood out to me: Lamine Yamal embracing Messi. No taunting or chest-pounding or disrespect, just respect from one generation to another. Like the old African Proverb says: “The lion doesn’t need to roar after every meal.”

Another image that resonated was seeing Lamine Yamal kneel in prayer amid the chaos around him while emotions boiled over after the match. While others argued, he prayed. That image reminded me that composure can be louder than confrontation.

Lamine Yamal has also shown a willingness to let people know where he stands on issues beyond football, including expressing solidarity with Palestine. Whether people agree with every public stance an athlete takes is almost beside the point. The point is that he is willing to recognize that his platform extends beyond 90 (or 120) minutes on the field.

Jackie Robinson wasn’t remembered simply because he stole bases. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar isn’t remembered simply because he had the most unstoppable move the NBA has ever seen. Colin Kaepernick isn’t remembered simply because of his dual-threat quarterbacking skills. Eventually the statistics become paragraphs, but character becomes chapters.

That’s why comparisons between Messi and Ali don’t really work for me. One changed football forever, but the other changed the world.

Some people have asked why so many Black Americans seemed emotionally invested in seeing Argentina lose. I don’t think it’s complicated. When you’ve spent your entire life hearing people tell you sports and politics should stay separate – but somehow they only say that after racism enters the conversation – you start recognizing the pattern.

People told Ali to “just box”. People told Kaepernick to “just play football”. People told LeBron James to “shut up and dribble”. People effectively accused Jaylen Brown of being “uppity”. Apparently athletes are free to use their platforms – unless they’re using them for something that makes people uncomfortable.

That’s always been the rule, until it isn’t.

This World Cup became about more than goals because people made it about more than goals. Racism made it bigger. Politics made it bigger. Silence made it bigger. For many viewers, supporting Spain wasn’t an endorsement of Spain’s history; it was simply rejecting what Argentina had come to represent in this particular moment. Sometimes cheering isn’t about choosing perfection, but about choosing the option that feels less harmful.

Maybe that’s why so many people found themselves drawn to this young generation. Not simply because they won, but because they represent the possibility that excellence and conviction don’t have to play on different teams. To quote Abdul-Rauf from our interview for my book Police Brutality and White Supremacy: The Fight Against American Traditions: “What you do speaks so loudly in my ears that I can’t hear a word you’re saying.”

I couldn’t agree more.

The children who loved a killer

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 08:00:09 GMT

The Carr family took in Steven Judy, hoping to ‘save’ a troubled teen. They didn’t know he would become one of the most hated men in America

Childhood returns to Traci Carr in fragments.

Night-time. She is five. She wakes to shadows on the wall, her room strange in the dark. Her footie pyjamas slip against the wood as she pads downstairs and climbs into bed next to her foster brother, Steven Judy.

He scoots over, and the monsters recede. She burrows under the covers, feeling safe.

Morning. Traci and Steve share Froot Loops, their favorite cereal, the milk turning pink. He teases her, tells funny stories, acts extra goofy to make her laugh.

Later, they play hide and seek. He’s all theater, snapping a belt in the air as he searches for Traci and her three older siblings. They collapse in giggles when he finds them.

Then one day, Steve disappears.

No one explains where he went. Her parents are away for long stretches, too. When they are home, conversations drop into whispers. Doors click shut. The television is switched off when she enters the room.

The year Traci turns seven, her parents take her on a car ride. At Conkle funeral home just outside Indianapolis, the room smells of carnations and furniture polish.

She is led to the coffin at the end of the room. She peers over the edge.

It’s Steve.

His eyes are closed, his face composed. His hair isn’t right – a wig, she’ll learn later. But otherwise, he looks like himself.

Her mother, Mary, leans close. Touch him, she urges.

I don’t want to.

Her mother insists. Don’t be afraid. Just touch him. Traci extends a single finger. It leaves a dent in his cold skin.

Three days earlier, on 9 March 1981, the state of Indiana had executed Steven Judy. Traci would not fully grasp this for years.

Decades on, she still carries the confusion of that day. It flickers across her face as we sit in her kitchen, a plastic storage bin between us filled with his belts, his wallet, his watch, letters, photographs: the small, stubborn evidence of a brother they once loved. A brother whose grave drew hate-filled handwritten notes decades after his death.

For decades, Judy’s crimes have been revisited in books, documentaries and true-crime retellings. His atrocities have been replayed, his psychology dissected. But Traci and her siblings are missing from those narratives. The families of condemned people are among the least visible casualties of capital punishment, even as the death penalty is on the rise again.

The Carr children loved and lost a foster brother the rest of the world called a monster. No one asked what it was like to be them. For decades, they were not ready to say.

I was there the day Judy died.

I was a young Associated Press journalist assigned to cover the family’s side of the story and had arrived in Michigan City on Sunday, the day before the execution.

As reporters and photographers gathered outside the prison, I sat in a hotel room with the family. Over months of reporting, I had quietly slipped into their orbit. I wasn’t a friend, exactly, but I had become a witness to their unraveling at a moment when most people looked away.

Eleven years earlier, a young man murdered my eighth-grade friend Cindy Winter in the Sonoran desert about a quarter of a mile from her home. We children had no language for this; neither did the grownups around us. After the first days of sorrow, we stopped speaking of Cindy altogether. Assigned to the Judy case, I did not yet understand that I was trying to report my way back into a story I already belonged to: violent death, bewildered survivors, and grief with nowhere to go.

That day, Traci had stayed home with a babysitter. In the afternoon, I went swimming with the other Carr children. We had lunch, and then dinner, though no one ate much.

Around 11pm, Judy’s foster father, Bob Carr, left for the prison. He had reluctantly agreed to Judy’s request that he witness the execution, which was scheduled shortly after midnight. By then, the kids were asleep, or appeared to be.

Mary thumbed through Polaroids of Judy that she had brought with her, sometimes glancing at the clock beside the bed. She smoked the way some people pray, steadily, wordlessly, through the waiting.

Shortly before 1am, Carr returned to our hotel with attorney Steve Harris. For Mary’s benefit, he described Judy’s final 71 minutes.

A shaved head. A cigarette. A phone call to a girlfriend who had sent him a last-minute telegram – Judy joked that if she proposed marriage, he might ask for a stay. A final Polaroid taken for the Carrs, never made public until now. A Valium to calm Judy’s nerves before the end. Some tears, some jokes.

At 12.04am, the guards blindfolded Judy and led him a few paces to the chair in the next room. Harris and Carr moved to the witness room.

“I don’t hold no grudges. This was my doing. I’m sorry it happened,” Judy said from the chair before the switch was thrown.

Mary soaked in every detail, hanging on every word, sometimes asking Harris to repeat himself. The ashtray beside her filled with cigarette stubs.

Within the month, she admitted herself to a psychiatric hospital for a brief period, shattered by what had happened. I visited her there. Wearing a hospital gown, she seemed emptied of the force that had animated her for months – defending Judy, raging at the state, willing him somehow to survive. The fight had fled her body.

I spent months with the Carrs, but I shed no tears for Judy. I did not mistake him for an innocent man. Still, I could not believe justice had been served by strapping him into a chair and killing him. The state had not restored his victims to life; it had only widened the circle of suffering. Our world, as I saw it, had room for outrage, punishment and fascination, but little space for certain kinds of grief.

I did not yet know that this story would stay with me for the next 45 years.

The facts of the case are these: on the morning of 28 April 1979, around 6.30am, Judy, 22, raped and murdered Terry Lee Chasteen, 21, along the banks of White Lick Creek outside Indianapolis.

When her three children – ages two, four and five – cried, he threw them into the creek to drown.

It wasn’t his first violent crime, but it was the one for which he would be executed.

The four bodies were discovered later that morning by mushroom hunters. Residents called it the worst crime Morgan county had ever seen.

A distinctive red and silver truck seen near the site of the killings was traced back to Bob Carr. He told police his foster son had borrowed it the night before. Judy was arrested the next day.

Public outrage hardened quickly. Even before all the evidence was presented, a grassroots group called Protect the Innocent demanded the death penalty.

At first, Judy said he couldn’t remember what happened. Later, he confessed. Harris, the attorney, initially pursued an insanity defense, but two court-appointed psychiatrists concluded Judy was legally sane.

After the guilty verdict, Judy made his preference clear: death over life in prison. Determined to eliminate any possibility of leniency, he proposed leaping across the table to attack the prosecutor before sentencing.

“You can’t do that,” Harris told him. “There are 50 officers in that courtroom.”

Instead, Judy asked to address the jury. He told them he knew their names, where they lived, where they worked, and would kill anyone who failed to vote for the electric chair. Then he turned toward the bench. “That goes for you too, bud,” he said to the judge.

The jury deliberated 20 minutes before recommending the death penalty.

Forty-five years later, one of the people I most wanted to find was Harris. He had witnessed the crime’s aftermath and Judy’s final hours. I wondered what remained with him after all this time.

Before Judy, Harris had handled three other murder cases. After the execution, he vowed never to take another death penalty case. “It was time-consuming and emotional,” he recalls now. “I just made the decision I would never do one again.” He represented only one other murder defendant, then gradually left criminal law altogether.

He drove me to the bridge overlooking the stretch of White Lick Creek where the killings took place, about a mile and a half from his office. State Road 67 hums nearby now, busy and indifferent. Round the bend, the creek remains as secluded as it was then; teenagers still go there to hang out beyond the sight of their parents.

A rope swing dangles beneath a railroad bridge where someone has painted: “THE DEVIL WAS HERE.” The water moves on.

Steve saved Randy Carr’s life when Randy was two years old.

Randy was playing in a mud puddle in the alley behind their house when a family friend known as Stinky climbed into Bob Carr’s truck and began backing it up, running over Randy’s legs. Steve saw the scene unfold and began yelling and waving his arms.

“He stopped him,” Randy says. “Another minute and Stinky would have run over my head.”

After that, Steve became Randy’s person. “The only one who paid me any attention,” Randy recalls. Saturdays were their day. Together, they cleaned the basement, mowed the grass. When the chores were done, Steve took him for ice-cream. “Never failed,” Randy remembers.

Steve entered the Carr family through a friendship with Randy’s Uncle Tony. On the day of the Chasteen murders, Randy, who was nine, and his brother Bobby, who was 11, helped Steve clean out the garage. They drove trash to the dump. They swept out their father’s pickup truck, the one Steve had been driving earlier that morning.

Then they went for ice-cream.

The next day, the police came. Steve was out with a friend, but they questioned the boys. They drove them back to the dump and asked where the trash had been thrown.

“I wasn’t going to tell them,” Randy says. “I pointed everywhere except where we dumped.”

Back at home, Randy went to the window with a pair of binoculars and watched as officers dusted the truck for fingerprints. He watched them wait for Steve to come back. “I didn’t grasp what was happening,” he says. “Dad never told us anything.”

After Steve’s arrest, children at school avoided Randy. He began fighting. “I would get mad if anybody told me Steve was guilty of this. I couldn’t see it in my mind. Steve couldn’t do this.”

Eventually, Steve told Randy himself.

“You’ve gotta let it go,” Steve said. “I’m guilty of this. It’s something I can’t control.”

He joked about the electric chair. “Man, I’m gonna ride that lightning.”

Randy thought he meant an amusement park ride. “I still didn’t understand,” he says.

Years later, Randy came to believe Steve deserved to die. He says that plainly now. But then he adds, quietly, tearing up: “To this day, I hate that he did that. Because he was everything I had in life.”

In the months before the execution, Randy started spiraling. He skipped school for the first time. He stole diet pills to get high. “I just felt like I needed to do something.” When his mother told Steve during a prison visit that Randy was acting out, Steve wrote Randy a seven-page letter about his own childhood, about how he had started screwing up.

In a letter to Mary, Steve mentioned that he had written to Randy, and offered her some parenting advice: “Listen, Mary, I just wrote Randy that letter we talked about. It was hard, too. I don’t know if it was exactly what you wanted but I think it will help if he listens. But you have to understand if you keep telling someone not to do this or that, it sometimes pushes them to do it anyway for spite.”

Randy read the letter “a thousand times” when he was a kid. He never skipped school again. “I loved Steve to death. I defended him for a long time. I broke a lot of jaws of people who didn’t really deserve it.”

Randy begged Steve to appeal against the death penalty. “I cried with him for a long time. Finally Steve said: ‘Look at me. Don’t bring this up again. It’s over with. Don’t be sad, because this is what I need.’”

Randy visited Steve the afternoon before his execution. “I was so upset. But Steve was laughing and carrying on like nothing was happening. It just blows my mind how he knows he’s going to his death, and he was just worried about how I was.”

A few months after the funeral, Traci noticed the spine of a book jutting from a stack of papers on the kitchen countertop.

Burn Judy Burn.

Published between Judy’s conviction and his execution, the book was written by Bette Nunn, managing editor of the Reporter-Times in Martinsville, Indiana.

Traci pulled it free and turned immediately to the photographs. One showed a small body just beneath the water’s surface. Another showed a little boy lying on a metal table, his shirt half pulled up from his torso.

They were children, very small. She could tell they were close to her age.

“I was starting to piece it together,” she told me. “I think I knew Steve had killed somebody. But I still didn’t understand what had happened to him.”

So she asked Randy. What happened to Steve? He told her what he could, as much as he understood.

She couldn’t reconcile the brother she knew with the killer described in the book. Yet she kept returning to the photographs. “I had a morbid interest,” she says. The more she grasped, the more terrified she became. The house itself seemed altered. When she returned from school and found no one there, she wouldn’t go inside, pacing the sidewalk instead.

She didn’t ask her parents any questions. She had already noticed the way her mother seemed always on the verge of tears, the way her parents argued in low, urgent voices. The whole house seemed stretched tight with things no one knew how to say aloud.

My editor at the Associated Press asked me to begin reporting on the case in early March 1980, 10 months after the murders of Terry Chasteen and her three children. Judy would become the first person executed in Indiana since 1961 and among the first handful nationally after the supreme court reinstated the death penalty in 1976.

I saw two possible ways into the story. I could try to reach Judy through his attorney, or I could try to understand the family waiting outside the prison walls.

I called Mary Carr. She invited me over immediately.

Mary worked as a drill operator at a manufacturing plant; Bob laid brick and stone for a living. Their house sat in a working-class neighborhood outside Indianapolis, small and crowded, every surface carrying its own accumulation of papers, toys, ashtrays, cups. Four children moved constantly through the rooms. Mary was not yet 31.

Bob was warm but reserved. Mary directed the energy of the house. Within minutes, she had seated me in a padded brown chair and placed a photo album in my lap. She pointed to photographs of Steven Judy.

“Look at him,” she said. “He’s handsome, isn’t he? He’s not cold and detached the way they say.”

I felt myself recoil. I understood that I could never look at Judy the way Mary Carr did.

When I was in eighth grade, my friend Cindy Winter was murdered in Tucson while riding her bicycle to a close friend’s house on a Sunday afternoon. Her body was found under a mesquite tree at the edge of a dry wash. The man who killed her was 24. He was arrested after he raped and killed another woman, leaving her two children alive beside the road.

The similarities between his case and Judy’s were striking. Before Cindy’s murder, we thought the desert between houses belonged to us. Afterward, the fear never fully left.

Meeting the Carrs conjured that dread back to life. After that first visit, I wrote in my journal: “Walking from my sturdy Scout to my apartment after midnight, the bushes seem to reach out as menacing men, and in the moonlight, I can see my fear.”

I could never understand the killer. But I wanted to understand the family living in the aftermath of what he had done.

I began to spend time at the Carrs’ kitchen table. I ate pizza with them, went swimming with the kids, phoned Mary to check in. Her warmth as a mother, I learned, was instinctive rather than structured. She wasn’t the kind of parent who tracked homework or studied report cards. What she offered instead was openness, noise, food, a place to belong. She believed that when her family took Steve in, they were finally giving him something no one else had: a loving family, a permanent place at the table.

“She thought she could save him,” Traci says. And that was exactly who Mary Carr was, a woman who believed in second chances, in the redemptive power of love and a full table. She had been raised by a mother who withdrew support, but Mary had chosen a different path: she made room. She fed people. She believed damage could be repaired if you loved hard enough and long enough.

This impulse would define the next eight years of her life, but Judy had arrived carrying damage the Carrs could not fully see.

In court records and later interviews, Judy described his childhood as violent and unstable. Both parents drank heavily. His father beat his mother and once, in a fit of fury, butchered a pet dog, leaving pieces scattered on the porch for the children to see. His mother brought men home; sometimes the children witnessed them having sex. She occasionally summoned Judy to kiss her while she was bathing or undressing, placing him on her lap and running her fingers through his hair. Pornographic magazines, he said, were kept openly in the house.

By age 10, he was pushing high school girls to the ground and molesting them. At 11, he began shoplifting; by 12, he was drinking. On 17 April 1970, at 13, he raped a 22-year-old woman and attacked her with a knife and a hatchet so severely that she required brain, abdominal and open-heart surgery to survive.

He was detained and transferred to the juvenile section of Indiana’s Central State hospital. Opened in 1848 as the Indiana hospital for the “insane”, central state closed in 1994 amid scandals over patient treatment and funding shortfalls. The old pathology building, where autopsies were once performed in search of the physical causes of madness, now houses the Indiana Medical History Museum. Brains sit in glass jars, labeled with names, dates, symptoms.

At Central State, Judy was diagnosed as a sexual psychopath. He became friends with Bob Carr’s younger brother, Tony, who also was a resident after getting in trouble at school and home. Through him, he met the rest of the family.

When Judy was released at age 15, Mary and Bob agreed to take him in. As a juvenile, he needed to be released to adults; this must have felt like astonishing good fortune to him.

He lived with the Carrs, ate at their table, and worked construction for Bob. But the violence continued: more assaults, more jail time, a robbery.

The Carrs even paid his bond weeks before the Chasteen murders.

Throughout, “Mom always loved Steve,” Traci recalls. “She never said anything bad about him, no matter what.”

Prison life became a world of letters. Steve wrote and received hundreds of them.

Mary kept many of them in a bedroom drawer: letters from strangers who prayed for him, or from women who had never met him but said they loved him.

For Mary and Bob, he described his life in prison with flashes of humor and longing. Without his television set, he would “go bonkers”, Steve wrote. “So far I’ve earned $15,000 on the Joker’s Wild, gotten three dates on the Dating Game, and outdrawn Marshall Dillon twice.”

“Tell the kids I said hi and I love them,” he wrote time and again. Sometimes he mentioned them by name: “You tell Traci I said hi and that I love her too and that I’ve got a get-rich-quick scheme for us. I’m going to write the cereal company and tell them me and her are going to quit eating cereal and put them out of business unless they pay us a million dollars (50 cents anyway, ha ha).”

During prison visits, Steve offered Mary tips on staying safe and told her to pass them on to his foster sisters. Lock the car doors. Watch the blind spot. Don’t pull over if a man waves you down.

After he was sentenced to death, Harris filed a routine appeal. But in October 1980, Judy told the court he did not want to pursue it, clearing the way for his execution six months later.

Steve wrote to his foster parents soon after. “I know you can’t accept what I’m doing but I hope you don’t hate me for it either,” he told them. Mary had cried during a prison visit, and he had avoided telling her in front of the boys.

“I’m sorry you had to find it out like you did,” he wrote. “I’m not going to get into my reasons and feelings on why I wanted it like this because I think it would be better to tell you here where we can look at each other’s faces.”

Steve was determined to carry through with the death penalty, but there were moments of fear. Right after he was transferred to death row in Michigan City, he wrote: “Mary, don’t ever let anyone tell you this isn’t bad, because it is, and I’m scared to death.”

Later he wrote: “I’m worried about how the kids are taking it all. There’s just so much on my mind that can’t ever be put into words.”

On 5 Febuary 1981, 32 days before the execution, he apologized for not writing. “I just let myself get so far down in the dumps that it was hard to do anything.” He warned Mary that people might try to persuade her to intervene. “I know a few of them might try and get you to interfere but I hope you don’t,” he wrote. “About the only thing you could possibly do is cause a short delay and that would only hurt me.” Then, as he often did, he turned back to the children: “Tell me, how are the kids doing? I really hope they’re taking all this okay. Tell them I said hello and I send my love.”

Steve considered Bob’s mother, Rosita Mary Colvin, his foster grandmother. He affectionately called her “the old lady” and asked about her in letters. She wrote him shortly before his execution: “I have loved you from the first time I saw you at Central, your blond hair flying around, you and Tony playing basketball. You was a beautiful child. If you had been my own son, I could not have loved you more. I’m so sorry, Steve. I don’t know what went wrong. I just want you to know you are loved by all of us and our lives will never be the same.”

His last letter was written to his attorney. Judy told Harris that he had committed about 50 robberies and burglaries and 15 rapes. He confessed directly to one additional murder, indicated there was a second, and said he’d left women tied up so there might be others. He promised to list all his crimes in a letter to be opened after his death.

That last day, he gave Harris a thick sealed envelope.

Police knew this list of confessions was coming and they were waiting. Immediately after the execution, Harris opened the envelope.

In front of him was one page of writing followed by seven blank sheets.

When I visited Harris this year, he spread the letter on his desk so I could read it: “I’m sorry Steve [Harris] but I’ve decided to handle it this way because I care too much for my foster mom and family. I hope you can understand. Thank you for all you’ve done for me. Steve.”

In his final photo, Judy stands next to Harris in the holding cell, minutes before the execution. His head is shaved. A cigarette rests between the fingers of his right hand. “I’m gonna give these things up,” he quipped to Harris.

“It was kind of scary that he could be so dangerous and actually a likable person,” Harris recalled. “He had a sense of humor.”

Steve asked that he not be interred behind Indiana state prison, where prisoners whose families don’t claim them are buried. The Carrs bought him a plot and headstone in Floral Park cemetery, less than a mile away from Central State hospital, where they first met him.

In the cemetery office, I asked for a map to help me locate the gravesite.

“Steven Judy,” the clerk said slowly. Hate letters were regularly left on Steve’s grave until about five years ago, he said. “Our groundskeepers removed them every morning. It became routine.”

The story of death penalty cases is usually told through a narrow cast of characters: the victims, the condemned, sometimes the families of those murdered or the legal teams. Almost no one asks what happens to the families who loved the condemned, especially when they are children.

Scholars who study capital punishment have identified those families as a distinct and largely invisible group. Sociologist Susan Sharp began studying them in 1996. In her book Hidden Victims, she describes them as living in a kind of moral exile.

“They are tainted by association,” Sharp told me. “We assume they must have done something wrong.”

Sharp estimates that roughly 30% of death row prisoners have no family contact, either because of long estrangement or because relatives cut ties after the crime. For the other 70%, she said, the family’s punishment can continue long after the condemned person is executed.

To outsiders, it can seem inexplicable that a family member can feel both horror for the victims and heartache for someone who has done monstrous harm. “We treat those family members as if they don’t have a right to grieve. We take away their right to be human,” Sharp says. “We fail to realize everyone is multifaceted. None of us is equal to the worst thing we’ve ever done.”

Families who provide primary support to prisoners on death row, as the Carrs did, are likely to suffer from depression, anxiety and PTSD that often go untreated or unrecognized, according to a report by the Texas After Violence Project, a non-profit oral history organization.

Sociologist and death penalty scholar Michael L Radelet is deeply familiar with the Steven Judy case; it partly inspired his first book, Facing the Death Penalty. “The family members of the executed are among the most powerless in our communities,” he told me. “The death penalty just doubles the number of innocent families who are mourning the loss of a loved one.”

With no institutional support and little public sympathy, many families carry loss, shame and sorrow for decades. “They are victims of the system,” Sharp said. “We need to find ways to intervene and help them make sense of it.”

After the execution, threatening and abusive calls flooded the Carr home. They took the phone off the hook for days, but the noise did not stop.

Inside the house, Mary and Bob fought constantly, often about Steve, and Bob moved out. Traci found her mom’s house chaotic and undisciplined so she went with her father; Randy and his brother stayed with Mary, who seemed unreachable, crying often, sunk in a sorrow with no clear edges.

Isolation hardened around them. Parents forbade their children from playing with the Carr kids. On the playground, though, the question surfaced anyway: Hey, what was he like, your brother? Traci refused to answer. “I wouldn’t talk about it. I just wouldn’t,” she recalls. “I thought we did something wrong. I was really ashamed of it.”

Randy kept getting into fights. Strong, athletic and ready to use his fists, he swung at anyone who tried to force him to accept what Steve had done.

The stain of being Steven Judy’s foster siblings followed Traci and Randy through high school and beyond. It entered rooms before they did.

When Traci moved into her first apartment, eager for the ordinary independence of adulthood, she slept with the lights on. “The dark terrified me,” she said.

Later, motherhood gave the fear somewhere new to live. She found herself watching her children obsessively, imagining dangers before they arrived. “The worst thoughts still pop in my head,” she says. “I have to mentally block them out.”

For a long time, Traci carried anger toward her parents for bringing Steve into their home, for not knowing more, for not protecting them better.

She has forgiven them now, at least mostly. “They grew later in life,” she said. They were young. They didn’t know the full extent of Steve’s crimes. “Mom had the best intentions. She was always trying to rescue people. Steve was charming so she really thought she could turn it around for him and make something good out of something terrible. She was trusting to the end of her life. And it’s a good quality.”

Bob died in 2005; Mary died in 2023. The bin containing Steve’s belongings went to Traci. After we spent a day going through the bin together, Traci carried Steve’s belongings back to a corner of her garage. She doesn’t love having his stuff. “Was he wearing that belt when he did that? And that watch. Was he wearing that?” she asked. “I know Mom loved him, but I would never have kept this if it were up to me.” But even now, the final act of throwing it away still feels impossible.

Asked what she would say to Steve today, knowing all she knows now, Traci hesitated.

“I’m sorry for what he had to go through as a child. It makes me sick to think about the things he had to witness.” She paused. “Some people can pull through,” she said, “and other people can’t.”

Mary’s attachment to Steve did not end with his execution.

For 20 years, on the anniversary of his death, Mary would check into a hotel room alone and try to connect. She said she could feel him. She said he came to her. The kids sometimes teased her about this, but she just laughed good-naturedly. She was not religious, but recalled her grandmother communicating with spirits. She believed she came from a psychic family.

Though she kept a connection with Steve, Mary cut herself off from her parents for a time after the execution. “If anyone ever needed support and love from their family, I needed it this month,” she wrote to her mother. “We buried Steve yesterday and not one member of my family was there. I think I know how Steve must have hurt when his family turned their back on him. My family did the same to me. And all I did was give a very lost kid some love.”

Traci says when she discovered that letter, “it broke my heart. She never told me about any of that.” It took Traci years to understand that her mother’s grief carried its own kind of exile.

For Randy, the spiral that began after Judy’s arrest never fully stopped. A star high school athlete, he later went to prison on drug-related charges. “Everybody always told me I was going to turn out like Steve, and I’m thinking I didn’t mind that because I loved Steve to death,” he said. “But I felt like everybody expected me to screw up, so it wasn’t no big deal to meet their expectations.”

Traci is married to a police officer. She works as a patient advocate at a hospital now. She sits with families in crisis, helping them navigate what they don’t understand. In the evenings, she knits thick blankets, the yarn moving through her hands row by row.

Her mother has begun appearing again in her sleep: Mary holding her, comforting. Almost as if speaking aloud what had been buried for decades had called her mother back.

“Everyone hated Steve, and we were told we should too,” Traci says. “For a long time, I thought we did something wrong, and I was ashamed. People treated us like we had raised a murderer. It’s still how people remember us. I don’t think Mom ever got to grieve properly. I don’t think any of us did.”

This year, somewhere in the United States, another family will be sitting in a hotel room like the one Mary sat in, waiting for a phone call.

Forty-seven executions took place in 2025, the most in any year since 2009. Fifteen more by early June of this year, with the federal government moving to add firing squads, electrocution and gas asphyxiation to how a life can be taken.

The methods have changed, but for families, what is on the other side of the execution has not.

Recently, I took a road trip with three friends I’ve known since elementary school. For the first time in decades, we spoke together about my childhood friend Cindy Winter, whose murder forced its way into our childhood before any of us really understood death, shattering trust and turning our Sonoran desert into a place of danger.

When Terry and her children were killed, Traci and Randy were younger than I had been when Cindy was murdered. What struck me in both cases was the force of the damage: how completely one person’s violence could unmake life for children who had nothing to do with it.

But the Carrs carried something I never had to carry. Cindy’s killer was a figure of fear to me. To them, Judy was the brother who was “everything I had”, the protector who made room beneath the covers, the boy Mary could not stop trying to reach.

They had to go on knowing the worst thing about him, without being able to unknow the rest.

My friends left Ukraine after the Russian invasion. Now I wonder if we live in the same world

The Guardian Wed, 22 Jul 2026 04:00:05 GMT

Anger, guilt, shame: the deepest unseen wound of this war is the rift between those who left and those who stayed behind

“Can we reschedule?”

Over the years of working with western colleagues, I had learned to accept that they don’t fully understand what war feels like from the inside. They would ask me to find someone in occupied Mariupol for an interview, or seem genuinely puzzled that I couldn’t just log on at a time that suited them. I made my peace with this long ago – they don’t have to understand. But this time, it was a Ukrainian who asked.

It was winter, the kind where every online meeting had to be carefully scheduled around power outage timetables – and sometimes around shelling timetables, as we had already begun to joke among ourselves in that dark way. The question about rescheduling the meeting came from a colleague who had left for Europe in 2022, and it hit me almost physically, precisely because she was the one to say it. That innocent query had no business feeling like an accusation – and yet it did. For a long time, I couldn’t understand why.

We knew that war would bring pain and rupture. But there are ruptures no one warned us about – ruptures that are quiet and slow, and for that reason the most devastating. One of them runs not between Ukraine and the world, but through Ukrainians ourselves – between those who left and those who stayed. Almost no one talks about it. But it’s there, and with every passing month it grows wider.

I would look at a friend’s social media post about a strike on Kyiv and realise that for them, the story began when it appeared in their feed. For me, it had begun much earlier – with the siren in the middle of the night, the explosions, the corridor where we had sat huddled with family, the silent wait to find out who hadn’t made it this time. And sometimes I would think: ”Oh, come on, what hypocrisy – to share a post about my city burning and then close the tab and go on with your lovely day.” I knew this was unfair. But the thought came anyway.

I understood something else the summer I managed to get away to another part of Europe and meet up with friends. We were sitting on a terrace in one of those beautiful cities where life looks orderly and safe, talking about work and plans. And then someone’s phone went off – the air raid alert – and within seconds everyone else’s followed. In Ukraine, everyone gets the sirens on their phones, but here, in this landscape, it sounded so wrong that we all fell silent, as if someone had cut the sound. Rita looked at her phone first and said: “Drones over Kyiv.”

A minute later came another alert – a MiG had taken off, cruise missiles launched, ballistic threat. I get these notifications every day, but in that moment I felt my heart drop, because in Kyiv there are family, people I love. Fear for them came over me suddenly and completely. And then I looked at my friends and saw on their faces exactly the same thing – like a mirror I hadn’t expected to find. The same fear, the same helplessness of someone who is far away and can do nothing. That was the first time I allowed myself the thought that maybe they were living through this war too – just differently. Through screens, through the helplessness of watching from afar and feeling they have no right even to their own fear. It occurred to me that perhaps neither group was misunderstanding the war. Those who left and those who stayed were simply no longer living in the same version of it.

I hear about their struggles – the bureaucracy, the loneliness, the uncertainty of being a refugee. And at the same time, I catch myself thinking: “God, how lucky you are. Not that your problems aren’t real, but they exist inside safety.” And underneath that, a quieter and uglier thought: “Do you think there is something I can do to help?” I never say any of this out loud. But the thoughts keep coming back, and with them the shame that they come at all.

A colleague – also Ukrainian, also among those who left the country after the full-scale invasion – was explaining why she hadn’t done her part of a joint project: depression. My first thought was ugly and I knew it: “Only I get to make excuses here. Are you really complaining about your depression while we are being shelled?” And then came the shame.

But I wasn’t prepared for what came next. “How long can people keep using the war to make the rest of us feel guilty?” my colleague asked.

The remark stayed with me, not because it offended me, but because it frightened me. I had long ago started to feel ashamed to mention too often the reality I was living in, worried it would sound like guilt-tripping, like competing to be the one suffering the most. Hearing it from her, from someone also Ukrainian, also inside all of this despite being in a safe country – it felt like a blow from one of our own.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

When my mother comes back to Kyiv, I think: “You’re here, you’re in the same world as me.” And then: “I am happy that someone I love has travelled from safety into a city that gets bombed regularly. I’m self-centred.” And immediately: “God, I’m such an egoist.” Then she leaves again, and so do all the others who have managed to visit Ukraine. They head back to Kraków, Berlin, Vilnius. I look at photos from their spontaneous weekends, their last-minute concerts, and I don’t just envy them. I’m angry. Every trip I take is like a military operation: no flights out of Ukraine, hours to the border, permits, logistics. Why is it so easy for them? Why not for me? I know why. That’s what makes it worse.

Once we lived in different cities but in the same world. Now my mother is in Bulgaria, Dasha is in Poland, Ira is in Germany, Katya is in Austria. The map of closeness has shifted so quietly that I didn’t notice until it had already changed. I don’t miss life before the war – I miss the feeling that the people I love are living in the same reality as me. Maybe that’s why my thoughts are so full of “I” and “they” – and so short on “we”. Not because we stopped loving each other, or because anyone chose the wrong side of a border, but because war has a way of placing people inside different versions of the same story.

And perhaps that is why I am always waiting for the next meeting on a terrace. Not in Berlin or Warsaw or Vienna. Here.

Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Israeli Banks Threaten to Cut Off Palestinian Economy, Deepening Crisis

The New York Times July 22, 2026

Global Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Two Israeli financial firms have long served as partners to Palestinian banks, handling transactions that make possible the West Bank’s imports and exports.

By David M. Halbfinger and Adam Rasgon

Reporting from Ramallah, Jerusalem and Tel Aviv

Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are routinely being terrorized by military raids and settler violence. But a more obscure menace is threatening to bring the entire West Bank economy to a halt.

Two Israeli financial institutions that have long served as partners for the 13 Palestinian banks — handling transactions that make possible imports to the West Bank of everything from food and clothing to gasoline, water and electricity — have signaled that they may abruptly end those relationships. That would cut the territory’s financial tether to Israel — and the outside world.

If the Israeli banks severed ties, officials say, it would amount to the imposition of a suffocating commercial blockade.

The banks have long been concerned they could be exposed to lawsuits over money laundering or terrorist financing, and have grown frustrated that Israel’s government is not better shielding them against these risks.

The prospect of being cut off has prompted Palestinian officials to appeal to foreign governments to intervene with the Israelis. A gathering on the subject set for Thursday in the West Bank city of Ramallah, sponsored by the Palestine Monetary Authority with the participation of officials from the United Nations, World Bank and International Monetary Fund, is titled “The Breaking Point: Sounding the Alarm Before Collapse.”

“There is a huge fear,” said Feras Milhem, who served as governor of the Palestine Monetary Authority from 2021 to 2025. “There is also a belief that this will not happen, that Israel cannot really cut the relations unless they want to push the Palestinians to anarchy.”

One of the two Israeli financial institutions, the Israel Discount Bank, has written to its Palestinian counterparts saying it will end its “correspondent banking” relationships with them by Sept. 1, according to a letter obtained by The New York Times. The other, Bank Hapoalim, told The Times that it was considering making the same decision.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Israeli finance ministry said the two banks had “announced their desire to cease providing correspondent services.” The ministry said that it was in talks with them to find a “safe and responsible manner” for them to continue those relationships, and that their termination could have “negative implications for economic stability in the region.”

Trade with Israel is responsible for 55 percent of Palestinian imports and 85 percent of exports, Mr. Milhem said. This commerce is handled by the correspondent banks, as is trade between the Palestinians and other countries.

The root of the potential crisis lies in the banks’ concern they could be exposed to international lawsuits alleging that they provide financing for money laundering or terrorism. The Israeli banks require that the Israeli government mitigate the risk by issuing letters temporarily indemnifying them against lawsuits, as well as immunizing them against potential prosecution in Israel. These letters come with expiration dates.

In recent years, Israeli officials have repeatedly threatened not to reissue the letters. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a staunch supporter of Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, has used the letters as leverage inside the government to extract concessions, including approval for settler outposts.

Each time, the government has backed down under international pressure, including a public intervention by U. S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen in 2024.

Since then, however, Mr. Smotrich has pressured the Palestinians by extending indemnification for shorter periods — often for as little as two weeks at a time — and waiting until the last minute to do so, officials said.

An aide to Mr. Smotrich, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said in a statement that the Palestinian financial system remained involved in terrorism and money laundering.

“The demand that Israel mitigate this risk instead of demanding that the Palestinian Authority cease engaging in terrorism and meet accepted international standards reflects the hypocrisy and racism of low expectations,” the aide argued.

Other experts counter that the Palestinian financial system has taken steps to prevent Hamas and other militant groups from gaining access to it.

“The Palestinian banking system is no friend of Hamas, quite the contrary,” said Daniel L. Glaser, who was assistant secretary for terrorist financing at the Treasury Department in the Obama administration. “And the Palestinian Monetary Authority is no friend of Hamas. It’s one of the few things that works there.”

Still, the Israeli government wants the Palestinian Authority to submit to a level of financial auditing that it says it has not previously undergone.

The most recent extension of indemnification was for six months, until the end of 2026. The two Israeli banks have made clear, however, that they have grown frustrated with the uncertainty and short-term extensions and want to end the relationships sooner, Israeli and Palestinian officials said.

The Israeli banks have never wanted to be in the correspondent banking business with the Palestinians, which they entered in the mid-1990s when Israel and the Palestinians were negotiating peace deals as part of the Oslo Accords, and the firms have pushed over the years to exit it.

The Israeli government has repeatedly promised to find a permanent solution that shields the banks from liability. In 2019, the government established a company that was meant to become an intermediary between the Israeli and Palestinian banks. But that company has never gotten up and running, and Israel would need to enact legislation for it to start operations, officials said.

With Israel in the heat of a political campaign ahead of elections later this year and the Israeli Parliament in recess, it appears unlikely such legislation could be enacted soon.

In a statement, Israel Discount Bank acknowledged “the importance of economic stability” but said that it had to consider the risks of providing correspondent banking services and its responsibility to depositors and shareholders. “We remain willing to assist with the operational solution, provided that the relevant responsibility and risk are assumed by the state,” it said.

Palestinian officials have searched for a backup plan in vain. They say that currency swaps, such as in dollars or euros, would suffice only for a few weeks. And a more permanent fix, like dropping the Israeli shekel as the Palestinian currency, carries the risk that Israel could choose to interpret it as a withdrawal from the Oslo Accords, which barred the Palestinians from issuing their own currency and made the shekel the primary legal tender.

That leaves the Palestinians contemplating the potentially cataclysmic consequences of the banking relationships coming to an end. The West Bank economy is already under enormous pressure from punitive measures imposed by Israel after the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel in October 2023. Those measures include the withholding of billions of dollars in import taxes that Israel collects on the Palestinian Authority’s behalf and the cancellation of work permits for tens of thousands of West Bank residents who used to work inside Israel.

Economic experts said essential goods would become unavailable in short order if the relationship between Israeli and Palestinian banks is undone. The West Bank gets 100 percent of its fuel, 93 percent of its electricity and 35 percent of its water from Israel, according to Mr. Milhem, the former bank regulator.

Many said they expected that a black market would emerge, with Israeli trucks making deliveries in exchange for bags of cash — an environment ripe for exploitation by terrorist groups.

“It’s not only a humanitarian issue, it’s a security issue,” Mr. Milhem said.

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

House Adopts $95 Billion G. O. P. Budget for Iran War

The New York Times July 22, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Republican leaders muscled through resistance in their own ranks to approve the budget blueprint for the war and other measures, but its prospects were far dimmer in the Senate.

By Catie Edmondson

Reporting from the Capitol

House Republicans on Wednesday won narrow approval of their $95 billion budget plan to fund the war with Iran and impose new election restrictions President Trump has demanded, muscling through dissent in their ranks to send the measure to a skeptical Senate.

The blueprint would pave the way for filibuster-proof legislation known as a reconciliation bill that would bypass Democratic opposition and provide up to $73 billion in additional military funding, $12 billion for farmers and $10 billion to enforce severe new voting restrictions championed by Mr. Trump.

It was approved in a 216-to-214 vote, with all but two Republicans in favor despite considerable concern in their ranks about its cost, its scope and voting to fund an unpopular war just months before the midterm elections.

The plan faces an uphill fight in the Senate, where the Republican leader has cast doubt on his chamber’s willingness to embrace it.

The debate featured little in the way of direct discussion about the war with Iran, for which the bulk of the money is intended.

Speaking at length on the House floor in support of the plan, Representative Jodey Arrington, Republican of Texas and the chairman of the Budget Committee, described the effort as “supporting our troops in their time of need.”

“Just base-line battlefield readiness,” Mr. Arrington said. “Bullets and bombs to finish the job, and to come home safely and victoriously.”

Representative Mike Rogers of Alabama, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, also omitted any mention of Iran, though he alluded to the conflict.

“No matter how you feel about the current events, these funds are necessary to ensure our fighting forces remain ready, our troops are paid and our nation is safe,” he said.

In the days leading up to the House vote, various Republican factions had quietly voiced grievances about the resolution. Budget hawks objected to the fact that none of the new spending would be offset by new cuts. Defense hawks said their party should use reconciliation to provide even more money to the Pentagon. Center-leaning House Republicans facing competitive re-election races were skittish about voting to fund a war that has driven costs up.

But as with most legislative initiatives that Mr. Trump demands, there was a sense of inevitability in the House about adopting the blueprint, and in the end, most would-be defectors swallowed their objections and fell in line.

In the end, only two Republicans, Representatives Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio, and one independent who aligns with the G. O. P., Representative Kevin Kiley of California, voted no.

Fiscal hard-liners said they were willing to add $95 billion in spending in exchange for a promise that the reconciliation measure would eventually include new voting restrictions that would require people to prove they are citizens when they register to vote, impose strict new identification requirements for voting and severely curb voting by mail.

The blueprint hews closely to an emergency spending request the White House sent Congress in June to provide more money primarily for the Pentagon. Republicans have sought to fund it through reconciliation, legislation that is not subject to a filibuster because nearly all Democrats have said they are opposed to the war and will not vote to allocate money for it. In the Senate, spending bills typically need bipartisan support — 60 votes — to advance.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader, called the legislation an “America Last Republican budget that will provide billions of additional dollars to Operation Epic Fury in the Middle East, which has been a complete and total disaster for the American people.”

It would be the third time in 18 months that the party has turned to reconciliation — a maneuver created to make it easier to pass bills that reduce federal deficits — to push through major elements of their agenda.

Yet it was far from clear that the budget blueprint would gain traction in the Senate.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, suggested at a news conference on Tuesday that the Senate would “hold” the House’s budget resolution — not acting on it immediately but keeping it available — until he was sure the Senate could move a stopgap funding bill to avert a government shutdown at the end of September.

“It’s a possibility that, if necessary, we could pull that budget resolution passed by the House and use it to fund the government,” Mr. Thune said.

Even before that, a number of Republicans in the Senate had questioned the plan’s viability. Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, has said he opposes it because it does not provide the Pentagon with enough money. Mr. Wicker has said he wants to ensure the military receives the full $1.5 trillion in funding Mr. Trump included in his budget request.

Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina both oppose the inclusion of the voting restrictions, known as the SAVE Act. Many Republican senators doubt that the measure will be allowed to remain in the reconciliation bill, which is subject to strict rules requiring that all provisions make direct changes to spending or revenue.

And Ms. Murkowski signaled she was wary that the Trump administration might interpret a vote in support of supplemental war funding as a vote by Congress authorizing the conflict with Iran. The president has not sought such authorization, and lawmakers in both parties have voted to require it.

In a hearing on Tuesday before the Appropriations Committee, Ms. Murkowski asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth whether he believed that a vote on “funding alone can substitute for explicit congressional authorization.”

Mr. Hegseth said he would defer to his legal team.

Catie Edmondson covers Congress for The Times.

House Passes Defense Bill Amid Iran War Divide

The New York Times July 22, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Republicans pushed through the $1.15 trillion bill over opposition from Democrats, who said backing it was akin to embracing the war.

By Robert Jimison

Robert Jimison, who covers foreign policy and defense issues in Congress, reported from the Capitol.

A divided House on Wednesday approved a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill as Republicans pressed ahead with a historic increase in military spending over the opposition of Democrats who voted against the plan in protest of the war in Iran.

Passage marked a victory for Republicans seeking to reshape the Department of Defense in line with President Trump’s aims, but the near party-line vote on what is normally a broadly bipartisan bill reflected major obstacles that could complicate its path to enactment.

In a 216-212 vote, all but a half-dozen Democrats opposed the measure, many saying that they could not in good conscience back a bill that ultimately would empower Mr. Trump to continue waging war against Iran without authorization or meaningful oversight by Congress.

Senate Democrats blocked that chamber’s version last week for the same reason, and G. O. P. leaders in the Senate lack the votes to overcome their opposition.

It sets up a clash over the annual defense policy bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act or N. D. A. A., that will likely to require significant bipartisan revisions if Congress hopes to send the legislation to Mr. Trump before the end of the year.

The bill includes a pay raise for service members, increased funding for missile defense production and additional resources to boost strategic investments in critical minerals. The sprawling legislation also contains a range of provisions directly related to how the U. S. military integrates and regulates artificial intelligence across the department.

It also would officially rename the Department of Defense the Department of War, part of an effort by him and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to rebrand the military in a way they argue better projects American strength and reflects the department’s core mission.

Republicans lauded the bill’s passage as another step to shore up Mr. Trump’s legislative agenda. Speaker Mike Johnson noted that the bill codifies “over 65 of the Trump administration’s executive orders and legislative proposals.”

The bill, which was supported by all but seven Republicans, would deliver the largest annual jump in military spending in modern history. It increases the national defense budget by more than $227 billion over the previous year, a boost Republicans say is needed to prepare the United States for a more dangerous world.

“For the first time in 40 years, we’ve been presented a budget that accounts for the true cost of American deterrence,” Representative Mike Rogers of Alabama, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee and the bill’s chief author, said.

He said that because of “decades of underinvestment in the U. S. military,” the United States no longer has the capacity to produce military equipment fast enough for a prolonged war, pointing to a shrinking defense industry and dwindling stockpiles of weapons.

Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee who joined his party in opposing the measure, argued that Republicans had transformed a bipartisan bill into a divisive one.

“Whatever else may be said about the N. D. A. A. — there’s a lot of positive aspects to it — it will continue to support the Department of Defense the president is using to wage this war,” Mr. Smith said. “And that makes it very difficult to support this.”

The debate came as Republicans had hoped the war in Iran was entering its final chapter after. Lawmakers had seen the signing of a memorandum of understanding and announced cease-fire last month as the pivot point necessary to allow them to spend their last days before a five-week summer recess highlighting domestic accomplishments and begin focusing on the midterm elections. Instead, the conflict has reasserted itself just as lawmakers prepare to leave Washington to campaign for re-election.

Mr. Smith said Republicans had blocked Democratic amendments and reshaped the legislation around the administration’s push to supercharge military spending at the expense of domestic programs that Americans depend on.

He argued that the administration’s broader goal of pushing military spending to above $1.5 trillion through three measures making their way through Congress — the defense bill, an emergency supplemental spending measure it has requested to pay for the war in Iran and a forthcoming reconciliation package that would include much of that money — was fiscally unsustainable.

“We’re making cuts to Medicaid and other health care programs in order to fund this,” he said. “The math just doesn’t add up.”

Mr. Smith faulted Republicans for continuing to fund an expanding war in Iran while declining to reassert Congress’s constitutional role in authorizing and overseeing the conflict, saying lawmakers were being asked to provide ever larger sums for military operations without meaningful debate over the strategy or its objectives.

Representatives Jared Golden of Maine, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, Adam Gray of California, Don Davis of North Carolina, Vincente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar, both of Texas, were the only Democrats to break with their party to support the measure.

Representatives Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, Chip Roy of Texas, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Eli Crane of Arizona, Tim Burchett of Tennessee and Josh Brecheen of Oklahoma all broke with fellow Republicans by voting against the bill.

The House measure is one piece of a broader effort by the Trump administration to bring military funding to unprecedented levels that proponents argue is necessary to rapidly expand the armed forces as the United States confronts simultaneous threats from China, Russia, Iran and other adversaries.

Appearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee this week, Mr. Hegseth described the strategy as a “generational investment” in the military, calling the emergency funding request an “urgent, necessary injection” amid a war that he said had so far cost $37.5 billion.

“Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Mr. Hegseth testified.

In recent days, Mr. Trump has abandoned the more optimistic tone that a diplomatic resolution could be met to draw the war to a close and has instead issued increasingly forceful warnings to Iran’s leadership.

On Wednesday, Mr. Trump warned that Iranian strikes against vessels navigating through the Strait of Hormuz would be responded to with attacks on key infrastructure.

“From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran,” he wrote in a post to his social media site.

Moments later, as he was preparing to depart for the dignified transfer of four American service members killed in the conflict, Mr. Trump previewed more strikes telling reporters that Iran was “going to pay a big price.”

“They’re getting decimated,” he added.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.
