Gen Z-ers Are Ditching Sex. They Might Be Onto Something.

The New York Times July 22, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Opinions

Is celibacy cool now?

By Nadja SpiegelmanChristine Emba and Carter Sherman

Produced by Vishakha Darbha

Data shows that Gen Z is in a sex recession. Technology, #MeToo and a growing emphasis on platonic relationships are reshaping how many people think about sex. As anxiety grows over falling birthrates and changing behaviors, Nadja Spiegelman, a Times Opinion culture editor, speaks with the journalists and researchers Carter Sherman and Christine Emba about why this shift might not be such a bad thing.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Nadja Spiegelman: In one word or a small handful of words, how do you feel about people having less sex?

Carter Sherman: I feel intrigued. It raises the question: Why, and what does it mean? And that’s been the guiding light of my reporting for the last several years.

Christine Emba: The word would have to be “mixed.” I actually feel happy for young people if they feel less pressure to do things that they don’t want to do. But I do feel concerned about what it represents about relationships more broadly, and their interaction with each other.

Spiegelman: Americans are having less sex, and it’s particularly visible among young people. There’s a recent study that shows that one in four Gen Z adults say that they have not had sex, and the number of young people who haven’t had sex in the past year has doubled from 2010 to 2024, from 12 percent to 24 percent. Christine, you’ve been reporting on sex and dating in the culture for a long time. What are you seeing about the causes behind this trend?

Emba: The trend is notable, especially among millennials and Gen Z. Gen Z is doing a lot of things less frequently than their older peers used to — or at least later. They started driving later; they’re moving out of their parents’ houses later; they’re drinking later or not at all. Sex is another thing that they are doing later than their peers.

But I think the causes behind it are both manifold and, when you think about it, kind of obvious. I think one is, frankly, the internet and smartphones, where there’s kind of a substitution effect. You could get dressed up and go out on a date and try to find someone to sleep with, or you could scroll your feed and watch pornography at home and not have to make all of that effort and fear rejection. So the technological climate has a lot to do with it.

Spiegelman: Carter, you’ve interviewed a lot of Gen Z-ers about sex. What have you seen or observed? Anything different from what Christine was saying?

Sherman: I definitely second Christine’s point, particularly about phones. This is not a trend that we’re seeing just in the United States; I think it’s notable that we’re also seeing it abroad, in countries like Japan and South Korea, which would point to there being some kind of global shared cause. And the emergence of smartphones and the social media that’s on them is a very obvious culprit.

That said, I don’t think that there really is just one thing that we can pin the sex recession, as it’s called, on. When I talk to young people, many of them bring up stuff like the political climate. It makes them feel more anxious to have sex right now.

After the overturning of Roe v. Wade, there was a study that came out which found that about 13 percent of millennials and Gen Z have become more anxious around sex, because of the overturning. We really have to look at what is going on overall in the climate when it comes to sex, and not just say, “OK, we can just change or fix this one thing and that will fix the entire dating crisis,” as some people have termed it.

Spiegelman: There are a lot of possible reasons behind this sex recession. Christine, you were talking about phones; Carter, you were talking about Roe v. Wade. I also wonder if #MeToo had an impact on young people and how they were thinking about sex.

Emba: That’s something that definitely came up in my reporting and with young people that I’ve talked to, millennials and Gen Z. I think one of the things that Carter was pointing out, very correctly, is that the entire social environment shapes how people move about, how they interact with each other, and maybe eventually how they have sex.

So, first of all, we have to know that Gen Z has come of age in a very anxious time. There was Covid-19 and the pandemic. Everybody was stuck at home. Our political climate is, frankly, insane. And #MeToo happened in 2017. So a formative age for many people in terms of thinking about sex and dating and how to relate to other people.

For young women, #MeToo served as a moment in which they could say, “The current sexual climate, our current sexual landscape, maybe actually doesn’t feel that great for me, and I feel like I’m allowed to say that publicly. There’s less pressure on me to assent to things.” Which is a really good thing.

I think for young men, however, they became really frightened, actually. There’s one guy I remember interviewing who said that after #MeToo, asking out a colleague in the workplace or hitting on a girl in public was like handing him a loaded shotgun. It was really dangerous and could have consequences for him.

And I was like, “That seems extreme.” But I think a lot of conscientious young men noted that #MeToo had happened. Women had been made uncomfortable in a number of circumstances that they hadn’t known about, and dialed back their own behavior — their own willingness to ask people out, to try to pursue sex on a date, to even try to pursue dating in some situations. And obviously, if you’re not talking to potential sex partners, it is far less likely that you will have sex with them.

Sherman: What I found in my reporting is that it’s different for the genders, as Christine has talked about. But what I found really interesting is that when I talked to young men — and I should say that for my book, “The Second Coming,” I interviewed more than 100 young people under 30, and I’ve also covered gender and sexuality for 10 years now — I found that young men actually weren’t all that moved by #MeToo, and I think this is partially an age thing.

Which, to Christine’s point, she’s talking about people being in the workplace. But many of the young people I was interviewing, they did not remember #MeToo, which was sort of a dagger to the heart the first time I heard it, because it was so pivotal to me.

And there was one young man I remember, 18 years old, who grew up in New York City, had just graduated high school right after we spoke, and he was talking about the ways that young men in his cohort talk about women, and he was using terms like “bop” and “ran through,” and things that really are not very friendly to women. Yeah, “ran through” was really the term that stuck with me.

Spiegelman: I don’t know the term “bop.”

Sherman: I mean ——

Spiegelman: Is it not appropriate for a New York Times podcast?

Sherman: It’s not family-friendly.

Emba: Yeah. I don’t know if we need to spell it out.

Sherman: No, look it up on Urban Dictionary if you feel so inclined after this. But what was striking to me is that he said this thing — he was like, “You’re talking about #MeToo, and #MeToo was about not sexually assaulting women, but I didn’t understand it as, like, treating women as people. Like, that’s not how I understood it.” And he drew a line between affording women and girls full humanity and just not sexually assaulting them.

I found that fascinating, because it suggests to me that #MeToo didn’t really do as much as we maybe would have liked it to do, that it didn’t actually really change some of these mores as permanently as we might have liked, because people just don’t remember.

The thing I will say about young women — I totally agree with Christine — I have found that they have become more anxious, and I think part of that is because, for the women who remember #MeToo, it helped them recognize, certainly earlier than I did, that maybe something that happened to them that was wrong was actually a violation — that they should recognize this as sexual assault or sexual harassment — and they deserve to seek redress for that. They deserve to be made whole.

But what these women have also found is that we didn’t actually really see that many institutional changes after #MeToo. Like, we have seen more H. R. trainings around sexual violence. We have seen some legislation around NDAs. But for institutions like colleges, we haven’t actually seen an overhaul of the way that we address sexual violence.

The same goes for K-12 institutions. And so these young women walk around with a greater knowledge of how pervasive sexual violence is, and an understanding that if something happens to them, their institutions are not necessarily set up to help them in that instance. And that is just a culture of fear. It’s a miasma of anxiety. And that makes you not want to engage in any of this to begin with.

Emba: I think that’s a great point. I think you’re right to point out this distinction between millennials and older Gen Z, who might have had their sexual memory working when #MeToo happened, and a younger generation who did not. One of the things that I’ve also noticed, as an age and gender split, is that in a post-#MeToo environment, where young women are more OK with talking about negative experiences, they share those, especially on TikTok and Instagram. A lot of women are more open to making reels about, “I had this bad experience with a man” or “I went on this date and it was awful, and here’s why.”

And there is just a lot more content about how men can be dangerous or predatory — or in social media dating advice parlance, narcissists or liars or something. And so it makes men feel both scarier and less responsive to female concerns. And there’s a whole dialogue that has grown, that is negative around dating men. It’s a term that I think The New York Times has published a number of pieces on — “heteropessimism,” right? This idea that, for a woman, trying to date a man is kind of a hopeless enterprise. And you might, in fact, wish that you were a lesbian or not interested in men at all, but alas, you are.

And then on the male side of the equation — if women are seeing feeds that are full of negative content about the opposite sex, and descriptions of unfortunate and scary occurrences that then shape their idea of dating — men are getting dating advice that is also really negative about women. These terms that we just used: All women are on OnlyFans; women can’t be trusted; women only want to date men who are tall, rich and handsome, and if you’re not one of those ——

Sherman: Six-four, blue eyes, and works in finance?

Emba: Yes, actually.

Spiegelman: I’ve also heard of this as like 6-6-6 — he needs to be six feet tall, make six figures and have a six-pack. Which I think is something that men believe women want.

Emba: And when men are told this by their dating advisers, like the “Fresh & Fit” podcast or Andrew Tate types — even Joe Rogan occasionally trades in this sort of discourse — they begin to feel really negatively toward women. And so, yeah, they aren’t really interested in being with each other in the same way.

Spiegelman: I have so many theories for why this is happening. One is something a friend of mine, who’s 21, brought up when we were talking about this: She was saying Gen Z is facing a lot of mental health issues, in part because of the anxieties of the world, and they are very medicated for their mental health.

They’re one of the most medicated generations, which, for anyone who’s been on antidepressants, can have an impact on your libido. She was positing that this might be one of the causes why Gen Z is having less sex. Has that come up in either of your reporting?

Emba: Not necessarily the medication effect specifically, but it is worth noting that something like one in four members of Gen Z has been in therapy at some point in their adolescence, which is more than any other generation. I think there is something to be said about mental health generally, and how Gen Z views protecting their mental health and protecting their space and peace in different ways than their older peers might have.

One of the things tying back to the reasons men are seemingly having less sex than women is that, for many young men at this point, this idea that you have to be the perfect man — you have to be the right model of masculinity, you have to be ready before you can be in a relationship — seems to be driving a number of men into taking a step back and moving into self-optimization, going into monk mode and thinking that they have to figure out every aspect of their lives before they can start dating, before it’s OK to approach anyone else. And so that moves having sex later.

And then, for young women, there’s this idea that your mental health is fragile. Other people can be anxiety causing. Relationships — and I think we can actually all understand this — can be really anxiety causing, can produce a lot of pressure. And to stay on balance, to keep oneself safe, the better thing to do is invest in yourself, invest in your mental health, invest in the relationships that you can control, your friendships, and maybe not experiment with sex and dating at this time because it seems too stressful and too fraught.

One thing I was genuinely curious about while working on this episode is the difference between solitude and loneliness. I kept wondering whether it's something you really only learn with age — or whether this younger generation has landed on something I missed in my twenties. Has being alone gotten easier or harder for you over the years?

Spiegelman: I was looking at a survey that asked Gen Z-ers: What is more important to you than regular sex? And they answered: success at work, friendships, a good night’s sleep was very high up there.

Sherman: Fair.

Spiegelman: Christine, you were talking about the amount of work and readiness that men think they need to do in order to be ready for a relationship, and I’ve noticed that, in my conversations with young people, much more so than when I was young — I guess I no longer am ——

Sherman: No, we’re all young forever.

Emba: No, you’re still young.

Spiegelman: OK, much more so than when I was in my early 20s. There’s a big focus on the idea of a long-term relationship as this venerated goal, this huge commitment. Part of it is that you see on social media that these relationships take huge gestures, financial and emotional, and part of that is just how an algorithm is designed — to promote performativity or the sale of a product.

But there’s this idea that a long-term relationship is this really serious thing, and that’s much more desired and much more the focus than casual sex. How have you seen the distinction about how young people feel between long-term romantic relationships and casual sex, and have there been shifts there?

Sherman: I found it very interesting how much young people are dismissive of hookup culture, as they put it. When I was growing up, as a millennial, I think we were very overwhelmed by the narrative of hookup culture. There was this real sense in the media that young millennials were having too much sex, that they were having sex so casual it verged on impersonal, and that this would imperil our ability later on, down the line, to get married, to have kids.

And guess what? We are getting married. We are having kids. We’re just doing it at a later point. I think that this narrative, though, has still trickled down to young people. They saw that millennials got roasted for hookup culture, and now they don’t really want to engage in that as much. They do want to be in these long-term relationships.

I understand that desire. I really do. Particularly for a group that feels very alone, having a person who feels like theirs, who feels like they are going to be a foundation for them and for their life — I don’t think that’s a bad desire whatsoever.

Emba: To go a little bit deeper into how that narrative has shifted, there was a spate of stories like “Cat Person,” the New Yorker short story that was just about a normal girl who goes on a date and hooks up with a guy and is grossed out by it. And there is an openness to this idea that millennial sex positivity — which I would not describe as sex positivity in the classic feminist sense, that sex is a good thing, but sex positivity in a kind of deterministic sense, meaning you need to go out and have a lot of sex, otherwise you’re not a good feminist or a modern young person, et cetera — was blown up a little bit.

Gen Z saw millennials dealing with the fallout of that culture and decided that they didn’t want to be part of it. And especially with some of the changes that had happened in sexual culture between millennials and Gen Z, so much of the sex that people seem to be having — that they’re reporting having as kind of abusive or unpleasant — was extremely porn-informed, for one thing. And so they have backed off from hooking up on the same level.

But then, when it comes to longer-term relationships, there’s the idea of the cornerstone versus capstone model of long-term relationships. Traditionally, long-term relationships — getting married, having a long-term partner — was seen as the cornerstone to your life. You find someone, and then you continue to build your life on top of that. Maybe you’re together and you go through grad school, you go through your careers, you’re joining your lives together. And maybe at the cornerstone, you’re not making that much money. You’re not that secure, but it’s OK.

Now, I think, in this more performative moment, where your big days, your dates are supposed to be celebrated as perfect on social media, a lot of young people feel like your long-term relationship should be the capstone of your life. That’s something that you only do when you’ve got all of the other bricks in a row: when you’re finished with school, when you have your career set up, when you’re making enough money — that’s when you can go for a long-term relationship.

Sherman: Just to complicate that narrative a little bit, because something that I do think comes up a lot, that sometimes frustrates me when we talk about Gen Z and the sex recession, is that millennials were also having less sex. So while we were having all of this discussion around, “they’re hooking up too much,” the reality is that they were having less sex than previous generations. And so when we think about the causes of the sex recession, we have to remember that this started before #MeToo.

This started before the pandemic. Gen Z is the inheritor of a trend that began among millennials. So whatever we’re seeing with Gen Z — how they see relationships, how they see hooking up — we have to be looking at both generations and thinking about things that have happened with both generations.

Spiegelman: Although I do think that there’s a shift that’s not so much about the having of sex, but the thinking about it in the culture. And for Gen Z, when sex is constantly being sold to you as a product — when it’s constantly over-available on your phone — it becomes uncool so quickly. We grew up in this very hypersexualized, “Girls Gone Wild,” culture that Gen Z is just a little grossed out because it’s so tied into a thing that’s being sold to them all the time.

Sherman: But is it uncool to not be able to have sex? Because I think it’s perceived as cool to choose not to have sex, but it’s not always clear that someone is making the active choice to be celibate versus just being unable to get laid.

It’s not cool to be powerless, right? It’s cool to be in control, and I think this is why people find the concept of virginity or the concept of being a virgin to be inherently embarrassing. Because that is a state you can’t change by yourself.

Emba: What you’re saying about people not wanting to admit to powerlessness — being powerless as being cringe and uncool — is extremely true. So, by going out and saying, “Well, actually, I’m choosing to be celibate,” or, “Actually, I am embracing loneliness and becoming a loneliness influencer,” or, “I’m decentering men; I’m a heteropessimist,” taking on the label for yourself feels like a reclamation of something that you might have otherwise felt powerless about.

Spiegelman: I’ve been thinking a lot about the difference between loneliness and solitude, which I think, in part, is a difference about choice. You’re lonely because you have no choice. Solitude is about choosing your own company.

But again, this might also be a way of reclaiming power over something that you don’t have a choice over.

I wanted to talk about loneliness influencers a little bit. Carter, can you explain what a loneliness influencer is?

Sherman: For folks who have not had this show up on their algorithms — first of all, I would love to know what makes you immune to this. Does my phone just think I am very lonely?

But basically, what loneliness influencers are — oftentimes women, which I find very striking, who are coming home and are taking off their shoes and making pizza, hanging out with their cat, and there’s text on the screen that says something like, “This is what your Friday night looks like when you are single and have no friends.” It’s very much selling the idea of a full life without anyone else in it, which I find really fascinating and inherently contradictory, because, of course, this is a person who is broadcasting their loneliness to the internet.

How much can I really believe that these people actually agree with the concept of loneliness? How many of these people are trying to change their circumstance? They’re a fascinating indicator of where we’re at in modern life, that these are an emerging system of influencers.

Emba: I think the rise of loneliness influencers speaks to another trend about Gen Z and millennial dating: One thing that has become clear to millennials and Gen Z is that, in a post-sexual revolution, feminist-inflected, if not feminist-winning world, is that women ——

Sherman: Definitely not feminist-winning. I don’t think the White House would identify as particularly feminist.

Emba: No. But a culture in which women are able to exist by themselves, where women have jobs, where women are going to college and graduate school at higher rates than men, where, in a lot of major cities, women are earning more than their male counterparts, you don’t have to get married or be in a relationship to make a life for yourself. And it’s felt as a liberating thing, at least, for younger women, millennials and Gen Z. And perhaps also for these older married women who maybe didn’t feel like they had as much choice in the matter, and so ended up with a husband and kids and a house and all of this stuff to deal with, as a way to feel like they were a part of and accepted by society.

So, the sort of romanticization of loneliness, I think, also speaks to a kind of romanticization of the idea that women can do it by themselves, that they don’t have to be in a relationship to be happy. They don’t have to have a boyfriend to be able to afford their, frankly, alarmingly clean apartments that are ——

Sherman: You and I are seeing the same woman, Christine.

Emba: Yes. It’s a little bit “American Psycho,” frankly.

Spiegelman: She has a lot of time to clean it.

Sherman: She does have a lot of time. This is the woman — if we’re thinking of the same person — who takes off her Louboutins when she comes in the door, which speaks to, again, her socioeconomic success, it seems like.

Emba: But I do think that there is something worrying about the loneliness influencer, because humans are wired for connection. It’s in our DNA to connect with people.

You can become physically and psychologically ill by being touch-starved, by not interacting with other people. Interacting with other people, whether in romantic relationships or simply friendships, is how you learn about the world, how you come to understand men or women or people in your office, how we know enough about each other to begin to create a civil society. The idea that we’ve decided that solitude is the best thing that you can have doesn’t really speak well for the future of our shared project.

Sherman: I guess I feel so conflicted about these influencers because the first time I came across a loneliness influencer, I was suddenly flung back to when I was, I think, 23 years old and had just moved to New York, and was working nights and did not have friends.

And I thought about how, if I had seen that content when I was that age, it would have really made me feel less lonely, because I would have realized that this is a life that other people are also living. Other people also struggle with making friends. The other thing is, when we think about the concerns that we have around young people not getting into relationships, not getting married, not having babies — which is another whole conversation; people are really worried about birthrates right now — I worry about how much importance we place on sex and relationships sometimes, because they’re really not a balm for all of the issues that plague us as a country, or as individuals.

Spiegelman: There’s so much moral hand-wringing and anxiety about the falling rates of people having sex, and I’m curious why it matters so much. We’ve been sold this one idea of a happily ever after for a very long time. But maybe, if we move away from that, there’s plenty of other reasons to be happy, ways to find happiness. People who say that they’re intentionally not dating say they’re focusing on self-improvement, on paying down debt, on getting fit, on traveling. Maybe there’s an abundance of other options for finding happiness?

Emba: One of the things that I wrote about in my book “Rethinking Sex” was a sort of critique of how sexuality — having sex and relationships and what kind of sex you’re having — became a defining factor of our self-identity. It’s something that people lead with; our relationship status, dating, is one of the first things that people ask about. One thing that we haven’t talked about is how dating has changed for millennials, but especially for Gen Z.

On dating apps, people get a volume of rejection, of people swiping past them and not matching with them, that is unparalleled in the history of dating. You might, 20 or 25 years ago, ask someone out and get turned down. On a dating app, you might swipe through and try to match with 50 people and get turned down by 49 of them.

That feels outside of your control, and also feels awful. And of course, it also doesn’t lead to dates in the real world. So I think some of the stigma around not having sex and not being in a relationship might also be what it reveals about your success in presenting yourself in this very specific forum that is the dating world today, where image matters a lot.

Dating apps are very picture-forward, where the ability to transition from the app into the real world is much harder and feels much more fraught for people. What I worry about, when it comes to young people not having as much sex or young people not having kids, is not necessarily the sex or the kids that might come from it, but actually just what it says more broadly about connection.

The first step to having sex or having kids is, ideally, being in a relationship of some kind with some person, which starts with just talking to people, having friends, getting to know people outside of yourself. And whether that leads to sex or dating or anything else, just this idea of connecting to other people is still really important — and it’s something that we have valued as a society and should value as a society.

And if our lower birthrates and our lower rates of sex and relationships are signals that we have forgotten how to do that, or a whole generation is struggling to make friends — and that is what the statistics are showing us, that younger people report higher levels of loneliness. They report higher levels of anxiety around relationships, but also around their state in life and security — the stuff that would allow them to form relationships — that seems like a problem to me. That is why I, at least, have been drawn to this question, because it speaks to the broader backdrop of discomfort.

Spiegelman: I think the discomfort is a really important part of it, because our phones can do so much for us that makes our lives completely frictionless. We live in a world of instant gratification. Porn can provide a version of sex that involves no risk, that almost involves no desire, because there’s no time to desire before it’s actively fulfilled.

And now intimacy can be met by our phones in so many different ways. I mean, you can have a very intimate relationship with an A. I. chatbot. You can have an intimate relationship with an OnlyFans creator, who can be texting you all day. And you can feel intimacy from your phone — a sort of version of it. You can get your sexual needs met from your phone, or a version of it. And if we want to make an argument for sex or dating, then we need to be able to make an argument that is actually for rejection, for heartbreak. Like, why would you put yourself through the friction and pain of these things? Can either of you make an argument for that? If I were talking to a young person who was like, “I have my needs met in this easy way. Why would I risk the pain of getting rejected or getting my heart broken?” I wouldn’t quite know what to say.

Sherman: I have had something of this actual conversation with a young person before, a year or two ago now. I was following around a group of young people who were at the Jersey Shore, and they were preaching the value of chastity, which is obviously a big sell to be making at the Jersey Shore.

Emba: At the Jersey Shore.

Sherman: I was like, “I’ve got to go report on this. This is so fascinating to me.” But I was talking to one of the young men, and he was not interested in having sex until marriage for religious reasons, which, I think that’s great; I think that people should obviously have sex according to their values. But what was fascinating to me is that he wasn’t even dating, and he was saying that this was one of the things he was thinking about: that if you aren’t dating for marriage, you’re dating for heartbreak. And that made me really sad, because I do feel like heartbreak is such — as you’re pointing out, Nadja — a formative experience.

When I had my heart broken, I learned so much about resilience. I have learned so much about anger. I have learned so much about art. I suddenly understood what all those Taylor Swift songs were about. And I feel like it turned me into the person I am today, to have gone through heartbreak. And to be able to feel that depth of feeling is a really special experience.

I don’t want people to get their hearts broken, but when it happens, it can be so enriching to your life. And I do think that young people are interested in more friction than they’re currently getting. I do actually think that there is a yearning for community. I don’t think we have to be making the argument that I was making to that young man. I think that there is an acknowledgment and an acceptance that friction is good for us. It’s better for us.

Emba: And to what you were saying, Nadja, about the idea that you can get your needs for intimacy met through A. I. or on OnlyFans — the question that was running through my head was: Can you really? Is that real intimacy? I think the thing with A. I. companions, and OnlyFans in particular — and this is my argument for friction — is that they’re meant to make you happy. They don’t fight you. They don’t push back.

Your A. I. flatters you and does what you want. It doesn’t get mad at you or tell you off, or say that it’s fine but you know it’s not fine, and then you have to figure out what’s going on. Those are the things that you have to learn to be in a relationship with real human beings. It’s how we learn how to move through the world with others. And without friction, you just don’t learn that, and I think that’s actually a pretty scary prospect.

Spiegelman: I want to keep pushing back. Why? If it’s enough for people, if it could be enough for people, then why do they really need to learn about all of the ways you can be hurt and unfulfilled by other people?

Sherman: The argument for friction is the argument for life. It’s the argument for being out in the world, for experiencing anything, and I understand that it’s scary and not always fun and feels rough, frankly — to make a pun using the word “friction” — but I do think people understand the inherent value of difficulty, and I think people understand that when I accomplish something that scared me or made me hurt or was just beyond what I thought I was capable of, they feel good.

In addition to that, I would make an argument around political power, and I would say that many young people are very fed up with our politics as it is. They feel very nihilistic. They feel like things are not going in the direction that they would like. And how do you make political change? You’ve got to build community. You’ve got to organize. You’ve got to talk to people. And of course, being on the internet can be helpful for that, but truly being in community with other people and meeting them and talking to them, and being able to have fuller conversations than you could possibly have on a screen — that is all essential to political power.

And so if you don’t want to do this because you feel very safe at home and you really love your A. I. boyfriend, that’s fine. But if you do want to change politics, maybe you should also try to experience other people.

Spiegelman: I heard you both say that an ability to be in community together is essential to politics. It’s essential to any kind of change. And from both the right and the left, there’s this feeling that we can’t just become completely atomized and isolated.

I’m also interested in the left-right divide. In part because, I think, it’s one of the things that’s going on with why young people aren’t having sex. Like, Gen Z has the largest political gender gap of any generation, with the men moving to the right and the women moving to the left.

When I was growing up, I associated the right with these Christian ideas of purity — of waiting for marriage, of abstinence — and I associated the left with a more pro-sex, sex positivity attitude. And to me, it feels like maybe there’s a bit of a reversal now.

The right wants people to have more babies, to have traditional values, whereas the left is moving further away from marriage and having children, and is making more room for ideas like asexuality or intentional celibacy. Do you guys agree with that analysis?

Sherman: I don’t know that that’s necessarily a fair characterization of either the left or the right. I do think that on the right — the right often gets painted as being anti-sex, and generally speaking, they’re not. There is a rich tradition within evangelical communities, for example, of promoting sex within marriage.

Emba: You have to have the right kind of sex. And at the right time, but you should be having it.

Sherman: Married, heterosexual, possibly procreative sex. That is the push among those on the right, and evangelicals have written a ton of very famous sex guides to that point.

And I think the left — yes, there is this sort of feeling that they’re not really pushing for sex, really, but these are also the people who are pushing for Pride parades. These are the people who are pushing for a more expansive view of gender and sexuality, and I think what often the left is really pushing is, let’s just not have strictures around what kind of sex is correct. Let’s take those away, and let’s make it more possible for more people to have the kind of sex that they want, and if that includes not having sex, then so be it.

I do think it is a major problem in our politics, and in our life, how much emphasis we place on sex as being a separate activity, as being something that is apart from the rest of our lives, and I just think that we all know that’s not true. When I come home from work and it’s been a bad day, it’s not like I can just go and have sex. My sex life does not exist in a parenthetical from the rest of my life, and I think we know that as individuals, and yet we seem to be unable to grasp that as a political concept.

Emba: I think for some on the further right end of the spectrum — with which I do not identify, frankly — some of the kind of Heritage Foundation-esque, Project 2025-ish characters, some of the motivation behind worrying about young people not having sex is more about the right kind of young people, wink wink, are not making enough babies and soon will be outvoted, and so they need to get to it so that we can continue to have political power.

I think there are other people who are really invested in this idea of not necessarily the sex, but the idea of a democratic society and people being able to interact with each other socially to build a politics in which we can live together. We’re losing those skills, and that’s really scary. That’s something that I identify with.

Spiegelman: I want to see if we can end in an optimistic place, and you’re fully welcome to disagree with me. Is there a world in which having less sex can mean valuing other forms of intimacy, creating more platonic bonds with people, valuing a sort of plenitude and solitude, figuring out other forms of happiness in the world that are not as focused as the millennial generation was on equating a rich sex life with the only way of being fulfilled?

Emba: For a long time, for most of its history, America has been focused on the relationship — the two-person romantic relationship, and then the near-nuclear family as the main segment of society.

And that meant that people who were not married or who didn’t have kids felt like they were off in the wilderness. And perhaps if Gen Z is having less sex and is less centered on romantic relationships, that actually does open up more space for people to explore relationships with their families, with their friends.

We’re seeing so much more discussion about people who are deciding to move in and build communities around their friendships, to have kids who have alloparents — who have relationships with godparents, friends, people who are not part of the nuclear family but who are still in relationships with them.

I actually think that this would be a great development. I think we have seen, over the past several decades, how the closed-off, tiny — two parents, 2.5 kids, we’re the only people who talk to each other — has failed to support both individuals and the broader society. If having less sex means that we have more relationships with other people overall, stronger relationships outside of the two-person pair, that’s a good thing.

Sherman: We were complaining at the start of this conversation about phones and how much those have really impaired young people’s ability to have sexual relationships. But think about how much time we all spend texting our friends now, or texting our parents, or texting the people who we care about and are intimate with.

We are more connected to those individuals than we ever have been before, and there’s a way to see that as a really beautiful thing. It is not just that, as technology develops, everything will get worse — we will become more friendless, we will not know our families, we will not know our neighbors. We are actually more connected than ever, and so it’s just a question of: How do we want to use that connection? What do we want to build with those connections?

Spiegelman: That is a perfect place to end. Thank you both so much.

Thoughts? Email us at theopinions@nytimes. com.

This episode of “The Opinions” was produced by Vishakha Darbha. It was edited by Kaari Pitkin, Alison Bruzek and Annie Galvin. Mixing by Carole Sabouraud. Video editing by Steph Khoury. The postproduction manager is Mike Puretz. Original music by Pat McCusker. Fact-checking by Mary Marge Locker. Audience strategy by Shannon Busta and Kristina Samulewski. The director of Opinion Video is Jonah M. Kessel. The deputy director of Opinion Shows is Alison Bruzek. The director of Opinion Shows is Annie-Rose Strasser.

With 2 Hires, Mamdani Blends Economic Development With Economic Justice

The New York Times July 22, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Anthony E. Shorris, a former deputy mayor and a partner at McKinsey, and Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, will lead the city’s Economic Development Corporation.

By Jeffery C. Mays

In a move that seemed designed to satisfy both business leaders and his democratic socialist supporters in New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday appointed two people to head the Economic Development Corporation whose vision for the agency might seem at odds.

Anthony E. Shorris, a veteran of city government and a partner at the global consulting firm McKinsey & Company, will serve as president. Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission and an advocate for strong government regulation, will serve as the board chair.

The announcement by Mr. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, comes as his administration has sought to shift the focus of the agency. The corporation, known as E. D. C., is a municipally run nonprofit designed to drive economic growth by creating jobs and encouraging economic development.

Mr. Mamdani has said he wants the organization to also focus on economic justice. The business community has expressed concerns about that shift and questioned whether the mayor was being inattentive to the city’s economy.

Those concerns heightened after The New York Times disclosed a memo, circulated by Julie Su, the deputy mayor for economic justice, that demanded that every E. D. C. program be re-evaluated to ensure the organization was not focused solely on economic growth, but also on justice.

Mr. Mamdani, speaking at a news conference at City Hall, said that he believed “that economic development and economic justice must go hand in hand. This is no radical concept.”

Mr. Shorris’s appointment was applauded by the city’s business, union and political leaders.

In a statement, Carlo Scissura, president and chief executive of the New York Building Congress, said Mr. Shorris would “truly bring together housing and economic development and growth.” Richard R. Buery Jr., chief executive of Robin Hood, an anti-poverty organization, said Mr. Shorris had the “cross-sector credibility” to spur job growth while focusing on “equity and economic justice” for city residents.

The city’s news release announcing the appointments did not include anyone other than the mayor or Mr. Shorris praising Ms. Khan, one of the most influential advisers helping to shape the Mamdani administration’s goals.

Ms. Khan is regarded as an antitrust crusader. During her time as chairwoman of the F. T. C., she sought to block acquisitions by Meta and Google. She filed suit against Amazon, accusing them of protecting a monopoly over online retailers.

During Mr. Mamdani’s transition to becoming mayor, Ms. Khan led a team that scoured city laws to find executive and regulatory actions that Mr. Mamdani could take during his first days in office to protect workers and lower costs. The administration has since unveiled several initiatives to protect workers, renters and consumers.

“It’s obvious the mayor is trying to strike a balance between his commitment on jobs and economic growth and economic justice,” Kathy Wylde, the former president of the influential business advocacy group the Partnership for New York City, said in an interview. “The appointment of Shorris and Khan does that.”

On Wednesday, Ms Khan praised the agency’s role in building the economy and driving growth. She emphasized that those goals were not out of line with economic justice.

“E. D. C. has key tools to drive projects that grow our economy, create good jobs, promote entrepreneurship and make life more affordable for New Yorkers,” Ms. Khan said at the news conference.

Steven Fulop, the current head of the Partnership for New York City, praised Mr. Shorris but said Ms. Khan’s appointment sent a “mixed message to the business community” that raised concern about the agency’s direction.

Ms. Khan’s reputation has been “built on an adversarial approach to large enterprises at the federal level,” Mr. Fulop said in a statement, noting that the Economic Development Corporation’s mission is to support growth and investment in the city.

“It’s unclear to us the ultimate direction E. D. C. will be taking and how this will play out over time,” Mr. Fulop added.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Jeffery C. Mays is a Times reporter covering politics with a focus on New York City Hall.

Women Are Too Controlling, She Wrote. Her Message Still Resonates.

The New York Times July 22, 2026

The message in “The Surrendered Wife,” the best-selling book by Laura Doyle, was provocative. Many women credit it with saving their marriages.

The message in “The Surrendered Wife,” the best-selling book by Laura Doyle, was provocative. Many women credit it with saving their marriages.

Laura Doyle, author of “The Surrendered Wife" and several other books, alongside her husband, John Doyle. Credit...

Supported by

By Vivian Yee

Photographs by Isadora Kosofsky

Vivian Yee writes about women in America. She visited Laura Doyle, read some of her books and talked to women who have practiced her method for this story.

Laura Doyle, best-selling author of “The Surrendered Wife” and several other books that promise to teach women to save their marriages, no matter how oafish their husbands might seem, has a question for me, the journalist who has come to Southern California to interview her. “Are you bossy?” she asks me, softly, almost shyly. “Are you controlling?”

I flash back to my ex, who labeled me controlling for pushing him to quit smoking, go out more, eat what I wanted to eat and take his shoes off inside my apartment.

“Um,” I stammer. “Some people would probably say so.”

Ms. Doyle is looking at me from her ivory couch, her husband of 36 years, John Doyle, next to her. “They would?” she says, her voice warm, with no judgment that I can detect.

I wouldn’t deny it, I tell her. But I have a question of my own. Given that Ms. Doyle considers herself a feminist, an ambitious, capable woman who was raised to be independent and has run her own company for nearly a quarter-century — given all that — does she hesitate to describe women, including herself, as “bossy” and “controlling”?

Because that is the premise of her books, the message she has been publishing, blogging, broadcasting, podcasting and teaching her international network of relationship coaches since 1999. That Ms. Doyle, 59, a self-described “former shrew,” thought she knew better than her husband as a young wife, “nagging” him to eat healthier, maintain the car on schedule and wear what she thought he should wear. That begging and cajoling only made him turn up the TV and drove him from their bed.

The message she is spreading is that with her marriage “in a ditch,” she reluctantly started taking the advice she received from happy wives to practice gratitude, apologize to her husband for emasculating and disrespecting him, metaphorically “duct tape” her mouth to curb her criticisms, make herself open to sex anytime, and relinquish control — even of their finances, even if it meant sitting in the dark because he forgot to pay the electricity bill (which actually happened). That taking care of herself (naps, beach volleyball) would help her show up better. That trying to change her husband got her nowhere, but changing herself gave her the marriage she had always dreamed of. That the intimacy returned so strongly that, nine years after marrying, she took her husband’s name. That the “intimacy skills,” as she came to call her findings, would work for other wives, even ones facing abuse, adultery or husbands with addictions.

That women are fundamentally different from men, whatever modern notions of gender equality might say. That a lot of women are controlling, and consequently, unhappy. That becoming a “surrendered wife” will save your marriage, but it might also save you.

The state of American gender relations is poor. Liberal-leaning straight women complain of heteropessimism, the conviction that dating men will end in tears. Young women increasingly reject marriage; divorce, in certain online spaces, is hot. Gen Z women are the most progressive Americans, speeding further left as more Gen Z men supported President Trump. Many of the far-right online ranters of the manosphere paint women as mere conquests, breeders who exist to serve men.

The women of a manosphere splinter sect, the “red pill women,” theorize that men (“captains” in marriage) are naturally dominant, and women (“first mates”) naturally submissive. Self-described red pill women may be a small minority, but they embody an increasingly visible axiom on the American right, that feminism is where it all went wrong. And if anyone asks them what to read, their answer is very often Laura Doyle.

Their philosophy has an apparent symmetry with Ms. Doyle’s, which holds that men, with their drive to protect and provide, “need respect like they need oxygen.” Women who want their husbands to desire and cherish them, she says, should “abandon the myth of equality.” Instead of acting like “smaller, less hairy men” and shouldering everything because they think he won’t do it or won’t do it right, they should practice softness, vulnerability and femininity — by which she means receptivity to gifts, compliments and help with suitcase-carrying, driving and household tasks. She used to tell women with abusive, alcoholic or adulterous husbands to leave, but later retracted that advice, saying that she had heard too many stories of such wives using the skills to save their marriages. If you want to leave, leave, she says, but if you want to fix your relationship, you can. You married him for a reason.

“Who am I to say?” she says in our interview. “I should have never said to stay, I should never say to leave, I shouldn’t say at all.” One of her mantras is, “you are the expert in your own life.”

The problem with reading Laura Doyle as some kind of manosphere apologist is that too many women of all types swear by her. Some would argue that’s only because patriarchy is baked into us all. Be that as it may, the straight women of America, and beyond, evidently crave succor from someone like her: a hetero-optimist in a hetero-fatalist world.

Since Ms. Doyle self-released “The Surrendered Wife” in 1999, eventually hitting the New York Times best-seller list, her books have been published in 19 languages across 30 countries. Friends surrendered, then friends of theirs, then women around the country and the world. Orthodox Jewish wives press her books on brides-to-be; evangelical Christian and observant Muslim wives have surrendered. But so have many secular or not particularly religious women who see themselves as strong and self-sufficient, doctors and lawyers and business owners and homemakers alike.

“I almost gagged myself when I saw the title,” said Darlene Davis, 66, a graphic designer in New Jersey who found “The Surrendered Wife” when her relationship was floundering. This was soon after Simon & Schuster published the book in 2001, adorning the cover with a red rose. “But within two weeks, I saw the difference.”

Pre-surrender, Ms. Davis described herself as a “big man-basher” who joked about male foibles with the best of them. Her post-surrender diagnosis: “Because I’m a strong, independent woman who knows how to get things done, I was doing all these things, telling him what to wear and speaking for him,” she said. “That’s great for business and all these other things, but it wasn’t good for him. He’s a very masculine man. He needs respect.”

She soon caught her future husband shopping for engagement rings.

Ms. Davis eventually became one of the first Laura-Doyle-certified relationship coaches, a group that now includes more than 600 women worldwide. The company — mission: “End World Divorce” — says more than 15,000 women worldwide have received Laura Doyle coaching through programs including “Ridiculously Happy Wives,” while others are receiving private coaching.

Amanda Blaine, 45, a nonviolent communication counselor, spent her 20s surrounded by progressives who embraced polyamory and avoided using gendered words, including “man” and “woman.” Uncomfortable with stereotypical femininity, she briefly identified as genderqueer. During the coronavirus pandemic, a breakup led her to “The Empowered Wife” (published in 2017). Within one chapter, she felt as if Ms. Doyle had been watching her relationship.

The skills soon reunited Ms. Blaine with her boyfriend. That December, she started coach training, which she said gave her the self-understanding to leave her boyfriend for good. (She wanted kids; he did not.)

Now happily married with a young son, Ms. Blaine coaches the skills to women, including one with a nonbinary partner, encouraging them to look past the old-fashioned language.

“You don’t have to be a woman with a man to relinquish control of your partner,” she said. “It’s just how to be a person in a relationship.”

But it wasn’t easy, admitting she was “a woman who wants to bear a child and wants to be doted on by a man,” she said.

Friends scoffed at the skills. Her coaching-program classmates were headed for divorce, one friend predicted. She fell out with another who asked, “Why do you have to call yourself ‘feminine’?” A mentor said being told to “respect” one’s husband made her recoil. It sounded like subjugation.

But Ms. Blaine, watching women in her circle get divorced, wished they had known the skills.

“Maybe there’s something you’re missing about what’s possible with this person who you wanted to spend your life with,” she said, “because of this other narrative around women’s empowerment.”

Listening to her reminded me of friends of mine who had gotten married despite questioning the institution of marriage, who’d had kids despite critiquing the traditional nuclear family — that classic woman’s quandary, freedom versus love, never resolved and especially fraught in the age of the tradwife. I had read surveys saying that women, in this day and age, still wanted men who could support their families. Reasonable! But also, tradition is hard to shake.

In her spacious living room in Corona Del Mar, Calif., the blue-tiled pool her husband built her shimmering through the sliding doors beyond, Laura Doyle tells me she knows she sounds old-fashioned, even backward. But she is no doormat, as she has been accused of telling other women to be.

Her ambition and independence remain, “but I think you can actually parse that control out,” she says. Control comes from fear, she says; she would rather put positivity in charge. Surrendering, she says, “helped me honor myself and be more successful in my career than I ever would have been.”

Honoring and respecting yourself, not only your husband, is one of Ms. Doyle’s main prescriptions. She and the Laura Doyle coaches I interviewed said the skills helped them prioritize their own desires, stop “martyring” themselves to children or chores, take care of themselves, ditch resentment and blame and gain dignity and humility.

“We ask, ‘What do you want?’ We never ask, ‘What does he want?’” said Marissa Zwetow, 49, a coach in Southern California. “That’s not submissive.”

They said they, too, wish men would do better. But if we’re stuck with the world we have, not the world we want, the only thing that makes these women feel empowered is changing themselves. It’s a sort of mental magic trick, transmuting what really seemed to me to be a form of hetero-resignation (and hetero-desperation) into hetero-hopefulness. (Though not absolutism: Ms. Doyle emphasizes that women can always leave.)

Ms. Doyle lays her hand over her husband’s, saying, “I think it’s OK if we want to be loved, not just have careers.”

I ask Mr. Doyle, 70, whether he thinks men could do more. He says his wife’s self-improvement helped him step up.

Before, “you feel that nothing that you do is going to be right,” he said. Now, “I feel more willing to help and to do things,” he said, “because there won’t constantly be a rejection or a criticism just for basically being who I am.”

Ms. Doyle was raised up the coast in Huntington Beach, Calif., the eldest child of a turbulent marriage. Her mother, a concert violinist and nurse, often pushed her father, who took X-rays at a hospital, to make more money. She raised Ms. Doyle not to depend on a man and played her the 1972 Marlo Thomas record “Free to Be … You and Me,” the groundbreaking children’s album that sang gently of an egalitarian world without traditional gender norms.

Ms. Doyle moved out in high school, when her parents’ marriage finally splintered for good. At San Jose State University, she met Mr. Doyle, a video producer who had moved in next door. They married when she was 22.

Four years later, she writes, she was convinced she had married the wrong guy. Too embarrassed for divorce, she sought advice from happily married women.

Their counsel horrified her.

“‘This stuff sounds crazy,’” she remembers thinking. “I was afraid I was letting all feminists everywhere down by staying in a relationship where I was being mistreated.”

Desperate, she tried it anyway. When tempted to criticize or micromanage, she writes, she asked herself which she wanted more, control or connection. She repeated “surrender” to herself, shorthand for “stop trying to control everything.”

Soon she was spreading the gospel to friends, who asked her to write it down for other friends. The Doyles self-published the result. When Simon & Schuster picked it up, the publisher wanted to dump the did-she-really-say-that title, she said, but it was already generating too much buzz. She went on “The View”; she went on the “Today” show. Later came four more books, a streaming TV show and a podcast, whose video version Mr. Doyle helps produce. “The Surrendered Wife” was reissued for its 25th anniversary this summer. An Adored Wife app is coming.

When I visit her, Ms. Doyle is perched on a powder-pink desk chair in her floral-wallpapered home office, nodding and beaming affirmations at the assembled acolytes on a Zoom call for coach trainees. She raises her arms and cheers as she calls each name (“Tess! Tess is heeere!”). There’s a lot to celebrate. In her world, the wives are ridiculously happy, and the husbands are all great guys.

“So sweet,” she tells one woman who recounts using the intimacy skills to allow her husband to deal with the dishes when she was exhausted and the dishwasher was broken. “You have a great guy, Catherine. That’s awesome.”

“Sounds like you’re just the princess at your house, like I am at mine,” she tells another woman whose husband cleaned the kitchen unasked. I can’t help but think of the feminist complaint that men get applause for every chore they do, while women are just expected to do it.

“Very, very surrendered, I’ve got to say,” she says to a third. Streams of red hearts keep floating across the screen as the other participants show support.

It’s hard not to be happy for all these women, even if some of the things they said startled me. (One coach told me a client ended up in bankruptcy after relinquishing the finances to her husband. She prioritized preserving the relationship over blaming him.) Still, I wondered: Is it really this easy? And also, does it have to be this hard?

A few interviewees acknowledged that it did not work for some women they knew, recalling one or two who had left their husbands. Then I found Jennifer Phoenix Allen, 45, a trauma therapist outside Minneapolis.

Her 12-year marriage hit rock bottom in February. She had spent years frustrated with his parenting; he had spent years lying about using porn. She’d caught him secretly recording her. He wanted a divorce.

She felt she needed to stay for their 8-year-old son, who has autism and A. D. H. D. Enter Laura Doyle. And … it worked.

“Cue the moral dilemma,” Ms. Allen said.

Because she was a feminist and she wanted her man, all men, to step up without her having to practice what often felt sneaky, like wearing a mask. Because she thought Laura Doyle advised being meek and demure, which grated. Because Laura Doyle told her to yield control of the finances, and she needed a separate bank account for security. Because she wasn’t even sure that monogamy and marriage were anything but artifices that capitalism had foisted upon us all. Because if she had to be married, couldn’t marriage be between two equal adults who made it work together?

“Why is it me having to do all these things, whereas he can keep on keeping on the way he always has?” Ms. Allen said. “I have a hard time not just taking a giant step back and looking sociologically at, how the F did we get here? Why are gender relations so incredibly messed up?”

But, indisputably: He had changed. And nothing else she had tried had worked.

“It’s been a shift from viewing him as, ‘Oh my God, you’re an abusive narcissist,’ to realizing I was being so critical and I needed to clean up my side of the street better,” she said. “Looking back, was I more harsh to my husband than I needed to be? I believe that I was.”

Was I harsher to my ex-boyfriend than I needed to be? Maybe. Probably.

The thing is, I’m no surrendered wife, and my current boyfriend is great anyway. I tell this to all the interviewees. Ms. Davis, the longtime coach, told me I must be practicing the skills subconsciously, and, after all this time in Laura Doyle’s world, who knows!

Ms. Doyle doesn’t tell me that. But she does seem to suggest, gently, that unless I change my ways, I might repeat the same mistakes. That’s what would have happened to her if she had exchanged husbands instead of changing herself, she says.

Instead: The morning before our interview, Mr. Doyle cleans the kitchen. He does the dishes, as always. He makes her tea. When a photographer arrives to take their portrait, they pose together. “Your eyes are so blue!” Laura Doyle exclaims, and smiles up at her husband.

Last year, a friend of mine who was having marital problems told me she’d gotten so desperate that she was reading a book called “The Surrendered Wife.” Given what I knew about her, I was pretty taken aback. Then she mentioned that she’d learned about it from a Reddit thread for “red pill women,” women who say men are naturally dominant over women, and I got even more curious. So I went to meet Laura Doyle last month.

She was warm and self-assured, and she very gently pushed back on my skeptical questions. And the more I talked to her, the more I started thinking about this push-and-pull that I think a lot of straight women like my friend experience — between believing in feminist ideals and independence and strength, and yet wanting love and marriage, and feeling like those desires are impossible to reconcile fully with their principles.

Vivian Yee is a Times reporter who writes about women in America, focusing on cultural and political shifts during the Trump years.

The Choice Facing Some Immigrants: Pay $1.8 Million in Fines or Leave

The New York Times July 22, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Tens of thousands of immigrants have received letters to pay up or leave, as the government enlists debt collectors and seizes tax refunds.

By Miriam Jordan

Miriam Jordan is a national immigration correspondent.

The Trump administration is aggressively deploying a potent tool to pressure undocumented immigrants into self-deporting — civil fines that can total as much as $1.8 million.

More than 100,000 people have received letters from the Homeland Security Department informing them that they owe $998 for each day that they have stayed in the United States after an immigration judge has ruled they have no legal right to remain in the country.

Fines for failing to heed a “removal” order have been permitted since the passage of immigration legislation in 1996. Until President Trump, however, no commander in chief had imposed such penalties. The effort to do so in his first term ran into logistical obstacles and never gained traction.

But after returning to the White House last year and starting his mass deportation campaign, Mr. Trump ordered “all appropriate action to ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties” from people unlawfully in the country.

Now, with the administration seeking to increase financial pressure on undocumented immigrants, the pace of fines has been accelerating, according to immigration lawyers.

For immigrants who receive one, the notices amount to an agonizing ultimatum: abandon the lives they have built, or face the threat of financial ruin if the government moves to collect on the debt. Even under a five-year statutory limit, the accumulated penalties can reach a $1.8 million per person.

Vivi Vasquez, a Mexican immigrant, has lived in the United States for 17 years and has an active humanitarian visa application. With a work permit, she has legally worked at a convenience store and cared for seniors.

Expecting an update on her visa application, Ms. Vasquez opened an envelope that arrived in April bearing a D. H. S. logo. Instead of news about her visa, she found a form letter in which the government had checked a box next to a statement that she had “willfully” failed to depart the United States.

She owed the government $1,820,352, according to the document, which was reviewed by The New York Times. Tucked in the same envelope was a flier titled, “Self-Deport with CBP Home and Leave on Your Own Terms,” referring to an app run by Customs and Border Protection. It offered “forgiveness” for all fines to those who used the app to self deport.

“I couldn’t sleep, and I was nervous every morning I left home for work,” said Ms. Vasquez, who has three U. S.-born children, ages 10, 12 and 14.

Legal aid organizations and lawyers representing individual clients have filed several federal lawsuits seeking to block the policy, contending that the financial penalties violate due process and the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on excessive fines.

In court filings opposing the motion to pause the policy, the government has argued that the fact that a person remained in the country to pursue other forms of immigration relief “is not a defense under the statutes and does not change the underlying determination that one willfully or voluntarily violated” the removal order.

Vast sweeps by federal agents in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis have been the most visible and volatile fronts in Mr. Trump’s crackdown. But the fines are part of a parallel effort by the administration to squeeze undocumented immigrants and make it harder for them to live in the United States.

The letter to Ms. Vasquez gave her 15 days, from the date it had been mailed, to contest the penalty. With barely a week to go before that deadline, her lawyer appealed. A month later, while awaiting a decision, Ms. Vasquez received a second, more menacing letter.

Unless she promptly paid, it said, the government would refer her debt to a private collection agency; initiate federal collection litigation; report her to credit bureaus, “which could adversely affect your credit rating”; and consider the debt in her future immigration proceedings.

“We started seeing this a couple months ago, and it’s become a big trend,“ said John Leschak, an immigration lawyer in New Jersey who represented Ms. Vasquez and was able to have the fines canceled.

“These are people who have homes, cars, businesses in their names,” he said. “The government says they stand to have all that confiscated.”

Prevailing, as Ms. Vasquez did, is not typical, according to a dozen lawyers interviewed by The Times. In case after case, they say, appeals have been denied, including for a 68-year-old man who is the primary caregiver for his wife, a U. S. citizen who has cancer.

The man was ordered removed in 2012 but allowed to remain in the United States after homeland security paused his removal. A few months ago, he received the form letter, saying that he had willfully failed to depart and owed the government $579,838.

“You can’t allow people to stay here and then turn around and just fine them for it,” said the man’s lawyer, Reem Khraizat, who practices in Detroit.

Ms. Khraizat filed an appeal that included letters of support from health providers attesting to his wife’s condition and her reliance on him.

“ICE reaffirmed the decision without even addressing the facts presented on appeal,” Ms. Khraizat said.

The Homeland Security Department said that between Jan. 20, 2025, and mid-July of this year, ICE had issued more than 103,000 fines to noncitizens who remained in the United States past a deportation order, seeking a combined total of more than $84 billion.

As of July 16, it had collected more than $1.2 million, according to the agency.

Desperate to protect their life savings, some immigrants have removed their names from property deeds or transferred their modest assets into trusts, according to two lawyers who assist immigrants with estate planning.

“This administration is just churning out as many fines as it can to intimidate and harass people into leaving the country,” said Charles Moore, a senior attorney with Public Justice, a nonprofit legal organization, who is representing immigrants in a Massachusetts lawsuit to block the practice.

The Homeland Security Department did not respond to questions about how many immigrants had chosen to self-deport to avoid the penalties and how many cases had been referred to debt collection agencies.

Even as the policy faces legal challenges, government enforcement continues to move forcefully. Mr. Moore, who is seeking class-action certification for the Massachusetts lawsuit, said D. H. S. has referred some debts to private collection agencies, seized tax refunds and garnished wages, and that the Justice Department has taken dozens of immigrants to court to compel them to pay.

Afissetou Tchedre, a Togo national married to an American service member, was sued by the Justice Department this year in its effort to collect more than $1.3 million. According to a counterclaim filed in federal court in New York in May, the government seized the full amount of the couple’s last tax refund, $10,662.

Ms. Tchedre has lived in the United States since 2011. After her asylum claim was denied, her husband, with whom she has four U. S.-born children, filed a petition to sponsor her for a green card.

Her lawyer, Hasan Shafiqullah, said that he believed D. H. S. had not even reviewed her case before assessing the fine, otherwise agency officials would have realized that Ms. Tchedre had the right to remain in the country.

“The government had knowledge that she was taking steps to obtain status,” said Mr. Shafiqullah, a lawyer at the Legal Aid Society in New York.

Ms. Tchedre lost her employment authorization as a result of the fine, and her lawyer is fighting to recover the seized funds.

During the first Trump administration, the notices were sent by certified mail, which obligates the recipient to sign for delivery — a requirement that led to many of the notices being returned to D. H. S. as undeliverable.

President Joseph R. Biden Jr. rescinded the policy upon taking office, but Mr. Trump resurrected it on the first day of his second term through an executive order and a swiftly enacted policy that carried steeper fines.

And this time, the letters were sent by ordinary mail.

Seamus Hughes contributed research.

Miriam Jordan reports from a grass roots perspective on immigrants and their impact on the demographics, society and economy of the United States.
