A Device Hidden in Cars Across the US Leaves Them Vulnerable to Hacking and Paralysis. Patch It Now

Wired July 21, 2026

As modern cars have evolved into multi-ton computers on wheels, drivers are beginning to learn they need to install security updates for their vehicles' code, just as they would for a phone or laptop. Yet not even the most tech-savvy car owners would expect they'd need to install a patch for an insecure third-party component they never installed or requested—and likely aren't even aware of—that's been wired into some of the most sensitive systems of their vehicle, leaving it vulnerable to stealthy hacking, tracking, and even roadside paralysis.

That's the disturbing discovery of a team of security researchers at UC San Diego, who found that a model of aftermarket car alarm known as the KARR Security System, installed in more than 2 million vehicles across the US by their estimate, can let any hacker within Bluetooth range send radio commands to silently unlock the car at will, turn off its alarm, honk the car's horn or flash its lights, or even disable its ignition and leave a driver stranded.

The KARR alarm devices are typically installed by car dealers, not manufacturers or owners, and used as a measure to prevent auto theft from dealer lots. Yet when the cars are sold, the alarms typically aren't removed, even if the buyer declines to pay for it as an additional feature. That means car owners across the US have a hackable device under their hood whose code they'll need to update to protect their vehicle—but one that, in many cases, they never purchased and have no idea is there.

The KARR Security System has been wired into the critical systems of more than 2 million vehicles by UCSD's estimate, all of which need the patch to protect them from hacking techniques that can track, unlock, and paralyze cars.

"This is a system added to cars by dealers, and unfortunately it has a severe vulnerability that allows anyone to gain access to any of these cars," says Aaron Schulman, the UCSD computer science professor who led the research. “It's designed to make cars more secure, but ultimately it's created a vulnerability that needs to be patched immediately across millions vehicles. We're trying to get the word out that you need to check your car for this device and manually patch it now.”

The company that sells the KARR Security System, Acrisure Protection Group, on Monday rolled out a firmware update for the vulnerable Bluetooth model of its aftermarket KARR alarm to fix the security issues UCSD uncovered. Car owners who already have the KARR Security smartphone app installed should receive an alert about the firmware update, the UCSD team says. Those who don’t have it installed will need to download the KARR Security System smartphone app (Android, iOS), connect it to their vehicle's KARR alarm, then tap “customer service” and “firmware update.”

Given that at least half of car owners who have the KARR device installed didn't ask for it to be in their vehicles, according to UCSD's estimate, you can check if your car has the device by looking for a KARR sticker on your car's driver-side window—or in some cases a sticker reading, “SWDS” for SouthWest Dealer Services, a subsidiary of Acrisure Protection Group—as well as a small button with a blinking light attached to the underside of your car's dashboard. Car owners in Southern California are most likely to have the device installed due to its popularity among car dealers in the region, but the UCSD researchers warn that they've found the devices installed in vehicles across the US and even in other countries.

That difficulty of getting word out to affected drivers, combined with the significant risk that the vulnerability could be used for theft, makes the KARR's security flaw “probably the worst” car hacking threat ever discovered, says Stefan Savage, another UCSD computer science professor who didn't work on the KARR alarm findings but did co-lead the first team to hack a car's steering and brakes in 2010 and 2011. “It affects a large number of vehicles, the manufacturer of your car can't fix it, and you don't even know you have the problem,” says Savage. “It provides all the elements a car thief would want, but you have none of the advantages we normally have in terms of defending it, because you're disconnected from the supply chain that put it there.”

When WIRED reached out to Acrisure Protection Group about the KARR security flaw, a spokesperson responded in a statement: “The vulnerability described in [UCSD's] research is highly complex and presents a low risk to customers under real-world conditions. Nevertheless, we responded promptly and developed a firmware update to address the issue.”

The company added that it will be alerting car owners to its patch via the KARR Security app, the KARR Security website, and via “dealer communications." It didn't share more about how it will reach car owners who aren't aware that they have the device installed, including owners of affected vehicles that may have even been resold to drivers who can't be reached by dealerships.

Despite Acrisure Protection Group's claim to have patched the flaw “promptly," it actually took close to 18 months to push out its patch. The UCSD researchers told the company about the vulnerability in January of last year, but the company didn't offer a fix until just weeks ahead of UCSD's planned presentations about its findings at the Defcon hacker conference and the Usenix security conference next month.

Acrisure's claim that the vulnerability represents a “low risk” under “real-world conditions" also merits some skepticism. In a series of demos for WIRED, all captured in the video above, the researchers showed that they could use their own Android app to send Bluetooth commands to vulnerable vehicles with KARR installed to carry out a wide array of potentially disruptive or dangerous hacking. The demo exploits can, with the tap of a button, unlock a car at a stop light to enable theft or carjacking, instantly paralyze a parked car to prevent it from starting, or even—with a “mayhem” button they built into the app—hack a group of cars to simultaneously and repeatedly trigger their horns and lights, as the researchers demonstrated for WIRED in a UCSD parking lot.

The UCSD team’s proof of concept app offers a menu of hacking options that the KARR vulnerability makes possible …

… as well as a list of nearby cars whose Bluetooth signals show they have the vulnerable KARR device installed.

The KARR Security System's vulnerabilities do not, fortunately, allow a hacker to start a car's ignition. But the UCSD researchers showed how a locksmith tool commonly available for resale online can, once a car thief is inside the vehicle, be plugged into a car's dash to create a working key within a few minutes and drive it away. Car thieves using that device would typically have to break a window or use car-door opening tools, potentially setting off a car alarm. But combined with the KARR vulnerability, they can stealthily get into the vehicle to carry out that theft technique.

The security flaw that makes all of those sabotage and intrusion tricks possible, the UCSD team found, is a single authentication key shared across all KARR devices. The UCSD researchers also spotted that key in the code of the KARR smartphone app, which customers who pay for the alarm can use to control it. With that key and a homemade app they created by reverse engineering the KARR app's code, they found they could spoof radio commands that would be accepted by any nearby Bluetooth-enabled KARR device.

The KARR device's insecurity is compounded by the fact that, even when a car buyer declines to pay for it as an add-on, it stays in the vehicle and continues to both beacon out and accept Bluetooth signals whenever the car is on, and also for as long as 10 minutes after the car is turned off. Though the KARR device is in a "deactivated" state for those drivers, the researchers found they could activate it with a radio command and then immediately carry out their menu of hacking techniques.

That activation does trigger a quick beep from the car's horn and a flicker of its lights, the only sign a car owner might have that someone has put their car into a hackable state. For the hundreds of thousands of KARR customers who did pay a dealer to enable the alarm system, they would receive no such warning.

A UCSD researcher, Nishant Bhaskar, first became aware of the KARR devices in 2018, while doing analysis of radio-enabled “skimmer” devices designed to steal credit card information from gas station point-of-sale terminals. He began to pick up Bluetooth signals from mysterious devices at the gas stations, and then soon realized that he was seeing the same radio signals on the highway from vehicles of all makes and models. That's when he began to search online for the text-based prefixes of those Bluetooth signals and saw in a Federal Communications Commission database that they came from the KARR alarm device.

Only years later, when then graduate researcher Jerry Yu was looking for a summer project in 2024, did Schulman suggest he take a look at the security of the KARR device whose signals Bhaskar had spotted. Yu quickly found the KARR app's universal authentication key, a glaring security flaw. “Once we reverse-engineered their application, we quickly realized after understanding their internal authentication protocol that it was so simple that we could extract it and re-implement it as our own application, which we did," Yu says. That app could, they discovered, unlock “every single car they've ever put this in.”

To get a count of how many vulnerable KARR devices are out there, UCSD researcher Yibo Wei used the open-source radio information database WiGLE, which crowdsources radio signals that contributors pick up with antennas all over the US and the world. He estimated as a result of those scans and extrapolating from the serial numbers of the devices that more than 2 million of the Bluetooth-enabled KARR devices have been deployed.

The UCSD researchers’ estimates of the locations of vulnerable cars across the US, based in part on radio signals collection crowdsourced in the WiGLE database.

Those WiGLE results are, however, more than just a measurement tool. They also potentially allow a hacker to track the historical locations of vulnerable cars based on their KARR device's Bluetooth signature and find places where the vehicle is frequently parked—a disturbingly easy scouting mechanism for finding opportunities to hack them for theft or sabotage.

In the UCSD team’s own scanning, they also found KARR-enabled vehicles virtually everywhere they looked. At one point, the researchers took me for a short drive around the outskirts of the university's campus while using their app on a normal Android phone to scan for cars with beaconing KARR devices. They found 97 vehicles with the alarms in just 20 minutes.

Schulman and his team now feel a responsibility to warn every one of those drivers about the hidden, hackable gadget in the guts of their vehicle. "When you install something by default at a dealer in every car that's sold, the pervasiveness of that vulnerability is going to be unimaginable," he says. “This is why we need to publicize this and get it out there, because the only way this will eventually get solved is if we get everyone on board and to fix it themselves.”

Stop Saying Kids Can’t Read

Wired July 21, 2026

Everyone is talking about the reading crisis. But inside the “Mississippi Miracle,” it’s all about comprehension.

It’s three weeks until Mississippi’s standardized test season begins, and Candace Hamberlin is feeling the pressure.

Evidence of what’s at stake hangs all around Jefferson County Middle School, where Hamberlin is in her first year teaching eighth-grade English. Inside her classroom, a large piece of black polyester with clear pouches labeled “Data Wall” shows the current reading level of each student. The school hallways are lined with posters listing schoolwide scores on an earlier practice test. One prominently displays the grade Mississippi would assign their school if that practice test had been the real thing: 175 out of 700 points, an F.

Jefferson County is one of the smallest in Mississippi; 6,800 people spread across 527 square miles along the Mississippi River. It’s also one of the poorest, with 32 percent of the population living below the poverty line. Fayette, where the only public elementary, middle, and high school are all based, is the only city in the county, home to about a dozen churches but not a single stoplight. The county is 13 percent white, but most of those families send their kids to private or parochial schools; 98 percent of the school district’s students are Black.

Inside Hamberlin’s classroom, it’s time for test-prep drills. This period has 20 eighth graders enrolled, but only 10 are present; six have been pulled out for remedial work with a consultant the district has hired to boost test scores, and the remaining four are absent for unclear reasons. The students in the room each grab a Chromebook and log in, at speeds ranging from feet-dragging to actively resistant. They open the StudySync software program, which shows them each a series of questions tailored to their weaknesses. Their faces look like they’re being marched to the guillotine.

Much of literacy instruction at Jefferson County Middle School now begins and ends with screens. In fact, Hamberlin doesn’t lecture at all on Wednesdays and Thursdays; students spend those class periods with StudySync and i-Ready, another adaptive software program, so each can focus where they need the most help.

The youngs are facing problems that didn't even exist half a generation ago. They’re handling it better than you think.

Their teacher can’t blame them for being sick of these exercises. The students’ lives, and hers, are dominated by the looming Mississippi Academic Assessment Program (MAAP), the set of annual standardized exams that measure their progress in language arts as well as science and math. Test prep is a year-round activity. Her students must learn how to decode the meaning of unfamiliar words, make inferences, identify the central idea of a passage, analyze tone and point of view. Every Friday brings a practice test.

Before moving to eighth grade, Hamberlin logged 25 years as an elementary school teacher. Eighth grade appealed to her because it’s all about analyzing texts, not just consuming them. That’s her idea of a good time. She remembers reading the first chapter of the first Harry Potter book four times just to make sure she didn’t miss a single detail. As she talks a group of students through a reading passage by Sojourner Truth, her passion is palpable—for the material, but even more for the puzzle-solving that reading comprehension requires.

“A lot of them think they’re studying the story,” she says afterward. “You’re not studying the story, that’s just the sprinkles on top. It’s what was she thinking, why did she say it, how did she convey her message?”

Candace Hamberlin, an eighth-grade English teacher at Jefferson County Middle School.

Despite her clear talent and enthusiasm for teaching, though, Hamberlin has thus far failed to convince many of her students to care about reading. Earlier in the year, barely half of the eighth graders scored high enough to pass the all--important exam, and less than 15 percent are scoring “proficient.” If that F on the final schoolwide practice test had been the real thing, it would have been disastrous; Mississippi’s letter grading system comes with steep real-world consequences. Low-performing schools can face state monitoring, while their funding is more likely to come with “accountability” strings attached. State law allows students to attend out-of-district charter schools only when their home district is failing, so low scores can result in a decrease in funding because fewer students are enrolled. Superintendents and principals know that their jobs are tied to increasing scores or at least not allowing them to drop.

Across the country, reading performance has slid for 14 years, and the problem is most extreme in middle and high school. Even in Mississippi, where the improvement in elementary school test scores has become the stuff of legend, older students are struggling. No one can quite agree on why reading scores have dropped so far.

And that’s just what the tests measure. Hamberlin’s true fears are more existential. Hamberlin wants her students to pass the exam, but what she really wants is to build them into readers; adults who can interpret a complex set of instructions, power through a confusing block of text, and—hopefully, maybe, at least a few—actually read books. “It’s as simple as understanding a conversation. How many times have you talked to someone and you’re talking about two different things?” she says. “All those skills from reading just transfer to life completely.”

Plenty of her students are smart and capable, but she’s never encountered a group less interested in reading. And neither she nor anyone else seems to have any idea how to fix it.

Panicking over standardized test scores is an American tradition. In 1983, a Department of Education commission published A Nation at Risk, a 36-page report that would become the foundation of education policy discussions for decades. Until then, standardized tests were generally administered locally, with little weight attached to scores. The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), which has since become “the nation’s report card,” had run trial exams in a small number of schools since 1969, but only for research purposes.

Citing a decline in SAT scores over the preceding two decades, A Nation at Risk’s authors framed their concerns in geo-political terms, warning that countries like Japan and South Korea were poised to overtake the US in global economic rankings if American students didn’t make significant gains. Their language was hyperbolic to the point of scare--mongering: “If an unfriendly foreign power had attempted to impose on America the mediocre educational performance that exists today, we might well have viewed it as an act of war,” the introduction read. “As it stands, we have allowed this to happen to ourselves.” One bullet point reported that one--quarter of Navy recruits could not read at a ninth-grade level, “the minimum needed simply to understand written safety instructions. Without remedial work they cannot even begin, much less complete, the sophisticated training essential in much of the modern military.”

In the four decades since, at least one of the authors of A Nation at Risk has backed away from its findings, saying the commission cherry-picked the data that best served their preexisting thesis that American schools were failing. They did accomplish their goals, though: The report called for the adoption of “more rigorous and measurable standards” in schools, and throughout the ’90s, states designed their own standardized tests to be administered across all school districts.

The march toward high-stakes testing crescendoed with President George W. Bush’s signature education reform program, No Child Left Behind, signed into law in 2002, which required standards-based exams in reading and math for every public school student in the country. Schools that didn’t meet standards risked state takeovers.

Hamberlin leading a session in her class of eighth-grade students.

The Data Wall in Hamberlin’s classroom shows the current reading level of each student.

Detractors have long questioned the validity of test scores, pointing to built-in bias among other issues. Even so, state testing has become the most important measure of reading skills by a huge margin. NAEP reading scores did rise, modestly, in the first part of the 21st century (at least among elementary and middle schoolers; high school scores stayed largely flat). Scores for 13-year-olds moved from 259 to 263 on a 500-point scale between 1999 and 2012; 9-year-olds improved from 212 to 221. The narrative that American schools were failing faded from conventional wisdom.

Then reading performance began to drop again. Among 13-year-olds, scores fell to 260 by 2020, nearly erasing the previous gains. The pandemic made things worse. By 2025, 13-year-old scores had plunged to 256, just a point above where they were in 1971. (Math scores have seen a similar decline.) Scores ticked up slightly among 9-year-olds in 2026 and remained at the prior year’s levels among 13-year-olds. One-third of 13-year-olds score “below basic” on standardized reading tests, meaning they can’t identify the main idea in a passage.

Panic roared back. Secretary of education Linda McMahon said the national results in 2024 “confirm a devastating trend”; The Atlantic said the country was “sliding toward illiteracy”; New York magazine labeled the drift “The Big Fail.” Much of the uproar sounded straight out of A Nation at Risk: “If policy-makers and education leaders fail to act now, students—and employers—will feel the impact of declining skills and knowledge gaps as the global workforce becomes more and more competitive,” the chair of the National Assessment Governing Board said in a press release.

Everyone had a pet theory as to what had gone wrong: smartphones, bad teachers, bad textbooks, lazy students, lazy families. A 2022 podcast called Sold a Story, about the problematic rise of the “balanced literacy” teaching method in elementary schools, revealed a pedagogical issue in the US: Many teachers were, basically, asking kids to guess at sentences instead of making them sound the words out.

As in-school apps began incorporating generative artificial intelligence, the fears intensified. Many schools now introduce AI starting in kindergarten, saying kids have to be prepared for a future in which it’s the norm. Maybe using AI tools will improve standardized test scores; it’s too early to tell. But it’s more difficult to believe those tools will improve literacy in the truer sense, that students will fully develop the cognitive skills to do the work themselves when they don’t have to.

“There’s no question that the engagement’s gone,” says Kevin Smith, an education scholar who co-leads the Adolescent Literacy Alliance at Florida State University’s Florida Center for Reading Research. “I’m not saying they’re not reading, but they’re not reading books for the love of books. They’re reading probably more than they ever have, but it’s snippets.”

Earlier this year, a team of researchers from Harvard, Stanford, and Dartmouth declared the US was in “a learning recession.” And suddenly, everyone was looking to Mississippi for the answers.

On the same small campus where Jefferson County’s eighth graders are scouring reading passages, the elementary school students are preparing for their own versions of the Mississippi Academic Assessment Program exams. State English Language Arts testing begins in third grade, and the first one is the most important. Under the state’s 2013 -Literacy-Based Promotion Act, any third grader who fails the test three times is automatically held back a year. (Students with documented learning disabilities, those who have already been held back twice, and students new to learning English are exempt from the policy.)

LaTasha Glass, 30, is in her first year teaching in Fayette after six years in her hometown of Natchez, a bigger, more touristy town on the river. With a daughter in fifth grade at Jefferson County Elementary, she brings a maternal air to class, providing warm encouragement and tough-love coaching in equal measure. She’s dressed for a day on her feet, in a lavender short-sleeved shirt over black stretchy pants and outdoorsy sandals, but her hair is stylishly braided, and silver bangles clink on her wrist. Glass started her career teaching second grade, but a previous principal convinced her she had what it took to get third graders over the test hurdle. That’s not an easy sell for many teachers; Jefferson County Elementary principal Shameka Woods says she’s asked the school district to pay third-grade teachers more because they’re so hard to hire. “No one wants to teach third grade!” Woods says. Glass pipes up, mostly joking but not entirely: “I asked her yesterday to put me back in second grade!”

Her first-block class makes clear why Glass is so valuable in the highest-stakes teaching role. From the time the bell rings, she has her students’ complete attention. The moment she senses she’s at risk of losing even a couple of them, she shouts out one of her bespoke call-and-response mantras that immediately brings them back:

Mac and cheese?Everybody freeze!

Class class?Ms. Glass!

Hocus pocus?Everybody focus!

Ready set?You bet!

Today’s lesson is about r-controlled vowels, a phonics concept about how the vowel sound in words like car or bird changes because of the r that follows it. Glass breaks down a few words on the smart whiteboard at the front of the classroom, but with plenty of pauses to ask for student contributions. To make things more fun, she plays a YouTube video from an education creator known as Mrs. Siravo, a parody of the Jonas Brothers song “Sucker” listing words shaped by this kind of “bossy r.”

Then it’s time for students to take turns coming to the board and diagramming their own words. “Circus,” a girl in a tie-dye fleece sweatshirt suggests, then writes it on the board as “curcus.” Glass lets the misspelling stand for the moment. The first task is to figure out the number of sounds in the word. Those who didn’t learn reading through phonics tend to assume the answer is two, but sounds are different from syllables. The actual answer is five: soft c, the growl of the r-controlled first vowel, hard c, “uh,” then s. The girl puts five dots under the word, and the whole class claps out the sounds. Now Glass returns to the spelling issue. Other r-controlled vowels can make that growling sound too, she reminds them. It must be an i, several students shout out. Their teacher grins, thrilled by their ability to sleuth out the correct answer.

She knows the test weighs on these 8- and 9-year-olds. She tries to praise them frequently, and makes corrections in a supportive way. “They have anxiety,” she says. “I let them know how much pressure it is, but I try to alleviate some of the pressure. When they make a mistake, I make sure they learn from it.” With just a couple weeks until the test, she’s feeling confident in her students: Only five of the 40 scored below a passing mark on the final benchmark exam.

LaTasha Glass in her third-grade class at Jefferson County Elementary School.

This is what the “Mississippi Miracle” looks like in the classroom. In 2013, Mississippi ranked 49th out of 50 on the federally mandated NAEP tests, confirming the conventional wisdom about how poor, Republican-dominated states have weaker education systems than wealthier, more Democratic ones. But starting in 2015—the test is given every two years—the poorest state in the country began a steady climb through the ranks of fourth-grade scores. In just two years, the state’s reading performance jumped five points, then another five points four years after that. Scores dipped during the pandemic, but by a smaller margin than in many other states. By 2024, 11 years after coming in second-to-last, Mississippi ranked ninth in the country in fourth-grade reading. The legend of the “miracle” began to take hold.

Jefferson County’s growth curve was even steeper. In 2013, the elementary school was among the worst performers in its underperforming state, earning an F rating. In 2022, just 43 percent of fourth graders passed the MAAP test. In 2025, 78 percent did, a 35-point jump in three years. Superintendent Adrian Hammitte, who’s in his seventh year as superintendent and his 16th in the district, was hoping for a 90 percent pass rate for third graders this year; preliminary data shows they landed in the mid-80s. “We want 100 percent,” he says, smiling, “but realistically, we’re shooting for 90.”

Debating the Mississippi Miracle has become the favorite sport of education observers around the country. Some scholars have argued that the story is simply too convenient, that common sense suggests the state is simply cooking the books. (Reports of cheating have undermined previous stories of miraculous test score improvements in Atlanta and Washington, DC, among other places.) Others suggest that the gains are the result of selection bias:The lowest performers in third grade are held back a year, meaning they don’t take the national fourth-grade test.

Most of these theories collapse under scrutiny. There is zero evidence that Mississippi’s improved reading scores are the result of widespread fraud. And simply preventing the worst readers from taking the fourth-grade test doesn’t explain the dramatic jumps in Jefferson County, where Hammitte says not a single third grader was held back in 2024 or 2025.

So why have elementary school reading scores jumped dramatically in places like Jefferson County, one of the poorest places in the poorest state in the country, at the same time national averages are plummeting? Hammitte believes the third-grade “reading gate” is in fact key to his district’s success—but not because it removes the weakest readers from the pool of fourth-grade test takers. Rather, he argues that third graders pass the test because their families see no choice but to pass; no one wants their child to be held back. Students who pass the third-grade state test are likely to repeat their success in fourth grade. “There’s so much pressure and so much emphasis on trying to get every child to pass the test,” he says, “not only because we know the state is going to report on it, but also because we know that if they don’t pass, they’re going to be retained.”

The reading gate is part of a broader array of accountability mechanisms, including letter grades for each district and school, that trace their origins to the No Child Left Behind era and that have been controversial among many progressive education advocates because they can punish students and schools without solving underlying structural inequalities. They can also lead to higher stress, lower morale, and more turnover among teachers. In Mississippi and many other states, the entire year’s curriculum is determined by what’s on the test. “Reading” doesn’t mean books, but exercises like the ones Glass’ class does every morning, each tailored to a specific skill measured by the MAAP exam.

Glass doesn’t design these lessons herself. As part of a move toward “high--quality instructional materials,” Mississippi strongly recommends that districts choose from a list of state-approved curricula, all tailored toward concepts on the spring exam. Those materials are based on scientific research into how children’s brains learn to read—not as an organic development, the belief that underpinned the “whole language” philosophy popular in the 1980s and ’90s, but through the building blocks of letters and sounds that make up phonics. To eliminate variability, Jefferson County classes use identical lesson plans; teachers can’t write their own material based on their students’ interests (or their own). Glass can’t just read from the script; the unplanned “curcus” conversation shows why even the best material still requires a teacher who can adapt on the fly. But as Glass walks through the concept of r-controlled vowels, the other third-grade language arts teacher down the hall is reading the exact same examples.

The reading gate and uniform teaching materials have gotten the most attention from those who believe Mississippi should be a model for the rest of the country. But sitting in on Glass’ class suggests that another part of the Literacy-Based Promotion Act may in fact be the most important key to improving reading performance.

Aside from its accountability measures, the law also provided $9.5 million in annual funding for literacy coaches and teacher training. (Today it’s up to $15 million a year.) Michelle Nowell, the associate state superintendent overseeing curriculum and instruction, runs a team of 57 coaches focusing on kindergarten through third grade, with 22 more due to be hired before the next school year. Those coaches float among districts, focusing on those that need the most improvement. “If you said, ‘Why do you think y’all been so successful in K-3?’ I would say it’s boots on the ground with our literacy coaches,” Nowell says. “We are not evaluative, we’re not punitive. We build relationships, and we’re there to help.”

Many districts, including Jefferson County, have carved out money for their own coaches. Last fall, Hammitte hired fourth-grade teacher Timothy Queen as the elementary school’s instructional coach. Queen, who’s also a cheerleading coach at nearby Alcorn State University, is a ball of energy and enthusiasm, constantly doling out hugs and fist bumps to students as his long braid bounces against his shoulders. His job is to train his colleagues, not work with students, but he can end up functioning as a second teacher during a given lesson.

With the all-important test approaching, both Queen and principal Shameka Woods are focusing much of their energy on third-grade classes. The result is that, at least during the spring, Glass is rarely leading her classroom alone. When she breaks her 20-ish students into small groups, she can check on half of them while Queen or Woods handles the rest. When a boy starts nodding off, Queen escorts him into the hallway to splash water on his face. As Glass talks through which letter combinations form which sounds, Queen jumps in to guide a brief discussion of the vowel sound in “cycle.” “What does that second letter sound like?” he asks, prompting one talkative boy to suggest “i.” “What’s the other letter” that makes an “i” sound, Queen responds. “Y!” the kids yell triumphantly.

Though they both lead English classes, Glass and Hamberlin teach profoundly different subjects. Glass’ goal is to get her students to read words and sentences, to connect “c-y-c-l-e” to an image of a bike and understand the basic series of events in a story. Hamberlin’s students have to be able to read a multi-paragraph passage, identify the main idea, find supporting details, and draw inferences.

As a result, third-grade class periods are a stream of engaging activities: diagramming sounds on the board, watching a YouTube song, calling out answers, doing call-and-response. Hamberlin’s eighth graders sit quietly and read long passages about topics ranging from how elephants use their trunks to 19th-century history. The Mississippi Miracle suggests the state may have cracked the code of how to teach basic literacy. The conundrum is that even there, success peters out when it comes to translating words into conceptual thinking.

“Sometimes students are distracted by the format of the test, and so they get the practice test and they read the paragraph and answer the questions,” says Laurie Lee, who co-leads the Adolescent Literacy Alliance, which ran a pilot training program for fourth- through eighth-grade teachers in three Mississippi school districts this school year. “But ultimately what will help is if the kids can actually read the texts and comprehend.”

Students do phoneme-grapheme mapping exercises.

Nationwide, middle-school reading scores began their decline a couple of years before elementary-school scores, creating a downward trend line that has lasted nearly 15 years. Eighth-grade performance on the National Assessment of Educational Progress is now one point shy of an all-time low. The number of eighth graders scoring “below basic” is the highest ever recorded. Among Mississippi eighth graders, the drop in reading scores began a few years after the nation as a whole, but the curve was even steeper, losing three points between 2017 and 2022 and remaining flat in 2024.

Theoretically, a class of third graders who excel on the reading standardized test would turn into a class of eighth graders who not only excel on that test but also apply those skills to the world around them, and then into a group of adults who are literate in a way that has nothing to do with tests at all. That’s not happening. A 2022 evaluation of adult literacy found that 28 percent of Americans cannot reliably compare and contrast information, paraphrase, or make basic inferences. Six years earlier, that number was 19 percent. Though the biggest drop was among adults who didn’t graduate from high school, even those with some amount of higher education got worse at reading. A 2023 National Endowment for the Arts survey, meanwhile, found that less than half of adults had read a book in the past year. Experts worry these trends stem from habits that started earlier in their lives.

In conversations with teachers and literacy experts, nearly everyone diagnoses the problem as one of attention span, not intelligence. “It’s really just about stamina,” Hamberlin says. “They have five to six passages. Some of them are informational, some of them are literature. And at a certain point they just don’t want to read anymore.” Students stop reading when they hit a word they don’t know, but they need to know how to decode unfamiliar words for the test as well as for the world. They lose focus if the subject doesn’t interest them, but they’ll encounter passages on all sorts of topics both on the test and in life.

Students’ backpacks in LaTasha Glass’ classroom.

“A lot of people don’t engage with lengthy text, and that’s a muscle like you build working out,” says Kevin Smith, Lee’s codirector. “I don’t know if a lot of our kids have built the muscle to read longer texts.”

The prime suspect is smartphones. A 2022 paper in the journal Developmental Neuropsychology synthesizing 11 studies found that 10 of them had identified a correlation between the amount of children’s screen time and their attention spans. Teens’ favorite apps seem to make the problems worse: Scrolling TikTok, which 61 percent of American teenagers do every day and one in five do “almost constantly,” means flicking away from a video the millisecond it becomes uninteresting. The more recent rise of generative AI, meanwhile, means never needing to struggle to understand a concept.

You can’t change the reading passage on a standardized test no matter how boring it is. You can’t ChatGPT your way to the answer. Hamberlin’s eighth graders aren’t using AI on their reading assignments. But they seem to treat reading passages like they’re TikTok. Sick of reading about a long-dead abolitionist? Make a wisecrack to a classmate, fiddle with your pencil, ask to go to the bathroom—anything but powering through the reading. Teachers like to talk about “productive struggle,” the idea of grappling with a concept you don’t understand rather than either giving up or asking a bot to solve it for you. Students already seemed to be losing that instinct before the rise of AI. Now there’s even less reason to do the work.

Screen time and social media don’t explain everything: The performance slide has affected some groups of students more than others, even though almost everyone has a smartphone. On some level, it doesn’t even matter how big of a problem they are, since kids aren’t going to stop using them. The thornier question for teachers and education officials is what can be done to improve reading scores in the world in which we live.

Conservative education reformers argue that America’s education system has strayed too far from No Child Left Behind, that focusing on equity and moving away from high-stakes testing as part of efforts not to punish students for being racial minorities or low-income—both of which are correlated with lower reading performance—means districts are no longer maintaining high standards. Mississippi is as committed as ever to high-stakes testing, but the stakes are higher in third grade than in eighth. Under this theory, one solution would be a requirement that students pass the standardized test at the end of every grade before moving to the next.

The research, though, is mixed at best about whether attaching harsher consequences to standardized tests actually results in better performance. And the decline in American reading goes deeper than the ability to pass a standardized test. Just 16 percent of Americans read for fun, according to a 2023 study, down from 28 percent in 2004. Only 41 percent of children under 4 are frequently read to, down 23 points since 2012. “I think there’s an important distinction between whether students are able to read and whether they’re willing to read,” says Jonathan Becker, a scholar of education policy at Virginia Commonwealth University. “If we want our students to be able to answer questions about a short reading passage, we’re going to have them read lots of short reading passages. There’s no real incentive on the tests or in a lot of the standards to have kids read whole books.”

As glass, woods, and Queen make the final push toward getting 90 percent of Jefferson County’s third graders to pass MAAP, Candace Hamberlin is hoping to beat last year’s eighth-grade pass rate of 50.7 percent. She won’t know whether they’ve done it until late August, after the next school year has already begun.

Mississippi’s definition of “passing” is counterintuitive. A student who passes MAAP is “approaching or at the level of difficulty, complexity, or fluency specified by the grade-level content standards.” In other words, they might not actually be on grade level. Students who show “solid academic performance and mastery” of skills at their grade level are scored “proficient.” Fifty-nine percent of Jefferson County third graders were proficient in reading last year, compared to just 24 percent of eighth graders. Even in Mississippi, the home of the most discussed miracle in contemporary education, teenagers are falling behind.

In April, the Mississippi legislature approved pay raises for all teachers, plus an extra $9 million to hire literacy coaches specifically focused on fourth through eighth grades. The hope is that expanding the Florida literacy scholars’ pilot program will give teachers across the state better tools for teaching reading, and add another adult in the classroom at least some of the time.

Students do semantic gradient exercises.

A hallway at the school is lined with posters about testing.

Literacy scholars agree that teaching reading across subjects is key. The ideal method of teaching students to read—rather than just passing reading tests—they say, is assigning them texts on subjects they’re interested in, whether that’s astronomy or the NFL. “I struggle to read things that are not interesting to me,” Becker says. “I do wonder how often we’re giving kids the option to read things that are interesting to them, so that maybe they can develop more stamina.”

Hamberlin’s eighth-grade students read what’s assigned by their state-approved instructional materials; whether they’re interested is beside the point. They don’t even read books for class; there’s no time if they’re going to get through the whole MAAP curriculum. America’s fervor for standardized tests is fundamental to its education policy. If schools like this one can extend the Mississippi Miracle to middle school, if America is going to pull itself out of this standardized test score slump, it will happen through skill drills, not students losing themselves in novels. “Human flourishing is not as easily measurable as student achievement,” Becker says. “It’s harder for people to commit to things that aren’t measurable, that aren’t tangible, that we can’t really document.”

This year, for the first time in her career, Hamberlin can’t think of a single student across her five periods who reads for fun, who considers her class anything beyond an ordeal to be survived. Even her strongest readers don’t particularly like doing it. “Usually in the classroom, somebody always has a book,” she says.

“I don’t have any of them that has a book.” Adding a reading gate at the end of eighth grade might make more of them pass the test, she thinks, but it certainly wouldn’t make any of them read books.

As Hamberlin works out her thoughts aloud, she notices a boy with close-cropped hair in a black Nike zip-up hoodie and black Air Jordans listening in. He’s supposed to be reading the assigned passage, but he’s gotten distracted a third of the way through. “You want to add anything about reading class and what kinds of things we do?” Hamberlin asks him.

The boy shrugs his skinny shoulders. “It’s really boring,” he says, then turns back to Sojourner Truth.

The Army Is Burning Through Its AI Tokens

Wired July 21, 2026

A little over a month after the Department of Defense (DOD) bragged that nearly half of its 3.5 million employees were using AI at work, members of the Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) received an email informing them that they were burning through tokens, and needed to limit use.

“Although the Army CIO announced in May 2026 that they were offering unlimited tokens, by mid-June the Army CIO pool was exhausted of tokens and had to re-establish limits,” the email reads. The email goes on to say that although the Army has chosen to renew token usage at “its current levels,” it’s unclear “if the Army CIO pool will be renewed after 1 Oct.”

The Army uses Ask Sage, a multimodal generative AI platform where users can run different large language models (LLMs), including Alphabet’s Gemini, Meta’s Llama, and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. “Apparently the whole Army burned through the whole year of tokens for just one service,” says an Army employee who spoke to WIRED anonymously because they were not authorized to speak to the press.

Ask Sage is used by the Army to “power its enterprise LLM workspace” and is “accredited for Controlled Unclassified Information.” It is also used by the DOD’s Chief Digital and AI Office (CDAO) for acquisitions. According to the Army’s website, Ask Sage was used to complete tasks like “reclassifying personnel descriptions, which involves defining and aligning job duties, experience and backgrounds.”

The Army employee says that the Army has been pushing its workers to lean into using generative AI. Employees were given an allotment of at least 200,000 tokens per month, according to emails viewed by WIRED, and were automatically allocated more if they burned through their initial allotment. Employees who had signed up for Ask Sage but were not regularly using it would receive emails encouraging them to use more of their allocated tokens.

In order to use Ask Sage, the Army had access to 100,000,000 tokens as part of an annual subscription to an “enterprise pack.” Tokens represent a unit of output, either in text or image, from an LLM. For the Ask Sage tool, a single token equates to about 3.7 characters, according to documents viewed by WIRED. The Defense Department burned through some 20 billion tokens per day during the 38-day Operation Epic Fury in Iran, according to Breaking Defense.

DOD didn’t reply to requests for comment; neither did Ask Sage. The Army responded to WIRED's request following the article's publication, citing the “robust and enthusiastic adoption” of generative AI tools. “Leadership actively manages centralized enterprise token pools,” says Colonel Marty Meiners. “The transition from initial testing to widespread operational use proves the success and demand for these tools.”

It’s unclear if the tokens used by regular DOD employees are drawn from the same pool as those who might be using AI tools on classified or secret information. This hasn’t stopped the Defense Department’s emphasis on AI. On Monday, the Intercept reported that the Pentagon has continued to lean into AI tools, and has cut the staff at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, whose jobs entailed preventing civilian casualties in conflict zones. Instead, the DOD is developing an AI tool to speed up the assessments that the Center’s staff would normally make.

The Army is not the first eager adopter of generative AI to rethink their near unlimited use. After encouraging employees to “tokenmaxx,” Meta quietly took down its leaderboard tracking token usage and is now trying to curb use. Last week, Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram at Meta, floated the idea of capping token use per engineer at the company. According to reporting from Fortune, Uber also saw its engineers burning through a year’s worth of generative AI tokens in merely four months.

The Army employee says they have not found the generative AI tools to be particularly useful for their work, and that when they have used the tools, they have found them to be unreliable. One model even asserted that it had completed a task that it hadn’t, they say. “I think there are definitely several aspects of the bureaucracy of the US federal government that these tools might be helpful with. But an unthinking application and use is not going to result in an effective, efficient, and trustworthy rollout.”

Etsy Is In Its Flop Era, and Sellers Are Fleeing

Wired July 21, 2026

In 2017, Emily Olson, a stay-at-home mom based in Boulder, Colorado, started selling prints and custom-made puppy portraits on Etsy.

Her watercolors were simple and relatively cheap—images of saucer-eyed corgis and malamutes in mini-tuxes, which she sold for $75 to $300 each—but dog owners adored them: “They were a labor of love,” she says. In 2021, she says she made more than $40,000 off her Etsy store, and her YouTube following ballooned to 180,000 subscribers.

But in 2022, she noticed something odd: Her sales started precipitously declining. Competitors flooded the platform, and she kept finding copies of her work on drop-shipping sites like Alibaba, where they were advertised as original creations. Then there were the AI-generated pet portraits, which were supplanting her listings in search results and selling for a fraction of the price.

The most frustrating part, she says, was that the AI-generated portraits were getting great reviews. “People were like, ‘Oh, this is the cutest image, I love it in my daughter’s bedroom.’ They didn’t really know or care who made it, they were just eating it up,” Olson says. In 2022, she says, her sales decreased by 30 percent, followed by 50 percent the following year.

In 2024, Etsy officially announced that it would continue to allow AI-generated art on its platform, provided sellers disclosed it as such. Frustrated with the policy and with her declining sales, Olson posted a video on her YouTube channel in January 2025 titled: “Etsy Was Great … Until It Wasn’t—Why I’m Walking Away.” “Etsy doesn’t align with my values these days,” she says in the video. “It feels like they’ve just become another giant corporation chasing profits above all else.”

Once a quirky bastion of amateur vulva jewelry and twee crocheted dolls, longtime Etsy sellers like Olson are now migrating from the platform in large numbers due to their frustration with policies they feel are lax. Competitors are emerging. Fybe, for instance, a new online crafts marketplace, will open to vendors August 1. It explicitly prohibits AI-generated content and drop-shipping on the platform, and will rely on volunteer moderators and direct conversations with sellers to ensure all products are human-made.

Both buyers and sellers on Etsy “are a little discontented,” says Rachel Powell, the founder of Fybe. “I figured if we could start a platform that has human moderation and only allows vendors that aren’t using AI or using drop-shipping, then we could be filling a very real need in the community.”

On the subreddit r/EtsyCommunity, there are dozens of threads from angry sellers griping about declining sales and the influx of what one user referred to as “AI-generated slop” that isn’t labeled as such. “Every maker I've talked to is basically screaming into the void about it, and Etsy doesn't seem to care,” one post concludes.

It isn’t just mass-produced mugs or T-shirts. Buyers have been inundated by AI-generated product listings for crocheting patterns, hermit crab pools, even medieval suits of armor. Longtime vendors say the hand-crafted aesthetics once prized by the platform are disappearing, thanks to a burgeoning market of online entrepreneurs promoting Etsy as a place for AI-driven side hustles.

“The whole AI side of things has really, really hampered Etsy for sellers, big time,” says Chloe Rose, an artist and content creator who for years sold stickers and original watercolors on the platform.

Viktor, a UK-based illustrator who has been on Etsy for 10 years, says his sales have decreased by 98 percent over the last year alone, thanks to people using the platform as “an easy way to make a quick buck.” “People have learned not to trust once-trusted sites like Etsy, because they are tired of seeing AI slop that is now infecting the site,” says Viktor, who goes by his first name online for privacy reasons. “Unfortunately, this has turned potential customers away from actual artists.”

Starting in 2021, the company's gross merchandise sales declined for a period of several years (though it did recently post back to back quarters of growth), which analysts have attributed to increased competition from sites like Temu and Shein. In late 2023, Etsy laid off 11 percent of its workforce. In recent years, however, the platform has largely maintained it loyal user base: Etsy has approximately 5.6 million sellers, according to a 2025 transparency report; and it generated $2.8 billion in revenue last year, a 2.7 percent increase from 2024.

As part of Etsy’s 2024 announcement allowing sellers to use works made with AI, the platform prohibited users from selling their own customized AI prompts and banned sellers from using AI to deceive buyers with their product listings; it also noted that sellers must disclose if they used AI in product listings.

But this mandate is not strictly enforced, and Etsy is largely unresponsive to complaints about AI content regulation, according to Etsy sellers who spoke with WIRED for this story. Olson says that the platform even flagged her own products as copies of other vendors’ works, despite her artworks being wholly original. Her efforts to reach a customer service representative were unsuccessful. “They are not easy to work with, at all,” she says.

In response to a list of questions, James Ossman, vice president of customer operations at Etsy, told WIRED the company knows “how deeply our sellers care about protecting human creativity.”

“Etsy is the marketplace for goods made, designed, handpicked, or sourced by real people,” Ossman said. “That includes original works created by sellers who may use AI as one of many tools in their creative process.” Ossman added that enforcing the company’s standards regarding transparency and AI is “complex, and we know we have a lot more work to do.” He said the company is “continuing to improve our ability to detect and remove listings that don't belong on Etsy.”

Olson has pivoted to Shopify, though she says sales there have been disappointing as well. “It is definitely harder to sell on your own website than on communities like Etsy,” she says.

But given the rising popularity of AI slop across platforms, there are also larger, more uncomfortable questions artists like her have to wrestle with, about whether there is even a future for handmade or crafted products in general. Sure, a hand-painted watercolor of a beloved shih tzu will have a different, more rough-hewn quality than a slick AI-generated portrait—but do consumers even care about the difference, particularly when the latter is so much cheaper and more accessible than the former?

“Face it, art is a luxury, and with all this economic uncertainty right now, it tends to be one of the last things people want to spend money on,” she says. “So I have empathy for people who don’t buy hand-painted works of art, but I also think we will always want to seek out things of beauty that are made by real people.”

How to Disable Music Videos in Spotify

Wired July 19, 2026

Spotify, it’s fair to say, has made some weird user-experience choices.

There are a number of panels in the app, and the layout is confusing. The service constantly tracks your activity. The app also seems to have an odd hostility to playing actual albums. This all works to create a general feeling that Spotify’s designers are trying to push you into using the service in a particular way.

It’s understandable, then, that some people are annoyed with the way music videos have been added to the platform. For the most part, they would start to play by default, in the background, whenever an artist had uploaded a video for the song. Some music videos have very different audio from the original tracks, particularly if they include sketches or sound effects, which can prove distracting if you prefer the album version of the song. And even if you enjoy music videos (which I do), the decision to have videos play by default—using up bandwidth and battery power—upset a lot of people.

There are a few other quirks. On Spotify’s desktop app, the videos are barely visible; they stay contained in the tiny album art panel until you manage to find the hidden, extremely small Now playing button that enlarges them. Also, the selection of videos that are on the platform, and the ones that are mysteriously absent, seems totally random. Because of this, I check YouTube first when I really want to watch a music video.

The most annoying thing, though, had been a lack of any obvious way to disable all videos. That changed recently—there’s now a toggle in the settings to disable music videos in Spotify entirely, alongside controls that disable the Canvas feature (animated album art) and video podcasts.

On mobile you can do this by tapping your user profile icon in the top-left to bring up the side panel. Then tap Settings and privacy, followed by Content and display.

In the Videos and Canvas section you will see three toggles: one for music videos, one for Canvas, and one for all other videos. This last toggle disables video podcasts, meaning you’ll get the audio-only version of podcasts instead. Turn all these off, and Spotify will use a lot less bandwidth.

On the desktop app, it’s a little different. Click your user profile icon in the top-right corner, then click Settings. Scroll down to the Videos and Canvas section to find the options to disable music videos and Canvas.

I tested this and it worked. The music video icon in playlists and albums disappeared, as did the collection of music videos on Artist pages. The only remnant of the disabled feature is a Switch to video button in the Now Playing sidebar, which appears below the album art. Click it and you’ll be told the video can’t play unless you turn videos back on in the settings. Odd, for sure, but for the most part turning this off means you don’t have to think about music videos in Spotify anymore.

I sincerely wish that Spotify would roll out music videos with more care. Sometimes I really do want to see a video—just not every time I play a track. Playlists of music videos might be welcome if they ran separately from the audio-only playlists. I just don’t want to get a music video when I’m looking for the album version of a song, and I don’t think I’m alone in that. I can only hope that Spotify’s future interface design choices will keep things more clearly separated.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method (Qi wireless charging is less efficient). You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (Programmable Power Supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours (WH). If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have onboard.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, however, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

The chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:

Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely source of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when it overheats. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

How We Test Power Banks

I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (currently an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

There are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.
